#6412. Deep-Sea Scientists Capture Extraordinary 4K Footage of a Fish With a See-Through Head

MBARI’s first 4K footage of a barreleye fish offers a rare chance to study how its unusual eyes work in the ocean’s dim twilight zone.

The day’s deep-sea research was over when a fish with a transparent head came into view. Research Specialist Shannon Johnson spotted it as MBARI’s pilots were “flying” the remotely operated vehicle (ROV) Doc Ricketts back to the surface for recovery, and she called for them to stop.

The animal was a barreleye fish (Macropinna microstoma), approximately 600 meters (1,970 feet) underwater and 90 kilometers (55 miles) offshore. For the MBARI scientists working aboard the research vessel David Packard, this was only the organization’s eleventh encounter with the species.

Senior Scientist Steven Haddock and researchers from MBARI’s Biodiversity and Biooptics Team were on the eight-day Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition, studying gelatinous animals such as jellies, siphonophores, and ctenophores, also known as comb jellies. They combined scuba diving in open water near the surface with ROV surveys hundreds of meters below, filming and collecting animals to better understand how they have adapted to life in the deep water column.

Most of the scientists had already moved to the ship’s wet lab to prepare to catalog the specimens arriving with the ROV. When news of the barreleye reached them, they ran back to the control room. The encounter was an unexpected finish to a long, productive week of research.

“Seeing a barreleye fish is a rare treat. Crew from across the ship joined the science team in the control room, mesmerized by this remarkable animal. Deep-sea animals capture the imagination, creating wonder and awe that we hope will inspire stewardship of the largest living space on Earth,” said Haddock.

The team spent approximately 20 minutes observing the fish with Doc Ricketts’ high-resolution 4K camera, examining its body and behavior and experimenting with different lighting conditions to show its transparent head shield. This was MBARI’s first barreleye sighting filmed in 4K and its first from the new flagship research vessel.

ROV Pilot/Technician Cameron Law also maneuvered Doc Ricketts close enough to record the fish with the vehicle’s virtual reality (VR) camera. The resulting 3D stereo imagery could contribute to future education and outreach efforts.

MBARI has completed roughly 7,000 ROV dives and recorded more than 41,000 hours of deep-sea video during nearly 40 years of ocean exploration. Its previous sighting of Macropinna was in 2021. This summer, MBARI researchers leading an expedition with Schmidt Ocean Institute in the mid-Atlantic Ocean recorded another species of barreleye, the binocular fish (Winteria telescopa).

Earlier MBARI observations by Senior Scientist Bruce Robison and Research Specialist Kim Reisenbichler helped reveal how Macropinna uses its unusual eyes to feed. In the ocean’s dim twilight zone, the fish’s large fins keep it stable and allow it to maneuver as it hovers, looking upward for the silhouettes of prey. Once it spots food, its large, tubular eyes rotate beneath the transparent dome to keep the target in view. The gelatinous shield also protects those eyes when the fish plucks small crustaceans caught in the stinging tentacles of deep-sea siphonophores.

The researchers did not collect the barreleye, but their footage will support continued research on this elusive species. The Biodiversity and Biooptics Team studies how marine animals interact with light and has extensively investigated deep-sea visual systems. Its close-up examination of Macropinna’s eyes will help researchers better understand vision in the twilight zone.

Pigments in the lenses of the fish’s eyes are thought to serve a similar function to the green pigments in the eyes of the strawberry squid (Histioteuthis heteropsis), a deep-sea neighbor the team has previously studied.

“Macropinna reminds us of the surprising ways that animals have adapted to thrive in the ocean’s midwater,” said Haddock. “So many of them survive by looking for subtle optical cues, like a shadow passing overhead, and this sets off evolutionary competition, pitting bioluminescent camouflage against increasingly sophisticated visual capabilities.”

The reentry of NASA's dead Swift space telescope is the end of an era for rapid-response space science.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's the end of an era: NASA's Swift telescope has reached the conclusion of its nearly 22-year mission, burning up in Earth's atmosphere after studying some of the universe's most powerful and mysterious events.

According to NASA, the spacecraft reentered the atmosphere at "7:39 a.m. EST Wednesday over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia, at approximately 3.4 degrees north latitude and 98.6 degrees east longitude." NASA expected most of the telescope's structure to burn up during its passage through Earth's atmosphere, estimating a 1-in-2,100 chance of any surviving debris falling over a populated area. No damage or injuries have been reported.

Weighing approximately 3,200 pounds (1,450 kilograms), the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory was initially designed for a two-year mission, but it far exceeded expectations. Over two decades, Swift became an important tool in the study of gamma-ray bursts, supernovas, black holes and other cosmic phenomena.

Launched in November 2004, Swift was designed to detect gamma-ray bursts, powerful explosions that occur throughout the universe. Its three onboard telescopes let scientists observe cosmic events across different wavelengths, including ultraviolet, optical and X-ray light. The telescope could swivel to focus on different sky targets in a matter of minutes, allowing it to rapidly follow up on sudden events like supernova explosions.

NASA estimates that Swift's scientific observations have contributed to approximately 7,000 research papers, leaving behind an extensive collection that scientists can continue studying for years.

Swift's return was driven by atmospheric drag, which eventually slowed the spacecraft and caused its orbit to decay. Increased solar activity intensified the drag, thus accelerating the space telescope's descent toward Earth.

Earlier this year, NASA explored an ambitious rescue mission to extend Swift's operational life. In August 2026, a privately developed robotic spacecraft built by Katalyst Space Technologies was intended to rendezvous with Swift and boost it into a higher orbit. However, the mission failed after launching, leaving the observatory on its path toward reentry.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

NASA officially ended Swift's scientific operations on Oct. 20 after its declining altitude made observations too difficult. For NASA and the broader astronomy community, Swift's story is a reminder that even missions designed to last just a few years can fundamentally change our understanding of our universe.

#6409. Scientists Engineer Rice That Fights Back Against a Devastating Crop Disease

An artificial intelligence-designed gene-editing tool has helped scientists develop rice plants resistant to bacterial blight, a destructive disease that threatens harvests across Asia and Africa. Researchers at the University of Missouri achieved the result using a technology previously tested in animal cells, opening a potential new route to protecting one of the world’s most important food crops.

The breakthrough centers on OpenCRISPR-1, a gene-editing system developed by California biotechnology company Profluent. Led by Bing Yang, a Curators’ Distinguished Professor in the College of Agriculture, Food and Natural Resources, the Missouri team adapted the technology for use in rice.

Gene editing allows scientists to make targeted changes to DNA, including modifications to genes that influence a plant’s vulnerability to disease. By studying how bacterial pathogens interact with rice at the genetic level, researchers can identify opportunities to strengthen the crop’s defenses.

OpenCRISPR-1 also offers an advantage over some existing gene-editing systems: it is freely available for research and commercial crop development.

“Unlike proprietary gene-editing tools that may require licensing agreements for commercial use, OpenCRISPR-1 is open source and free for research and commercialization of crop genome editing,” Yang said. “That accessibility gives researchers and companies greater flexibility to explore new genetic solutions and develop crop varieties with valuable agricultural traits.”

Bacterial blight can severely reduce both the quantity and quality of rice harvests. In regions where rice farming supports millions of livelihoods, outbreaks can have serious economic consequences and threaten a vital food supply.

“Bacterial blight can wreak havoc on rice crops, reducing both yield and quality, which creates serious challenges for farmers who depend on the staple grain,” Yang said. “Our lab investigates how bacterial blight interacts with rice at the genetic level — knowledge that helps us identify ways to strengthen the plant’s natural defenses.”

Although the researchers have successfully developed resistant plants, the work remains at the laboratory stage. The next challenge is transferring the findings into commercially grown rice varieties, followed by additional testing, regulatory review, and partnerships with companies capable of bringing the crops to market.

Farmers may have to wait several years before rice varieties developed through this research become available. Meanwhile, Yang’s team sees potential applications beyond bacterial blight, including improving resistance to other diseases and helping crops withstand environmental stresses.

Corn and soybeans are among the crops that could eventually benefit from similar genetic approaches, although such applications would require further research.

“Our recent breakthrough paves the way to explore genetic solutions to a range of challenges that farmers face across Missouri and nationwide, from devastating plant diseases to drought and extreme temperatures,” Yang, an investigator in the Bond Life Sciences Center, said. “By developing crops that are better equipped to withstand these stresses, we can help farmers protect yields, strengthen agricultural resilience and prepare for an increasingly challenging growing environment.”

Reference: “AI-designed OpenCRISPR-1 enables efficient targeted mutagenesis and prime editing in rice” by Ajay Gupta, Rabia Ahuja, Bo Liu, Mark Adero, Dung Thi Pham, Wolf B. Frommer and Bing Yang, 20 May 2026, aBIOTECH. DOI: 10.1016/j.abiote.2026.100054

#6408. Melting permafrost has birthed a new type of large landslide

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Wildfires and water underneath the ground could dislodge large chunks of frozen earth

In 2018, an immense landslide in Canada’s Mackenzie Valley dammed the Redstone River (shown) and created a 3.5-kilometer-long lake. Researchers say the event was a new type of large landslide called a permafrost detachment slide.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In 2018, a strange and enormous landslide occurred in Canada’s Northwest Territories. A slab of earth roughly equivalent in volume to seven Great Pyramids of Giza suddenly began sliding downhill, leaving behind a barren scar in the forested landscape. But what puzzled scientists was that the slide had initiated in frozen ground that had been glued in place for years.

An analysis of the event reveals that it represents a new class of catastrophic landslides called permafrost detachment slides, researchers report in the Sept. 28 Geophysical Research Letters. The slides may be set in motion by wildfires that occurred decades earlier, destabilizing the ground and opening cracks through which water infiltrated deep underground. Over time, that water may have thawed the frozen layer from below, eventually unleashing the entire frozen layer in a catastrophic slide.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Large landslides don’t normally mobilize so much still-frozen material, and when they do begin in thawing layers they usually move slowly, says Dmitry Nicolsky, a geophysicist studying permafrost at the University of Alaska Fairbanks who was not involved in the study. But he says this new research suggests scientists need to better study what’s occurring beneath the surface in permafrost regions, because “we don’t know how [the ground] will move — it might go slowly or it might go catastrophically.”

The inspiration for the research manifested in 2019, when permafrost geologist Joseph Young, based at the University of Alberta in Edmonton, Canada, at the time, was helicoptering to a field site in the Northwest Territories to assist a colleague’s research. In some of the valleys out there, the slopes were “just collapsing with landslides everywhere,” says Young, who is now at an engineering firm in Edmonton. That was surprising because they were in an area where the permafrost — ground that has been frozen for at least two consecutive years — shouldn’t have been thawing much.

Once on the ground, more puzzling details emerged. “Traditionally with permafrost, it melts from the top down, and that releases this slurry of muddy material,” Young says. But at some of the landslide sites, large blocks of still-frozen ground seemed to have been moved hundreds of meters, he says.

Young and his colleagues studied two of the largest slides in the region that had moved big chunks of permafrost. These were the 2018 slide, which mobilized 18 million cubic meters of earth and dammed the Redstone River, and another event in 2017 that moved 4.5 million cubic meters of material.

Field observations revealed that both events had initiated along flat sliding surfaces roughly 20 meters underground, where the permafrost layer’s base was identified. Meanwhile, satellite observations showed that the ground at both sites had been gradually moving meters each year for decades.

Young and his colleagues hypothesized that climate warming and wildfire had somehow played a role in causing the slides. They set up instruments nearby that tracked ground temperature from 2020 to 2022, focusing on spots either with undisturbed forest or where wildfire had burned about 25 years earlier.

They then plugged that data into computer simulations to estimate how the ground would have evolved in the decades after a fire. Based on the results, the researchers concluded that wildfire and extreme summer temperatures can warm and weaken the frozen ground surface, causing it to start creeping and form tension cracks. As these cracks grow, water can penetrate deeper into the frozen ground and eventually reach beneath the permafrost layer, causing it to thaw from below and eventually detach.

More than 150 other slides in the region, identified via satellite observations, may also have been permafrost detachment slides, Young says. This could occur wherever there’s a relatively thin and warm permafrost layer and a rapid warming event to set things in motion, he says.

Permafrost is thawing in cold regions around the world, and these huge slides are very visual manifestations of that, Young says. “This is a direct reality of a changing climate.”

J.M. Young et al. Recent intensification (2004 – 2020) of permafrost mass‐wasting in the central Mackenzie Valley foothills is a legacy of past forest fire disturbances. Geophysical Research Letters. 2022. doi: 10.1029/2022GL100559

#6407. The 9 Best Dishwashers of 2026

Our top recommendations from Bosch, Whirlpool, Midea, and more can knock out dishes with minimal disruption.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you’re tired of scrubbing pots and pans by hand, a good dishwasher is one of the best investments you can make for your home. The latest dishwasher models are smarter, quieter, and more efficient than previous generations, with soil-sensing cycles that adapt to your load, adjustable racks to accommodate dishes of all sizes, and quiet motors that won’t disrupt movie night. It’s the same kind of quality-of-life upgrade you get from buying a washing machine. Once you have one, it’s hard to imagine life without it.

Whether you’re replacing an aging unit or adding one to your home, the best dishwashers can make your kitchen routine easier. They may even help you save money on your water bill, too. To help narrow down your options, we focused on aspects like reliability, cleaning performance, and drying power, so your dishes come out spotless and ready to put away.

Adding a dishwasher to your home is an important decision, especially since it’s something you’ll be using a few times per week. To find the best models, we researched the top-rated machines from trusted brands like Bosch, Whirlpool, and GE, analyzing customer feedback and consulting expert reviews. We also relied on previous Popular Mechanics testing and extensive research to weigh the features that matter most in daily use.

Specifically, we prioritized quiet operation (favoring models under 50 decibels that won’t interrupt a conversation), adjustable racks and foldable tines, and proven cleaning performance. We then cross-referenced these insights with long-term reliability reports to ensure every pick on this list is built to last.

For our most recent update, we revisited the current dishwasher landscape to ensure every recommendation still holds up. We added new picks that offer a strong value, smart features, and a great fit for specific needs, like compact kitchens and busy households. We also re-evaluated our existing selections to confirm they remain competitive on price, performance, and availability.

The Bosch 300 Series checks all the right boxes as a top dishwasher. This front-control model cleans thoroughly with seven cycles, and it uses sensors and targeted spray arms to track soil and adjust as it runs. It’s quiet at 46 decibels, so you can run a cycle anytime without it interrupting your dinner conversation.

Storage is flexible, too. You get a standard third rack for utensils and other small items, plus a middle rack that adjusts to nine positions to make room for pots below and stemware above. Fold-down tines on the upper and lower racks accommodate lids and other cookware, and all three racks move smoothly. It also uses a condensation system for drying and leak protection that can automatically stop water intake if it detects a possible leak.

Other features include the ability to control and monitor cycles from your phone and hands-free voice control when paired with Amazon Alexa or Google Home. We only wish it had an auto-open door drying feature to top it all off, but this isn’t a major con by any means.

For around $500, the Frigidaire top control dishwasher is a dependable, modern dishwasher that offers Energy Star efficiency, a quick wash cycle, and a DishSense feature that helps adjust the wash based on how dirty the dishes are.

Meanwhile, Frigidaire’s Maxdry feature cranks up the heat for noticeably better drying than most entry-level models, so you’re not hand-drying half the load afterward. The fingerprint-resistant stainless steel finish also does a nice job of hiding smudges, helping it look cleaner for longer. It has a child lock, delay start, and a removable silverware basket, rounding out a feature set that feels surprisingly robust for a budget pick.

At 52 decibels, it won’t compete with high-end models that offer quieter performance, but it’s perfectly acceptable at this price point.

This dishwasher has nearly everything you want: a third rack, an adjustable second rack, and a handful of cycle options to thoroughly clean your dishes, including a quick wash and a high-temperature wash that helps remove grease. It also offers enhanced, fan-powered drying technology that ensures your cookware doesn’t come out damp. At 51 decibels, it’s not the loudest, but not the quietest either.

Other notable features include a presoak cycle to clean off stubborn food and folding tines to fit larger items like mixing bowls and large pots. Unfortunately, there is no WiFi support or app compatibility, limiting the dishwasher’s convenience compared to other models.

Dishwashers are more flexible than ever with multiple racks and ample space for efficient organization. This Midea top-control model stands out with a third rack and spray arms for each level, making it easy to customize the interior to get thorough cleaning.

You can raise or lower the middle rack by up to 2 inches to make room for big pots, baking sheets, or tall plates below, so you don’t have to go through the effort of hand-washing cumbersome dishes. The Midea also features a dedicated third rack for utensils and flat cooking tools, along with jets that spray directly into reusable water bottles.

Beyond organization, a three-stage drying system combines heated dry, auto-open door, and air circulation, so you’re not toweling dishes off after the cycle finishes. And with a 47 decibel sound rating, it runs quietly enough that it won’t disrupt conversations. The only thing we noticed was that some reviewers had complaints about the latch on the door rusting, and the racks breaking. That said, it may be less reliable in the long-term compared to higher-end models.

If you actually want the “smart” part of a smart dishwasher to pull its weight, this LG model is an easy standout. We like that WiFi and LG’s ThinQ app let you fire up or pause a cycle from the couch, check how much time is left, and get pinged when it’s done, while Alexa and Google Assistant support hands-free control. The app keeps an eye on water supply, drainage, and leaks, and sends alerts if something looks off. It also nudges you when it’s time for routine maintenance.

The smart features extend to how it runs, too. A sensor wash cycle automatically adjusts time and water based on how dirty your dishes actually are. LG’s one-hour wash and dry program also uses four multi-directional spray arms for deeper cleaning and then circulates heated air throughout the tub for faster drying.

An auto-vent feature pops the door open slightly at the end of a cycle to vent steam, and a status light projects onto the floor so you’re able to see when it’s done at a glance. These features combine to make cleaning your dishes a little smarter and less painful.

While the upper rack gets fold-down tines for odd-shaped glassware and bowls, the lower rack doesn’t, so it’s a bit trickier to load large pans and bakeware than on models with fully flexible lower racks. However, if you normally hand wash large pots and pans, this may not be an issue.

The Whirlpool Eco Series 24-Inch Top Control Dishwasher is a great pick for families that go through dishes like a small restaurant. It’s built to keep up with real-life cleanup, using a three-rack layout so you can load more dishes in one go. Below, the lower rack has fold-down tines for bulky cookware, making it easier to run a full day’s worth of dishes.

The Sensor cycle uses AI technology to monitor soil level, load size, and water temperature, then adjusts as it goes. There are also cycles that add soak time and longer wash phases to help reduce the need for pre-scrubbing. A sanitizer rinse option targets food-borne bacteria, while a high temperature wash helps cut through grease. Meanwhile, the combination of heated and condensation drying features mean you’ll have dishes that are ready to put away when the cycle finishes.

There is no app control or remote monitoring features, but this dishwasher does offer a fingerprint-resistant stainless exterior and a relatively quiet sound rating of 47 decibels. That means you’ll be able to throw it on without ruining family movie night.

The GE Profile 18-Inch Top Control Built-in Dishwasher is great for smaller apartments where cabinet space is tight. It offers full-height racks, an adjustable upper rack, and room for everyday dishes, glasses, and cookware. With a three-level wash system, you don’t have to pre-wash anything in the sink. It even features a cycle that automatically adjusts time and water based on how much dirt it detects on your dishes.

The GE also features a stainless steel tub, an ADA-compliant low-profile design, and a sound rating of 47 decibels, so you can run it while you’re watching TV without having to raise the volume. There is no third rack, but it does have fold-down tines and a removable silverware basket, providing you with more flexibility when loading dishes. As someone who dealt with a basic 18-inch dishwasher at a previous apartment, the GE is a big upgrade.

The Midea 18-Inch Built-in Dishwasher is a great budget pick if you want a true built-in dishwasher in a small space without spending a premium price. At 18 inches wide with room for 8 place settings, it tucks into narrow apartment kitchens, bar nooks, or RV islands while still handling daily dishes for a small household.

You get six wash settings, including Heavy, ECO, and Quick, plus heated dry and a sanitize option. The stainless-steel tub feels more durable and premium than its price suggests, and users call out how quiet it is while running. The main trade-offs are a somewhat fussy lower rack for full-size plates and long normal-cycle times; however, if you’re prioritizing price, small-footprint installation, and solid cleaning over bells and whistles, this Midea is an excellent and affordable option.

Sometimes you don’t feel like washing a small amount of dishes by hand, but running a full cycle on a dishwasher feels like a waste of energy and water. This double-drawer model from GE is here to try to solve that problem.

You can run the two drawers separately or together, whether you need a quick rinse for a few plates and glasses, or a deeper clean for multiple place settings. This is especially convenient because you can continue loading dirty dishes while the other drawer runs through a cycle.

The dishwasher has six wash cycles, plus sanitizing and extra dry options. There are four adjustable shelves per drawer to accommodate plenty of dish and glass sizes. The detergent compartment is a little harder to fit pods, so you may be better off with a liquid or powder cleaner.

Some dishwashers might have to be hardwired to a dedicated circuit rather than using a plug-and-play connection. Hardwired dishwashers are more secure and permanent, while units with power cords are easier to install and offer more convenient disconnection in case of repairs. Both styles require access to a 120-volt, grounded outlet. Check the specs of the dishwasher you’re considering to ensure it aligns with your desired connection type.

Most households will be fine with a standard built-in dishwasher that slides under the counter and hooks into existing plumbing. However, portable and countertop models have come a long way and are now legitimate options for renters and small kitchens. Options like the GE Portable Freestanding Dishwasher, roll to the sink when needed and store away when you’re done.

Meanwhile, countertop dishwashers live on a counter or sturdy cart, and are ideal for smaller spaces like studios, where a full-size unit may not fit. Just know that compact models often compromise on features like noise reduction and capacity due to their smaller size.

For most households, dishwashers generally come in two widths: the standard 24-inch and the compact 18-inch. A 24-inch model is usually the best choice for families, having enough room for bulky cookware and larger loads. In contrast, an 18-inch model is a space-saving solution for small kitchens or narrow cabinet cutouts. I used an 18-inch machine in a previous apartment and found it filled up fast, forcing us to run cycles more frequently.

Manufacturers like to quote capacity in “place settings,” but what really matters day to day is interior flexibility and vertical space. Look for a tall tub design, which maximizes interior height so you can fit oversized items like baking sheets and pots on the bottom rack. A model with a third rack and an adjustable second rack, like the Whirlpool Eco Series Top Control Dishwasher, will give you enough flexibility to wash an entire day’s worth of cookware in a single load.

One of the biggest differentiators between modern dishwashers and older models is noise, which is measured in decibels (dB). Anything around 50 decibels or below is generally considered very quiet and shouldn’t overpower a normal conversation. Standard units that produce sound at around 51 decibels are more noticeable, especially during spray and drain cycles.

If you’re particularly sensitive to noise or often run the dishwasher at night outside of your energy company’s peak hours, look for models that promise quieter performance. Many of the newest dishwashers run quietly enough that you’ll barely notice them in the background. There have been multiple times when I’ve opened my Samsung dishwasher at home mid-cycle because I didn’t hear it running.

One of the most frustrating parts of using a dishwasher is opening the door to find wet dishes. Fortunately, modern dishwashers utilize several methods to ensure they come out bone-dry.

Some rely on traditional heated dry cycles, which raise interior temperature to evaporate moisture. Others take a more energy-efficient approach called condensation drying, where residual heat from the hot rinse water evaporates moisture against the cooler stainless steel walls. Newer models, like the Midea 24-Inch Top Control Built-in Dishwasher, have an auto-open feature, which automatically pops open the door at the end of the cycle to vent steam and ensure that even plastic containers dry completely.

Modern dishwashers pack more features than ever. When shopping around, you’ll see things like third racks for utensils, height-adjustable upper racks, soil sensors, foldable tines, and WiFi and app control. Many of these features give you the flexibility to load your dishes more efficiently, which means you can wash more items in a single load and are less likely to need to rewash plates or glasses.

Also consider where a dishwasher’s controls are (hidden on top versus front-facing), whether the tub is stainless steel, and other things that could potentially enhance your experience. Just remember that every added feature usually nudges the price up. Whatever you buy, make a habit of cleaning your dishwasher a couple times per year to keep it running like new.

Most households will be fine with a standard 24-inch dishwasher, which offers enough room for everyday dishes and larger cookware. But if you’re working with a smaller kitchen or apartment, an 18-inch model saves valuable real estate. “Your choice depends on available space, how many dishes you typically wash, and the size of the pans you cook with,” says Glenn Lewis, president of Mr. Appliance, a Neighborly company.

Yes, and it’s worth checking before you buy. “They need a dedicated 120-volt electrical connection, a water supply line, and a drain connection, all of which must meet local building codes for safe operation,” Lewis says. If you’re replacing an existing unit, the connections are likely already in place, but if you’re adding a dishwasher for the first time, you may need to hire a professional to set up the plumbing and electrical.

It’s possible, but proceed with caution. “You can if you have basic plumbing and electrical knowledge, but improper installation can lead to leaks or electrical issues, so many homeowners opt for professional installation,” Lewis says. If you’re swapping out an old unit and the connections are already there, a DIY install is more manageable. But for a first-time installation, professional help is usually the safer bet.

An Energy Star certification means the dishwasher meets strict efficiency standards that might save you money over time. “Energy Star-certified models use less water and electricity, not only to run the dishwasher but to heat the water used by the dishwasher,” Lewis says. “Lower energy means lower utility bills and reduced environmental impact over time.” If you’re choosing between two similar models, going with the Energy Star-certified option is usually the smarter long-term investment.

#6406. A Healthier Form of Salt Could Prevent Nearly 3 Million Deaths Every Year, Scientists Say

A global study spanning 193 countries suggests that a simple change to everyday salt could prevent millions of deaths and cases of cardiovascular and kidney disease each year.

Replacing ordinary salt with a potassium-enriched alternative could prevent nearly three million deaths worldwide each year, according to a new study covering 193 countries. Researchers estimate that a global switch could also prevent more than ten million new cases of cardiovascular and kidney disease annually, offering a potentially powerful way to reduce the health burden of high blood pressure.

The analysis, led by The George Institute for Global Health, examined how different levels of salt replacement might affect the world’s 4.6 billion adults. The findings suggest that even limited changes, particularly among people already diagnosed with high blood pressure, could produce substantial health gains.

Potassium-enriched salt replaces part of the sodium chloride in regular table salt with potassium chloride. It looks, tastes, and performs much like conventional salt in cooking but contains less sodium and provides additional potassium, two changes that can help lower blood pressure.

“Consuming too much sodium and not enough potassium are well established causes of high blood pressure, a major risk factor for life-threatening conditions like strokes, heart attacks and kidney disease. Switching to potassium-enriched salt addresses both these dietary issues at the same time, with substantial health benefits,” said Bruce Neal, Senior Professorial Fellow at The George Institute.

High blood pressure (hypertension) affects approximately 1.4 billion adults aged 30 to 79 worldwide, or roughly one in three people in that age group. Cardiovascular disease (CVD) caused 19.2 million deaths in 2023, nearly 50 percent more than three decades earlier. In 2025, the World Health Organization (WHO) endorsed potassium-enriched salt as a way to reduce blood pressure and cardiovascular risk.

The researchers modeled several scenarios, including replacing all salt consumed at home, in restaurants, and in processed foods. Switching only household table salt could prevent approximately 1.85 million deaths and 6.19 million new cases of cardiovascular and chronic kidney disease annually. Replacing salt exclusively in processed and restaurant foods could prevent another estimated 1.56 million deaths and 5.46 million new disease cases each year under that separate scenario.

More targeted approaches also showed considerable potential. If 80 percent of people with diagnosed hypertension switched their household salt, the model projected approximately 590,000 fewer deaths annually. Among those receiving treatment for hypertension, a comparable level of adoption could prevent about 480,000 deaths each year.

“While a global shift from regular salt to a potassium-enriched substitute is aspirational, this is a starting point to get countries thinking about the opportunity, with much greater potential and at much lower cost than many drug-based treatments,” Neal said.

The projected benefits varied considerably between countries. Under a complete replacement scenario, China could prevent approximately 1.08 million deaths and 3.61 million new cardiovascular and kidney disease cases annually. India could avert nearly 400,000 deaths and 1.53 million new cases, while the United States could prevent approximately 105,000 deaths and 492,000 new cases.

Achieving these reductions would require strategies tailored to how people consume salt. In many countries, household cooking accounts for a substantial share of sodium intake. In Europe and North America, however, processed and restaurant foods contribute more than 70 percent, making cooperation from food manufacturers and restaurants essential.

“To realize the maximum benefits from switching to potassium-enriched salt, we need to see the food industry in Europe and North America, where over 70% of salt intake comes from processed and restaurant foods, get on board. This would also require investigating ways to scale up the production of potassium chloride to meet demand,” Neal said.

Although potassium-enriched salt can help lower blood pressure, it may pose risks for people whose kidneys cannot effectively remove excess potassium from the bloodstream. This can lead to hyperkalemia, a potentially dangerous condition that can disrupt the heart’s electrical activity. People with advanced kidney disease and those taking certain medications that increase blood potassium levels require particular caution.

The study’s modeling suggested that the overall health benefits could outweigh the risks even among people with advanced kidney disease. However, that population-level finding does not mean potassium-enriched salt is safe for every individual.

“People with serious kidney disease and those taking medications that significantly raise blood potassium levels need to take precautions. Risks for this group can be managed effectively through patient education, product labeling, and clinical oversight,” said Professor Vivek Jha, a nephrologist and Senior Professorial Fellow at The George Institute in India.

Reference: “Global health outcomes from replacing dietary sodium chloride with potassium-enriched salt” by Liping Huang, Xiaoyue Xu, Kunihiro Matsushita, Tammy M. Brady, Lawrence J. Appel, Ewout J. Hoorn, Aletta E. Schutte, Jason H. Y. Wu, Maoyi Tian, Leopold N. Aminde, Kathy Trieu, Bruce Neal and Matti Marklund, 4 November 2026, Nature Health. DOI: 10.1038/s44360-026-00216-9

#6404. Popular Dairy Alternatives Could Be Leaving You Short of Essential Nutrients

Replacing even a modest amount of dairy with plant-based alternatives could significantly reduce essential nutrient intake, according to a new study from the University of Surrey. Researchers found that substituting just 20% to 35% of dairy products increased the estimated prevalence of inadequate iodine intake among adolescent girls from 54% to 65%. Among women ages 19 to 49, the figure rose from 32% to 42%.

The study also identified reductions in calcium, riboflavin, and vitamin B12 intake. However, researchers found that fortifying plant-based alternatives and other foods could help prevent these nutritional shortfalls.

In the first UK study of its kind, researchers from the University of Surrey and Queen’s University Belfast analyzed dietary data from more than 3,500 people, ages 18 months to 100 years. Using the National Diet and Nutrition Survey, they modeled how replacing milk, yogurt, and cheese with commercially available plant-based alternatives would affect intake of four essential micronutrients.

Dr Katie Nicol, a research fellow at the University of Surrey and co-author of the study, explained:

“With the growing need to address environmental sustainability, many dietary recommendations are focused on plant-based diets and the reduced intake of animal products.”

“With the rise in plant-based alternative foods, we need to know whether they are like-for-like replacements for the micronutrients that are found in dairy products. This is particularly important for vulnerable groups, including young children and adolescent females, who are more likely to be deficient in certain micronutrients, which could affect their overall health.”

Iodine was the nutrient most affected by dairy replacement. When researchers modeled completely replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives under current fortification levels, the estimated prevalence of inadequate iodine intake reached 80% among adolescent girls and 72% among adolescent boys. These figures reflect modeled dietary inadequacy, not confirmed clinical deficiencies.

Iodine is essential for producing thyroid hormones, which regulate metabolism and support growth and brain development. It is particularly important before and during pregnancy, when iodine requirements increase.

Dr Sarah Bath, associate professor at the University of Surrey and lead author, said:

“The UK is particularly vulnerable to iodine insufficiency due to a lack of an iodine fortification policy such as universal salt iodization, which many other countries have.”

“People may also be unaware of the importance of iodine, which is needed to make thyroid hormones to regulate our metabolism, support healthy growth, and brain development. Iodine is particularly important during pregnancy, when the requirement increases, but it is also essential prior to pregnancy to ensure that stores are optimized. People are also unaware that dairy products are a major source of iodine, particularly in the UK, and that plant-based alternatives, unless fortified, have a very low iodine content.”

The researchers found that mandatory fortification of plant-based dairy alternatives could prevent declines in micronutrient intake. However, even with fortified alternatives, an estimated 59% of adolescent girls would still have inadequate iodine intake. Adding iodine to bread reduced that figure to 37%, suggesting that combining both fortification strategies could be more effective.

Dr Nicol emphasized the importance of aligning nutrition policies with environmental goals:

“Nutrition policy must evolve in tandem with environmental targets; however, it is important that shifts towards more sustainable diets do not compromise on public health. Fortification of foods is one way that this could be achieved; however, government policy is needed to make this happen.”

Dr Anne Nugent, from Queen’s University Belfast, described how the team identified dairy-containing foods in the UK National Diet and Nutrition Survey and modeled replacing them with equal amounts of plant-based alternatives. The researchers accounted for differences in the nutritional content of available products and tested whether fortification could prevent deficiencies without causing excessive nutrient intake.

“During the analysis, we first identified all foods and recipes containing dairy produce (milk, cheese, and yogurt) in the national food survey for the UK, the National Diet and Nutrition Survey. Next, we conducted a series of replacement scenarios whereby we substituted the dairy present with an equal weight of plant-based dairy alternatives. As the nutrient composition of dairy alternatives available on our supermarket shelves can vary, we also applied a condition to make sure that every dairy alternative we had identified in our previous market survey had an equal chance of selection. The last step was to examine the impact on dietary intakes of key nutrients following either the reduction or removal of dairy from the diet, replacing it with the dairy alternatives as above, and asking whether a series of fortification options could mitigate against any shortfalls in intake while avoid situations of excess.”

Reference: “The impact of replacing dairy products with plant-based dairy alternatives on iodine and other micronutrients: a modelling study and evaluation of policy options to support population intake” by Katie Nicol, Anne P Nugent, Jayne V Woodside, Kathryn H Hart and Sarah C Bath, , The Lancet Planetary Health. DOI: 10.1016/j.lanplh.2026.101515

An analysis of plant fossils preserved in amber from Myanmar revealed that the West Burma Block, a chunk of crust that broke off of Australia, seeded Southeast Asia's lush tropical forests.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Southeast Asia's tropical forests owe their rich biodiversity to a tiny fragment of Earth's crust that split from what is now northwestern Australia roughly 150 million years ago, a new study reports.

The fragment transported hundreds of flowering species and a flourishing collection of other ancient plants north across the prehistoric Tethys Ocean, the research reveals. The findings contradict previous theories that the fragment originated closer to what is now Southeast Asia and that Southeast Asia's tropical forests evolved sometime after the extinction of the dinosaurs around 66 million years ago.

At the time the fragment formed, Australia was connected to Antarctica and India within the ancient supercontinent Gondwana, which the Tethys Ocean separated from another ancient supercontinent, called Laurasia.

After drifting northward for 100 million years, the microplate eventually collided with Southeast Asia, seeding tropical forests that evolved into the lush ecosystems found in this part of the world today, the researchers said.

"The rich tropical rainforest flora of [Southeast Asia] is not endemic but owes much of its biota to the great southern land, Gondwana," study co-author Byron Lamont, a distinguished professor emeritus in Curtin University's School of Molecular and Life Sciences in Australia, told Live Science in an email.

But the collision with Southeast Asia was far from smooth, Lamont said. The fragment, which is known as the West Burma Block (WBB) or the Burma terrane due to its location in western Myanmar, wasn't the only piece of crust crossing the Tethys Ocean around 100 million years ago. The Indian subcontinent was also moving north, and it was doing so at a relatively rapid speed of 4 inches (10 centimeters) per year.

Around 80 million years ago, the Indian Plate bumped into the WBB, altering the fragment's orientation. The Indian Plate continued to shove the WBB until they both collided with Asia. The Indian Plate then slid beneath the Eurasian Plate to form the Himalayas, and the WBB ground to a halt to the west of present-day Myanmar, where it created a deep valley between mountain ranges about 35 million years ago, Lamont explained.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Both the Indian Plate and the WBB "took some time to stop," he said.

From the time the WBB broke off from Gondwana until its collision with Southeast Asia starting 50 million years ago, the microplate spent tens of millions of years hovering near the equator, where it was humid and hot like it is today. This climate and the fragment's isolation provided a refuge where ancient plant lineages could survive and diversify, Lamont said.

For the study, Lamont and his colleagues examined more than 3,000 plant fossils from Myanmar that were preserved in amber around 100 million years ago. The fossils included flowers, leaves, fruits and seeds. They belonged to at least 392 types of flowering plants and a vast array of conifers, ferns, mosses, cycads and liverworts that reached Southeast Asia by floating on the WBB.

Amber has been mined from the north end of the WBB valley for at least a century, Lamont said. "Its beautiful fossils, preserved in 3D, have long attracted interest for their novelty value alone and there has been much commercial interest in them, especially from Chinese traders," he noted.

Some of the study's co-authors acquired chunks of amber from traders at least a decade ago, and they have been studying these pieces ever since. Advice was often required from experts at other institutions around the world, which is how Lamont got involved in the study, he said.

The findings, published Oct. 27 in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution, reveal the deep evolutionary roots of the tropical forests that grow in Southeast Asia today. The WBB didn't strip Australia of its ancient flora, because the descendants of many plants found in the 100 million-year-old amber still exist in the country's Northeast, which is hot and humid, Lamont said.

It's hard to say what kinds of animals arrived in Southeast Asia via the WBB, because only creatures small enough to be preserved in amber are represented in this fossil assemblage.

"The animals present in the amber are small insects, such as ants and mosquitoes," Lamont said. "Typical Australian vertebrates, such as marsupials, emus and nectar-feeding birds, arrived from South America in Australia over 100 million years later [after the WBB split off], and of course they would not have got caught in the resin even if they had been around."

#6400. Scientists Discover Something Unexpected 90 Kilometers Beneath Earth

A rock from Papua New Guinea was hotter than expected during its descent into Earth, challenging models of a process that influences earthquakes, volcanoes, and climate.

Earth recycles its own surface. In regions called subduction zones, one tectonic plate, a vast slab of Earth’s outer shell, sinks beneath another as the plates collide. These zones are sites of earthquakes and volcanic activity, and they help stabilize Earth’s climate over millions of years by recycling molecules such as carbon dioxide.

A rock from Papua New Guinea has revealed a gap in scientists’ understanding of the temperatures inside these regions. Four million years ago, it descended more than 90 kilometers, or about 56 miles, below Earth’s surface. But roughly halfway down, it was already much hotter than current models would predict.

An international research team led by Göttingen University reconstructed the journey by studying eclogite, a red and green rock that forms under the high pressures found in subduction zones. Minerals within the rock preserve evidence of the conditions it experienced underground, allowing researchers to piece together its history. The findings were published in Nature Geoscience.

Using a combination of analytical techniques, the researchers found tiny inclusions of coesite trapped inside another mineral during the rock’s formation. Coesite is a mineral that requires extremely high pressure to form. Its presence helped the team conclude that the rock had reached a depth of at least 90 kilometers, where it experienced temperatures of around 800°C, or 1,470 °F.

At about 45 kilometers, or 28 miles, however, the rock had been only 100°C cooler, a difference of 180°F. In other words, it had already reached around 700°C, or 1,290°F, at roughly half the depth. Those shallower conditions were unusually hot, while the deeper conditions fit the more common, relatively cold pattern of subduction. Calling the deeper conditions cold does not mean the rock cooled as it sank. It means that its temperature was lower relative to its depth than it had been earlier in the journey.

Dr. Jan Schönig at Göttingen University’s Geoscience Center explains, “Finding this change from hot to cold subduction was unexpected, as this contradicts our current thermal models of subduction zones.”

Researchers have found rocks that recorded unexpectedly high temperatures before. This is the first time, though, that a rock’s journey from shallow to deep conditions has so clearly shown an accompanying shift to relatively colder temperatures for its depth.

One possible explanation is that shearing stress, produced as plates move against one another, heats rocks at shallow depths more than scientists have assumed. Another is that the subduction zone had not yet had enough time to develop the lower temperatures expected there. Both processes could have contributed.

Understanding these temperatures more accurately could help researchers assess how subduction affects earthquakes, volcanic activity, and the movement of chemicals through Earth, including the long-term carbon cycle. It could also clarify how subduction has operated over millions to billions of years and how it continues today.

Reference: “Geothermal gradient change during subduction recorded by ultrahigh-pressure eclogite” by Jan Schönig, Silvio Ferrero, Kerstin Gresky, Dominik Sorger, Axel K. Schmitt, Bernd Wunder, Suzanne L. Baldwin and Adam F. Holt, 1 October 2026, Nature Geoscience. DOI: 10.1038/s41561-026-02110-1

The research was supported by funding from the German Research Foundation (DFG).

#6399. Newborn survival improves when families receive financial support

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Rx Kids, a cash transfer program, boosted infants’ health in Flint, Michigan

Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield announces Rx Kids' Detroit debut in 2025. The program began in Flint, Mich., in 2024. “We know how to deliver this support efficiently and with dignity," pediatrician and Rx Kids director Mona Hanna told Science News.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Extra financial support during pregnancy and after birth can help more babies thrive in their earliest days.

The Rx Kids program in Flint, Mich., launched in January 2024, provides extra cash to pregnant residents and their infants, unconditionally. Researchers compared neonatal deaths — those in the first four weeks of life — in 2025 with those in 2021 through 2024 in Flint. The city’s neonatal mortality rate dropped from 10 deaths per 1,000 live births to 5 deaths per 1,000 live births, researchers report November 2 in JAMA Pediatrics. The early neonatal mortality rate, covering deaths in the first week of life, fell from 8 per 1,000 to 2. For the rest of Michigan, rates were stable over the study’s time period.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“As a pediatrician, there is no outcome more important than babies surviving,” says Mona Hanna of the Michigan State University College of Human Medicine in Flint, who is also the founder and director of Rx Kids. “These early findings suggest that something as simple as providing families with financial support during pregnancy and infancy may help save babies’ lives.”

Income tends to drop and expenses rise in the months before and after a birth, making the perinatal period especially difficult financially for many families. Economic precarity can expose moms and babies to health harms. For example, housing instability and homelessness is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight.

Backed by public and private funds, Rx Kids got started in Flint, a city with a high rate of child poverty that has been dealing with the public health fallout of lead contamination in the water distribution system. Nearly 100 percent of the community participates in the program. Flint families receive $1,500 once during pregnancy and $500 per month in the baby’s first year. Anyone who is a resident, at least 16 weeks pregnant or with a newborn up to six months old can enroll. Families have put the extra cash toward diapers, transportation, housing and safe places for their babies to sleep, Hanna says.

“Every day, we hear from moms who tell us, ‘I can breathe’ or ‘A weight has been lifted off my shoulders.’ They tell us they feel less stressed, more hopeful, more supported and more loved,” Hanna says.

The support has had a measurable health impact, with studies linking the program to more access to prenatal care, a decrease in the preterm birth rate and in low-weight births and fewer neonatal intensive care admissions.

Rx Kids has now expanded to dozens of communities in Michigan and Ohio.

Tired of using loud and unsightly window air conditioners or clunky and underpowered portable air conditioners? Even if you don’t have the means to install a fully ducted HVAC system in your home, you can still upgrade to a more powerful cooling system with a ductless air conditioner.

Ductless air conditioners, often called mini-splits, cool targeted areas of your home without relying on the ductwork. Instead, they connect a compact outdoor condenser to one or more indoor air handlers, which are usually mounted on a wall or ceiling.

To help narrow down the best ductless air conditioners, I compared models across capacity, efficiency, installation requirements, noise level, smart features, and overall value. I also spoke with HVAC expert Kim Lincoln, who has 25 years of industry experience, for guidance on how mini-splits work, when they make sense, and what shoppers should know before buying.

Many come with features like programmability, dehumidification settings, and, in a few instances, smartphone functionality.

As an added perk, most of these contraptions also double as heaters—which is useful during cooler months. I leaned on my experience with different types of cooling units, as well as product specs I reviewed during my research. The final list below represents the best in each category, including best budget and best for DIY installation.

For this update, I relied on the expertise of Lincoln, as well as my own experiences with several types of ductless air conditioners. I asked her a variety of questions about mini-splits, touching on topics like the differences between this type of air conditioner from other units, installation, and more. I also updated the products I recommend to reflect recent advances in smart home technology and energy efficiency.

This highly-rated AC unit from Senville comes in a number of sizes, ranging from 9,000 BTUs all the way up to 30,000 BTUs, and it comes in 120- and 230-volt models. You can control all of its settings via the included remote. The air conditioner comes with an installation kit, including a communication cable and copper lines, but it’s important to note the brand requires professional installation for the unit’s five-year warranty to be valid.

Great for climate control storage and small bedrooms, the WYS009A-20 is an Energy Star-certified machine that’ll help you save money year-round. It cools as low as -13 degrees F and heats up to 122 F.

It has a permanent washable air filter and a remote control for easy operation—though you have to buy an additional remote to use Wi-Fi capabilities. It also operates at only 25 decibels, making it one of the quietest machines on this list, and it has four modes: cooling, heating, dehumidification, and ventilation. After installation, Pioneer provides free tech support and five-year coverage on replacement parts and the compressor.

This model from Della is a great value. It delivers 24,000 BTUs/hour, making it suitable for rooms up to 1,500 square feet. It’s also the sleekest model we found.

In addition to cooling, this unit has settings for heating, dehumidification, and ventilation, and that versatility extends to its selection of impressive features, including a 24-hour timer, sleep mode, energy-saving mode, and multiple fan speeds. You can easily adjust all of these using the included remote control and the Della+ app. The app allows users to control the settings, set timers, and control various Della units from one screen for whole-house control.

The Della Mini-Split comes with a full installation kit, including a line set, and it operates at 51 decibels. Some installers report the directions are confusing and have had to rely on online guides for extra help, but most reviewers are happy with this unit.

Suppose you want the ability to adjust your air conditioning from your smartphone. In that case, this model from Senville includes built-in Wi-Fi connectivity, allowing you to operate it remotely from an Android or iOS device.

It’s suitable for large spaces, thanks to its four-zone setup and 36,000-BTU output. Plus, it also has heating, dehumidification, and fan settings.

The unit has a turbo mode for even more versatility, and it automatically switches from cooling to heating based on the ambient temperature. The Senville Mini-Split comes with an installation kit that includes a 16-foot line set for your professional installer.

If you plan to install your ductless air conditioner in a large room, this model delivers 36,000 BTUs, making it powerful enough to efficiently cool spaces up to 1,500 square feet. It can be used for heating and cooling, operating in ambient temperatures between 5 and 122 degrees Fahrenheit, and it comes with a comprehensive installation kit.

You’ll get an insulated and pre-flared 25-foot line set, communication wires, a drainage extension, and remote control. The unit can even be equipped with wifi if you purchase the brand’s USB adapter (sold separately).

The large, rectangular indoor units that come with most ductless air conditioners can be a bit cumbersome on your wall, and if you prefer a more streamlined appearance, this unit uses a ceiling cassette instead.

The 9,000-BTU system can be used for heating and cooling in spaces up to 350 square feet, and it comes with a 16-foot line set and all necessary installation equipment. The system has a 24-hour timer, sleep mode, turbo function, and three indoor fan modes. It operates at 31.5 decibels, making it ideal for bedrooms.

If energy usage is your top priority, DELLA’s 12,000-BTU mini-split is one of the most efficient systems commonly available online. Its efficiency rating sits around 22–23 SEER2 (which is a newer efficiency standard that prioritizes real-world performance), and that means it uses significantly less electricity than many other entry-level mini-splits.

The inverter compressor automatically adjusts output instead of cycling on and off, which helps the unit maintain steady temperatures and reduces power consumption. (You’ll really notice this feature during periods of extreme weather that tend to spike utility bills.)

The unit is well-sized for bedrooms, offices, or small living areas, and it cools and heats spaces up to about 600 square feet. The built-in Wi-Fi control and quiet operation round out the package.

One drawback: While DELLA has great reviews, it’s a smaller company and may offer less customer support, based on some user feedback.

If you’re looking to cool a smaller space like a bedroom or home office, Costway Blast Series is a solid pick for a bedroom, office, or other small room where you want more permanent cooling than a window unit can provide. Its 9,000-BTU output is sized for spaces up to 450 square feet, so it’s a better fit for modest rooms than the larger 18,000- or 24,000-BTU systems in this category. It also offers quiet operation, a display-off function, a timer, and a remote control you can use from bed.

Like many of the units we looked at, this product is more versatile than a cooling-only AC, too. It has cooling, heating, dry, fan, and sleep modes, plus ECO, turbo, and iFEEL settings. The washable filter and self-cleaning function are also helpful for keeping routine maintenance manageable.

The tradeoff is that this model requires 208- to 230-volt power, so it may need electrical work before installation. Its 17 SEER2 efficiency rating is respectable, but not as high as some more expensive bedroom-friendly mini-splits. Still, for a smaller space, it offers a useful mix of performance, basic heat-pump functionality, and good value.

This high-efficiency mini-split system is specifically designed for DIY installation—and no special tools are required. It’s compatible with Google Assistant and Alexa, and it comes with features like an auto restart if there’s a power outage, leak detection, and sleep mode on the remote to adjust the temperature automatically during the night.

The unit heats and cools with 24,000 BTUs of power, which is more than enough, but considering the model's premium price, it's a little on the low side. Its SEER rating is 20.5, and operation is relatively quiet.

Overall, it’s a great package, albeit a pricey one.

Compared to window or portable air conditioners, ductless systems are more permanent, more powerful, and typically quieter. They also give you more control over specific rooms, so you can cool the spaces you actually use instead of the whole house at once. There are some drawbacks, though.

Ductless ACs run pricey (even setting aside the cost of installation). They’re also more visible than central air vents, and you need to size and place them carefully to cool a room evenly. DIY installs or wrong-sized units can cause issues in the long run.

Maintenance can also be difficult, as not all HVAC professionals are familiar with these products. However, for an older home with radiator heat (like mine is), it’s the best way to add efficient air conditioning without blocking most of our windows.

First, decide how many indoor units you need and where you’ll place them. Unlike window units, mini-split systems are permanent fixtures, so carefully consider where they’ll be most efficient within your home.

Generally, a single ductless air conditioner can handle cooling a targeted area or a single room. If you’re cooling down multiple rooms, consider a multi-zone system so that you get even temperatures throughout your home.

It’s also essential to select a unit that’s powerful enough for the room it’s in—too small and it may not cool your space. The cooling capacity of air conditioners is typically measured in British Thermal Units, or BTUs, per hour.

As a general rule of thumb, choose a unit that delivers 20 BTUs per square foot of living space. So, a 200-square-foot room needs at least a 4,000-BTU air conditioner. Those sensitive to noise should consider units with a quiet mode feature.

It’s also important to consider the electrical system in the area you plan to install the mini-split. Many larger mini-splits require 208- to 230-volt power, which works with both commercial 208V electrical service and the 240V circuits typically used for major appliances in homes, while smaller systems may run on standard 120V outlets without any needed upgrades.

Quieter units are more desirable for bedrooms, living rooms, and nurseries, where a peaceful environment is essential. Look for ductless air conditioners with noise levels between 19 and 30 decibels, since this range can be compared to the sound of leaves rustling or a soft whisper.

Units with levels between 30 to 40 decibels are still suitable for other areas of the home, since this range is comparable to background noise or casual conversation.

While shopping for your ductless air conditioner, you may see “SEER” with a number next to it. SEER stands for Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio, which measures how much energy your air conditioner uses during the annual cooling season. The higher the SEER rating, the less energy your unit uses to cool your home.

You may also see “SEER2,” a newer efficiency standard introduced in 2023 that uses updated testing conditions meant to better reflect real-world performance. SEER2 numbers are typically slightly lower than SEER ratings for the same unit, but they represent the same idea: higher numbers mean more efficient energy usage.

A product with an Energy Star certification has been rigorously tested by the United States Environmental Protection Agency for its energy efficiency. EPA-recognized laboratories test products to Energy Star specifications to ensure manufacturers produce energy-saving products.

Although testing guidelines change per product category, all items must prove they consume less energy than standard models without compromising performance.

Mini-splits are more permanent and expensive than window or portable air conditioners, so they make the most sense when you plan to cool the same space for several seasons. Most systems also require professional installation, and larger units may need electrical upgrades before you can install them.

They’re also not invisible. The indoor air handler usually stays mounted high on the wall year-round, which may bother homeowners who prefer the low-profile look of central air vents. Proper sizing and placement matter, too, since an oversized, undersized, or poorly positioned unit can lead to uneven cooling, wasted energy, or poor humidity control.

Ductless air conditioners cool your home without using the network of ducts that central HVAC systems rely on, says Lincoln. “The way I explain ductless cooling to homeowners is simple: the system conditions the room directly instead of trying to send cooled air through ductwork first,” she explains.

Instead, ductless air conditioners connect a small outdoor condenser to one or more indoor air handlers using refrigerant lines. Because there’s no ductwork involved, these types of units are often more efficient and easier to install in older homes, additions, or finished spaces where running ducts would be difficult. They also allow for “zoned” cooling, meaning you can control the temperature in individual rooms instead of conditioning the entire house at once.

These systems are also more customizable than a whole-house system. “Where mini-splits really shine is zoning,” explains Lincoln. “One outdoor unit can support multiple indoor heads, so different parts of the house can be conditioned based on how those spaces are actually used.”

Yes. “A mini-split is just a ductless system made up of an outdoor condenser and one or more indoor air handlers,” says Lincoln. The terms ductless air conditioner and mini-split are generally used interchangeably, as we have in this guide.

Both describe systems that pair an outdoor condenser with one or more indoor air handlers connected by refrigerant lines instead of ductwork. The “split” part refers to the system being divided between indoor and outdoor components.

Some mini-splits provide cooling only, but many modern models are actually heat pumps, meaning they can both cool and heat your home using the same system. Adding air conditioning to an older home that previously utilized radiator or baseboard heat can be tricky—squeezing ductwork into closets and unused corners feels a bit like remodelling Jenga. These units solve that issue without much fuss.

Usually, yes. In most cases, it makes sense to hire a professional. Installing a mini-split usually involves mounting indoor and outdoor units, running refrigerant lines, and making electrical connections, which is why many manufacturers recommend professional installation.

“Installation is where good equipment gets made—or wasted,” advises Lincoln. “Mini-splits look deceptively simple once they’re on the wall, but installation is not casual work. Line sets, electrical, drainage, vacuuming the system down properly before startup…those are the steps that determine whether the unit runs the way it was engineered to run.”

Some systems are more DIY-friendly, but even those can be complicated if you’re not comfortable working with electrical systems or HVAC equipment. Professional installation also helps ensure the system runs efficiently and may be required to maintain the manufacturer’s warranty. If you are a very seasoned DIY pro who’s handy with a YouTube tutorial, you might be okay. Otherwise, we recommend budgeting for an installer.

Companies size mini-splits systems based on BTUs, which measure how much heating or cooling power the unit can deliver.

“When people ask how to calculate the right BTU for a room, the honest answer is that manufacturer charts are a starting point, not a finish line,” says Lincoln. “For a window unit, those charts can get you close. For a mini-split, a proper load calculation is the better answer.” This is another reason it’s great to work with an expert installer before ordering—they can guide your purchasing based on your needs.

Lincoln explains that it’s not a straightforward calculation, in most cases. “Room size is only the starting point. Sun exposure, ceiling height, insulation, window size, window direction, occupancy, and heat from electronics or appliances all change the cooling load,” she adds.

Smaller systems around 9,000 BTU often work for bedrooms or small offices, while 12,000–18,000-BTU systems handle larger living areas. As a rough rule, most homeowners look at units sized for the square footage of the space they want to heat or cool, but must consider all of these other factors, too.

#6397. Scientists Finally Crack a 1,600-Year-Old Roman Glass Mystery

More than 1,600 years after the Romans created the famous Lycurgus Cup, a University of Sheffield technician has found a way to reliably reproduce its extraordinary color-changing glass.

A glass cup made more than 1,600 years ago has puzzled historians and glassmakers for centuries.

When light reflects off its surface, the cup appears jade green. When light shines through it, the glass turns a striking ruby red. Despite knowing much about the science behind this unusual effect, modern glassmakers have struggled to reproduce it consistently. Now, researchers at the University of Sheffield have developed a recipe that recreates the remarkable color-changing properties of this ancient Roman masterpiece.

The Lycurgus Cup, created in the fourth century AD and housed in the British Museum, is made from a special type of glass known as dichroic glass. Its appearance changes depending on whether light reflects from the surface or passes through the material. The cup is one of only 40 surviving Roman glass cage cups and among the most complete. It is also the only surviving example known to display this extraordinary color-changing effect.

Its craftsmanship is just as remarkable as its colors. The decoration depicts Lycurgus, a mythical Thracian king, entangled in vines as punishment for his misdeeds. In 2022, an international panel of artists and conservators recognized the cup as one of the seven glass wonders of the world, honoring its artistry, unusual colors, and exceptional preservation.

Scientists believe the secret lies in tiny amounts of gold and silver added to the glass by Roman craftspeople. Under the right conditions, these metals can form layered nanoparticles thousands of times smaller than a grain of sand. Because the particles are smaller than the wavelengths of visible light, they absorb light strongly and produce vibrant colors that depend on their size and shape.

Understanding this process, however, is different from knowing exactly how to recreate it. The precise techniques used by Roman glassmakers remain unknown, and previous attempts to reproduce the effect have met with varying degrees of success.

The challenge took on new life when Christina Metcalfe, project manager for the Molecular Photonic Breadboards project, asked University of Sheffield technician Dr. Lisa Hollands to recreate the glass for the university’s LightFest in 2025.

“I knew that making a glass of this type was likely to be a complex task, as it is not just a case of adding nanoparticles to glass,” said Dr. Hollands, from the University’s School of Chemical, Materials and Biological Engineering.

“I’ve studied and worked with glass for over 25 years, so I used the knowledge and experience I’ve gained, coupled with a modern scientific understanding of what I was trying to achieve.

“To start with, I worked with a leading Roman glass expert, Professor Caroline Jackson, to research what was already known about glass of the time and developed a base glass using modern materials to mimic what the Romans might have used. Then came the more difficult part of trying to get small amounts of gold and silver into the glass in the right form.

“Although if the Romans could have seen me experimenting, they’d probably laugh and ask: ‘Why does she not know how to make this?’”

Hollands experimented with different types of furnaces, starting materials, and oxygen levels, even testing the addition of sugar. After numerous attempts, she developed a glass that appeared opaque green under reflected light but turned red when illuminated from behind. The successful sample demonstrated that the distinctive optical effect of the ancient cup could be recreated using modern materials and experimental techniques, although it did not establish the exact recipe used by the Romans.

The first piece was exhibited at LightFest, an event held in Sheffield by the Molecular Photonic Breadboards project in partnership with the Universities of Sheffield and Bristol. Funded by the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC), the project focuses on developing materials that harness light for sustainable technologies. These materials could support fields important to the United Kingdom’s economy, including solar energy, quantum technologies, and healthcare diagnostics.

With the glass recipe established, the team wanted to create something that would showcase its unusual properties while paying tribute to the original Roman artifact.

“The next step was to commission a piece worthy of paying homage to its illustrious predecessor.

“We approached Elliot Walker, one of the UK’s finest glass artists and winner of season two of Netflix’s Blown Away, who accepted the challenge and was commissioned to create a contemporary sculpture using Dr Hollands’ recipe,” said Metcalfe.

For Walker, working with a material inspired by ancient glassmaking offered a rare connection to the craftspeople who had mastered similar techniques centuries earlier.

“It is a very rare thing to have the opportunity to work with glass developed from ancient mixtures and recipes, and it is always a very exciting one.

“You can really get an idea of how the glass makers of the past would have adapted to this sort of glass; it’s like shaking their hands.”

Walker drew inspiration from both the story depicted on the Lycurgus Cup and the classical Farnese Atlas sculpture. His design also needed to make the unusual optical effect visible to viewers, which influenced the final form of the artwork.

“I wanted to keep the sculpture quite classical in form and to carry through the original story of Lycurgus shown on the cup, but we needed a blown element within this to really show the dichroic glass,” Walker explained.

“The piece is a blend of the Lycurgus story and the Farnese Atlas sculpture, with the globe replaced by a cup.”

The completed sculpture is scheduled to be unveiled at the Millennium Gallery during the University of Sheffield’s Festival of the Mind, running from November 6 to 15, 2026. After the festival, it will become a permanent exhibit at the Turner Museum of Glass, located within the university’s School of Chemical, Materials and Biological Engineering.

“We set out to create something tangible to help the public understand what is possible when these tiny nanoparticles are embedded in something,” Metcalfe said.

“What Lisa and Elliot have managed to achieve has surpassed all our expectations. The incredible historic narrative really captures people’s imaginations, and I like to think we’ve created something that people will marvel at for years to come.”

Although this particular glass is expected to have mainly decorative uses, the knowledge gained from recreating it could contribute to the development of new photonic materials and advanced glasses for managing radioactive waste.

The project also connects with ongoing research led by Professor Russell Hand at the university’s Immobilisation Science Laboratory (ISL), within the School of Chemical, Materials and Biological Engineering. His work focuses on immobilizing complex nuclear wastes in glass, a process intended to keep hazardous materials safely contained.
