A half-built neutrino telescope on the floor of the Mediterranean Sea searched for cracks in one of physics' most basic invariances. It came up empty, but its limits rival those of detectors many times its size.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The view from inside a detector building block, with the yellow buoy of a nearby detection unit clearly visible.

A particle-detecting telescope sunk more than a mile beneath the sea off the coast of France has tested a core principle of Einstein's relativity and found no cracks.

The detector, called Oscillation Research with Cosmics in the Abyss (ORCA), detects elusive particles called neutrinos. As a doctoral student, Alba Domi rode onto the Mediterranean aboard one of two boats that helped build the telescope, lowering some of its first detection units to the seafloor about 1.5 miles (2.4 kilometers) below the waves off Toulon, France.

Now, data from those first detection units have been used to test one of the founding rules of Einstein’s relativity: the idea that the laws of nature look the same no matter which way you face or how fast you move.

The team found no sign that this rule, called Lorentz invariance, is broken. But even with a detector only a fraction of its planned size, they set limits that compete with those of far larger and longer-running experiments.

The results were published Wednesday (Nov. 4) in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics.

Physics rests on two successful theories: general relativity, conceived by Albert Einstein more than 100 years ago, and the Standard Model of subatomic physics.

"General relativity describes the universe well on a cosmic scale, and the Standard Model of particle physics describes the microscopic scale; really, the single particles, how they behave," said study co-author Lukas Hennig, a doctoral student in advanced physics at Erlangen-Nürnberg.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Both theories assume Lorentz invariance to be true. But in extreme settings, such as the first moments after the Big Bang, the two theories don't mesh. That has fueled a decades-long hunt for a theory of quantum gravity that unites them. Some candidates, including versions of string theory and loop quantum gravity, suggest that space-time might have a hidden "grain" at the tiniest scales — and that Lorentz invariance, "one of the most basic assumptions we make about our universe, might be violated," Hennig said.

Any such violation would be extremely small. To spot it, physicists would need a probe that could travel long distances and barely interact with anything along the way. Enter the neutrino.

Neutrinos are nearly massless particles that pass through Earth every second and carry zero charge. They barely interact with anything and come in three types: electron, muon and tau neutrinos. As neutrinos travel, they morph from one type into another in a predictable pattern that physicists call neutrino oscillation.

An optical module attached to the Dyneema ropes of the detection unit.

If Lorentz invariance were broken, that oscillation would change, with the effect growing more pronounced the farther the neutrinos traveled. So the team focused on neutrinos created when cosmic rays slam into the atmosphere elsewhere on the globe before traveling up through the planet to the detector. Some of the tested neutrinos crossed the entire 7,900-mile (12,700 km) width of Earth.

ORCA is part of the KM3NeT neutrino telescope. Each of its detection units is anchored to the seabed and holds 18 glass spheres packed with 31 light sensors apiece. When a neutrino collides with a particle in the water, it produces a faint flash of blue light that the sensors catch. The many sensors in each sphere help the team pin down which direction the light came from, Domi said.

Earth itself serves as a filter. The researchers selected only particles traveling upward through the planet, and they were able to weed out the flood of other particles from the atmosphere that would otherwise swamp the signal. "Only the neutrinos can get through," Hennig said.

That setup differs from that of IceCube, the Nobel Prize-winning detector buried in Antarctic ice. "Ice scatters the light more than water, but on the other hand, water absorbs the light more than ice," Domi said, which changes how each team reconstructs a neutrino's energy and path.

The researchers used 5,828 neutrinos collected over about 17 months between 2020 and 2021. They found that the oscillations matched standard physics. That means if Lorentz violation exists, it must be weaker than the limits the team set.

Those limits matter for theorists. If a model "predicts a Lorentz invariance violation [stronger than the new limits], the data rule it out. In that case, you can be pretty sure that this model is not correct," Hennig said.

The team also set the first direct limits on a kind of violation that would treat muon neutrinos and tau neutrinos differently.

The detector's limits on several key measures are competitive with those from Japan's Super-Kamiokande, which used 12 years of data, and from IceCube, which used two years of data from its full array.

"I'm surprised that we have competitive results with only six detection units," Hennig said. Today, 44 units are in the water, and the collaboration plans to activate 108 by 2030.

The best tests may still lie ahead. Because Lorentz-violating effects grow with distance and energy, neutrinos from distant cosmic sources are "actually the best candidates to do this kind of research," Domi said. The team plans to repeat the search using ORCA's sister detector, ARCA (Astroparticle Research with Cosmics in the Abyss), which sits off the coast of Sicily and is designed to catch those high-energy cosmic travelers.

If space-time does have a grain, those particles may be among the first to feel it.

Adriani et al. (2026). Atmospheric neutrino constraints on Lorentz invariance violation with the first six detection units of KM3NET/ORCA. Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics. https://doi.org/10.1088/1475-7516/2026/11/012

New findings suggest that "food challenges" can help prevent children from being saddled with unnecessary allergy diagnoses.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A peanut allergy diagnosis in infancy can mean years of avoiding the food or undergoing treatments to build tolerance. But a recent study suggests that more than one-third of babies thought to have the allergy may stop reacting badly to peanuts within months of that diagnosis.

In an analysis published in The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology: In Practice, researchers conducted supervised "food challenges" with infants diagnosed with a peanut allergy. These challenges involved giving the babies increasing amounts of peanut protein, with the intention of confirming whether they indeed had an allergy.

The team found that more than 1 in 3 infants who underwent the food challenge tolerated the peanut protein, meaning they didn't experience symptoms of an allergic reaction.

"This rate is much higher than we thought," study co-author Dr. Timothy Brettig, a pediatric allergist at the National Allergy Centre of Excellence in Australia, told Live Science.

Between April 2024 and October 2025, Brettig and colleagues retroactively reviewed the medical records of 1,275 infants who had been referred to Australian public hospitals after having a reaction to peanuts before their first birthday. These babies had first been assessed by allergy specialists at a median of 10 months of age.

For their initial diagnosis, the babies had to have a history of an allergic reaction to peanuts and show evidence of peanut sensitization on an allergy test. These tests included a skin-prick test, in which peanut extract is placed on the skin before it's lightly pricked, to check for a local reaction; and blood tests that detect antibodies against peanut proteins.

"Children under 1 year of age are an interesting group, as their immune system is still in rapid development and existing allergy tests may not reflect their allergic status well," said Dr. Alexandra Santos, a professor of pediatric allergy at King's College London who was not involved in the study. While these tests can hint that a child is sensitized to certain foods, they don't necessarily confirm that a baby will have an allergic reaction upon eating said food; the tests can also give false positives.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Of the 1,275 infants, 778 later underwent a food challenge roughly six months after their first recorded allergic reaction; at that point, their median age was 13 months old. They were given up to seven gradually increasing doses of peanut protein, ranging from 15 to 1,300 milligrams. These doses were given at 15-minute intervals while medical staff monitored the children for signs of an allergic reaction.

Nearly 35% of the participants — 271 kids — completed the challenge without reacting.

"This is an excellent article," said Dr. Drew Bird, a pediatric allergist at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center who was not involved in the study. "The take-home message is to strongly consider a supervised oral food challenge when an infant's peanut allergy diagnosis is uncertain."

Bird emphasized that these challenges should ideally be done before a child starts oral immunotherapy, a treatment in which patients regularly consume carefully measured amounts of the food they are allergic to. The dose is gradually increased under medical supervision, with the goal of helping the patient tolerate greater amounts of the allergen and reducing the risk of reactions from accidental exposure.

An incorrect diagnosis can prompt families to unnecessarily avoid exposing their children to peanuts.

The starting dose is often determined through a similar oral food challenge to the one used in this study, though. So in theory, that challenge would help reveal whether the child needs treatment in the first place.

Bird cautioned that food challenges should be performed by a board-certified allergist-immunologist and an experienced allergy team in a setting equipped to treat anaphylaxis — a severe, potentially life-threatening allergic reaction.

In this study, 507 infants reacted during the food challenge, and of those, 61 developed anaphylaxis and were treated with epinephrine (the hormone in EpiPens).

"In an ideal world, with infinite resources," Santos said, "all patients except for those with a history of severe reactions would have a food challenge for diagnosis."

Because that is not the case, the families of infants whose allergy diagnosis is uncertain may be advised to avoid peanut products while they await a formal food challenge, she noted. But in the interim, they may miss an opportunity to help the child develop tolerance and, in turn, increase the risk that their allergy will persist.

Food challenges should be prioritized for infants whose allergy diagnoses are uncertain, she said. This would include babies who have low levels of peanut-specific antibodies in their blood or who show only small welts on skin-prick tests.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Brettig, T. W., McDonald, E., West, D., et al. (2026). #6393. A drug-free diabetes treatment? An implant lowers blood sugar in mice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The device banishes extra blood glucose by converting it to a compound excreted in urine

Excess blood glucose (shown in white in this illustration) is the target of a new experimental device. In mice, the sugar gets converted into a compound which the kidneys can excrete in urine.

NEMES LASZLO/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A wireless implant that clears excess sugar from the blood could someday offer a drug-free way to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity.

In mice with both conditions, the under-the-skin device brought high blood sugar back to normal within 60 to 90 minutes of being switched on, researchers report October 22 in Science. After six weeks, the treated mice lost up to 10 percent of their body weight and had lower triglycerides, a type of fat in the blood.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Diabetes affects about 830 million people worldwide. Conventional type 2 diabetes treatments like insulin and GLP-1 drugs require careful dosing. Even experimental diabetes-controlling implants still rely on the hormone insulin, which clears sugar from the bloodstream but doesn’t rid the body of it, says Martin Fussenegger, a bioengineer at ETH Zurich. The new implant instead removes glucose from the body without added drugs, genes or living cells.

The 3-centimeter-long device contains a catalyst made of gold flakes and platinum particles on spongelike graphite. When electricity powers it, the catalyst converts glucose into gluconate, a compound that is easier for the kidneys to flush out in urine. With less glucose available for energy, the body may turn to its fat stores instead, Fussenegger and colleagues suspect. In mice, that shift showed up as higher blood levels of chemicals released when fat breaks down, such as ketones. “This system kind of targets the root cause, which is the energy surplus by glucose in the body,” Fussenegger says.

The implant works like an automatic sugar-removal system: A wearable glucose monitor detects high blood sugar levels and sends readings through a smartphone that switches the implant on. When levels return to a safer range, it switches off. The automated system ran for two weeks in eight mice. The catalyst itself remained able to convert glucose after up to three months under their skin, though the study didn’t establish how long the entire device would last.

And it’s still unknown how well the device would work in people. “This is a potentially promising method,” says David Klonoff, an endocrinologist at Sutter Mills-Peninsula Medical Center in Burlingame, Calif., who was not involved in the study. “But the risks are significant and must be carefully ruled out before it can be safely tested on humans.”

Researchers need to determine how much gluconate the kidneys can clear, Klonoff says. If it builds up, it could disrupt the body’s acid-base balance, causing symptoms such as nausea or confusion; excreting it could also deplete electrolytes such as sodium and potassium, he notes.

Scaling up the device is another challenge. Humans consume about 250 grams of carbohydrates daily, compared with two grams for mice, Klonoff estimates. Meeting that demand could require a much larger implant or multiple devices, he says. In a lab test, a larger device cleared nearly all glucose from about 5 liters of solution, roughly an adult’s blood volume, though not a full day’s glucose intake.

Fussenegger’s team plans to test the device in pigs and sheep before considering human trials. If proven safe and effective, it could offer an alternative to existing diabetes treatments and a new weight-loss option for people regardless of whether they have diabetes, he says.

#6392. The 6 Best Portable Solar Panels for Renewable Power Anywhere

Coupled with a portable power station, these solar panels provide efficient, portable power for emergency backup at home or powering devices wherever you roam.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Over the last decade, growing interest and competition in portable power stations and solar generators have driven huge improvements in solar panel performance. When I started playing around with them in the late ’90s, they were little more than a novelty, with low wattage that limited their usefulness. Today, they can theoretically draw and store enough energy to charge a power station in a few hours, giving you a true solar generator.

Once you’ve harnessed that energy, you can use it to power whatever you want. While they generally fall short of the large, permanently installed panels that homeowners use for power, they can still deliver ample power to a wide range of devices and setups. That may mean topping up phones and gear at a campsite, powering the appliances in an RV, or even storing it for a modest home backup in an emergency. I recently tested a set of highly rated models from the most trusted brands in the field to find the best portable solar panels on the market right now.

I’ve tested dozens of portable solar panels over the past five years. From 2021-2024, I lived and worked out of a converted van and used a portable solar generator to power all of my appliances and electronics as I drove all over the continent.

For this round of solar panel testing, I spent the past two months using eight new panels from brands I’ve tested and trust, and found five options that I strongly recommend, including the Bluetti 200W and the EcoFlow NextGen 220W. Each one was tested in real-world conditions, either on the road or camping, in tandem with many power stations across many brands and sizes. I tried them in both direct sun and partial cloud conditions, judged their portability, and considered any unique design elements.

I also added two panels I’ve tested in the past and still recommend. I didn’t test either the Jackery SolarSaga 100W or the BougeRV Arch 200W in the past few months, but I have used both extensively and feel they offer valuable alternatives to my latest test picks.

Thanks to all of this rigorous testing—I tend to be pretty hard on my gear—you can rest assured that these are the best portable solar panels you can get right now.

Bluetti has emerged as a leader in the portable solar game thanks to its durable, effective gear, and its 200W solar panel hits a sweet spot between portability, durability, and performance.

It’s about as lightweight and portable as a 200W panel can get. It packs down to roughly 2 feet square, which is easy to pack and carry. At the same time, its 23.4 percent efficiency rating is among the best you’ll find for a panel this size.

In terms of toughness, I’ve put one through a ton of mistreatment—I really cannot overstate how rough I am with my gear—and can report that it is as durable as they come. I’ve crushed it in storage, tossed it around a campsite, and left it out through a downpour: It still works just fine.

For most solar power seekers, the Bluetti 200W is a great building block for any solar generator, whether you use a single panel to draw a modest amount of power or chain two to three together to power a more robust setup.

Jackery’s 100-watt bifacial SolarSaga panel is lightweight and thin, making it easy to pack and carry. Its 23 percent efficiency is above average, so you’re getting more energy during quick bursts of sun on a cloudy day. The panel also features a bifacial design, so it can absorb both direct sun and light reflected off the ground behind it. Plus, SolarSaga is arguably the most durable panel I’ve tested. I have a set that I have flung like frisbees, and it’s no worse for wear.

My only gripe is really a general issue with 100-watt panels. The SolarSaga 100W can absorb enough energy to provide a small amount of steady power, but the panel is roughly the same size as Jackery’s SolarSaga 200W panel. (Of course, the 200W costs nearly twice as much, so there’s plenty of reason to go small if you don’t need much power.) As with the Bluetti, though, the option to expand your generator with multiple panels makes the SolarSaga 100W a viable component of any size solar generator–just be prepared to buy a couple if you need more juice.

Typically priced under $300, the BougeRV Arch is an affordable 200W panel with a flexible design that snaps onto the curved tops of vans, boats, and other vehicles. (Though you can set it up anywhere).

It’s lightweight, thin, and durable, with an anti-scratch surface that protects it from damage from passing branches, cleaning brushes, and other threats. At the same time, its 23 percent efficiency rate is comparable to my other recommendations, but high for a flexible panel.

While it’s technically designed for rooftop installation, it packs easily whether flat or rolled and can be set out in the sun like any other portable panel, though it lacks legs for standing and angling. Versatile, durable, and decently high-wattage, it’s a highly versatile pick and budget-friendly to boot.

This more powerful, 350-watt version of my top recommendation is wider and a bit more cumbersome to carry and store, but that’s a fine trade-off if you’re using it to power a converted van or RV. As with the 200W panel, it offers an excellent 23.4 percent efficiency rate, and a 350-watt max charge rate can sustain a light to medium solar setup on its own. It’s also quite durable for a large panel, so it can roll with the punches while living on your vehicle’s roof.

Of course, “less portable” doesn’t mean “non-portable,” though. At 32 pounds, it’s still light enough to move around a campsite or adjust outside your home. And it folds down to a size that isn’t that much larger than the 200W panel, so it is fairly easy to store. (Pro tip for RVers and van campers: I found that a great place to keep mine was beneath the mattress in my camper bulkhead.)

I was already a big fan of the EcoFlow 220W solar panel, but the brand’s redesigned NextGen version is an appreciable leap forward. Its bifacial design gathers more sunlight and increases efficiency to 25 percent, up 23 percent from the previous version: I found that it works especially well on terrain that can reflect light, like sand.

The previous model relied on an attachable stand, but NextGen has built-in stands and is significantly easier to deploy. It also features an integrated solar angle guide that helps you find the best possible position. Meanwhile, the panel is lighter and more portable than its predecessor.

My one gripe is fairly technical: I wish it had 8mm rather than photovoltaic connectors, which are increasingly common in solar generators. That's a small nitpick, though, and it may or may not matter depending on what power station you’re using.

I’ve watched enough of my camping neighbors struggle with setting up solar panels to know that a good, intuitive setup process can make a big difference for a lot of people. Goal Zero’s Boulder 200 Briefcase gobbles up sunlight, but its easy-to-use design is what really shines. As the name suggests, it features a briefcase-style design with a sturdy top handle for easy carrying when folded, plus a hard exterior shell that protects the panels between uses.

When you set it up, the Boulder 200's latching kickstand legs snap into place, slip far less than other panels, and keep the setup from tipping in the wind. When you’re ready to pack it up, magnetized corners hold everything together so it won’t open while you’re carrying it.

While some panels slow to a trickle under cloud cover, the Boulder 200 provides a steady flow of power. With a max capacity of up to 200 watts, you’re getting a lot of power for each deployment. If you want to cut down on camp setup, the Boulder’s snap-in-place legs are hard to beat.

If your solar generator needs to provide a steady stream of power for a hungry campsite or home, you’ll need larger, high-wattage panels that can absorb enough energy to keep the lights on. For maximum potential, I think EcoFlow’s 400W panel is the best high-wattage option that still feels genuinely portable.

The EcoFlow 400W can churn out plenty of power in a surprisingly mobile package, though its 35-pound weight is a bit hefty and cumbersome to move and set up. A grip handle helps with portability, eyelets around the rim let you hang it or tie it in place, and the whole thing is plenty durable. Its efficiency is a few tenths of a percentage point lower than the rest of this list, but it’s still decently efficient. With one of these in good sunlight, you’ll have lots of power flowing. Double it up, and you can max out the charging speed on most power stations.

First and foremost, if a solar panel doesn’t deliver the wattage you need, then it’s not much use to you. A solar panel’s charging capacity, which we casually refer to as wattage (W), indicates the maximum amount of electrical power it can produce from the solar energy it absorbs in an hour. Though all brands advertise panels based on their maximum capacity, the power you get at any given time depends on several factors, including how you position your panel and environmental conditions like cloud cover.

While “mini” handheld solar panels can charge a small device like a phone, I generally recommend focusing on large, foldable panels designed to pair with a portable power station or plug into a controller that connects directly to a vehicle or home electrical system. Generally speaking, these panels start at 100 watts and go up from there. To provide continuous power to an array of devices, especially large appliances, you may need to grab several hundred watts per hour. That means you’ll need either a high-yield panel or several small ones chained together.

For example, if you’re car camping or traveling with a small van setup, a single 100- or 200-watt panel may provide enough power to charge a few devices and maybe keep low-draw items like a string of lights or a portable refrigerator going. If you’re supplying power to a larger van or RV with lots of lights or small electronics, such as a coffee maker or TV, you will need substantially more solar capture capacity–call it 200 to 400 watts. Finally, if you need a solar generator to create a comfortable off-grid living space with uninterrupted power or use a high-draw appliance like an air conditioner, aim for 600-800 watts.

Beyond maximum solar capture, look at a panel’s energy conversion efficiency, which measures how much of the sunlight that hits the panel converts into usable electricity. I recommend looking for portable panels that can deliver 22 percent efficiency or higher. (There are a lot of cheap panels out there: A sub-20 percent efficiency rate should be a big red flag.) A few percentage points might not seem like much, but it may be the difference between getting the power you need before the sun sets or in less-than-ideal weather.

Some portable solar panels are more mobile than others. The panels that can produce the amount of electricity that you need to power many devices and/or appliances are generally quite large–at least a few feet across and a foot or two high. A larger panel allows you to absorb more energy.

Luckily, all of these panels can fold into a more compact size that’s relatively easy to carry and store. They’re also thin and relatively light, and a good model will have a handle or grips that make it easier to move between uses. For example, the Bluetti 200W panel is 6 feet wide when deployed, but folds down to roughly the size of a pizza box, making it much easier to move and pack.

Solar panels have to take a beating. They often get banged up in transit, you’re constantly opening and closing them, and they need to withstand long days sitting out in rain and/or bright sunlight for hours or even days on end. Heavier high-wattage panels tend to be a little more fragile than foldable and/or flexible panels. The further off the beaten path they need to travel, the more important it is to sacrifice wattage for durability.

With most portable solar generators, I’ve found that it’s difficult to generate more than 1,000 watts per hour, no matter how many panels you use. That’s a lot of electricity, especially for a temporary or portable setup, but it can start to feel like a cap when you’re trying to create a backup generator for your home or take it off-grid. Realistically, in those scenarios, you will want to invest in a permanent solar generator setup with heavy-duty panels installed on your roof or a flat patch of land on your property.

Arrange your panels to face the sun as broadly as possible, then adjust them regularly throughout the day to follow the sun’s movement, ensuring the entire panel gets direct sun. If that sounds like too much work, position the panels facing directly south if you’re in the Northern Hemisphere (or north if you’re south of the equator) to get as much sun as possible throughout the day from a single position.

Whether you plan to adjust them or not, never place solar panels close to shade: Even the dappled cover from an overhanging tree branch can significantly diminish the amount of sun your panels absorb.

Technically, you can—sunlight through the clouds still provides solar energy. That said, as with other kinds of shade, cloud cover will impact how much energy your panels absorb.

I’ve used solar panels in sub-optimal sun conditions plenty of times. A bit of overcast will drop your wattage, but you can still get a decent charge if your panels are well positioned.

Nick Hilden is a writer, globetrotter, and jack-of-many-talents who has written gear reviews for the likes of  Runner’s World, Popular Science, Men’s Health, Thrillist, the Daily Beast, the Los Angeles Times, Greatist, and the Manual, and his lifestyle, culture, and tech writing has also appeared in Scientific American, Afar, Salon, Vice, Healthline, and many others. Before entering journalism some 15 years ago, he worked as a bartender, brewery manager, sound engineer, recording and touring musician, cook, teacher, and in a variety of other trades. These days, he lives all over the world, performs music sporadically, and spends a lot of time thinking how to best improve his Honda Element conversion.

#6390. Octopus brains challenge what scientists know about learning and memory

Scientists found a chemical switch that keeps octopus brain connections strong, offering clues to how these animals remember.

Learning changes the connections between brain cells. In animals such as mammals and sea slugs, making those changes last usually requires new proteins.

But octopus brain tissue did something unexpected. Its nerve connections stayed stronger for at least 10 hours, even when researchers blocked the cells from making new proteins.

A gas called nitric oxide may help explain why.

The researchers propose that it keeps the enzyme that produces it active, creating a continuing supply that helps nerve connections stay strong.

Binyamin Hochner’s lab at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem worked with Tal Shomrat’s group at the Ruppin Academic Center.

Ana Luiza Turchetti-Maia carried out most of the experiments, using living brain tissue from common octopuses caught by fishermen off Israel’s Mediterranean coast.

Octopuses solve problems and learn from experience. They have about 500 million nerve cells, giving them the largest nervous system of any animal without a backbone.

A brain region called the vertical lobe helps them learn through sight. It serves a similar role to the hippocampus, which helps people and other vertebrates form long-term memories.

A brief burst of strong activity can strengthen connections between nerve cells in this region.

Scientists call this long-term potentiation, and they think it is one way brains hold on to what they learn.

In 2008, Hochner’s team strengthened connections across the lobe as far as they could go, and the octopuses then struggled to form new long-term memories.

A 2023 map found about 25 million nerve cells in the lobe, most receiving input from just one incoming nerve fiber.

Nitric oxide already looked important: studies in the 1990s found that blocking it disrupted learning through touch and sight.

Later, the team’s tissue tests showed that the enzyme that makes the gas was especially active in the vertical lobe.

For the new study, researchers stimulated incoming nerve fibers with four rapid bursts of 20 pulses each. They then measured the connections’ responses every 30 seconds.

They also used drugs to block nitric oxide synthase, the enzyme that makes the gas. These drugs worked reliably only at much higher doses than researchers usually use.

Scientists often expect nitric oxide to help start the strengthening process. Yet the octopus connections still grew stronger when the blockers were already present.

A thin carbon-fiber sensor placed in the tissue detected a rise in nitric oxide after stimulation.

One roughly calibrated measurement suggested levels about 1,000 times higher than those needed to activate its best-known signaling pathway.

Across five experiments, however, the average rise came later and was less clear.

The researchers suspect that at such high levels, nitric oxide attaches to proteins and changes how they work.

Drugs that targeted its usual signaling pathway did not affect the strengthened connections.

The picture changed when researchers added blockers after the connections had strengthened.

Given 10 minutes later, one drug reduced the strengthened response by an average of 63%, while another reduced it by 82%.

A mirror-image version of a blocker, which cannot block the enzyme, reduced the response by 23%. That smaller drop could have happened by chance.

When researchers washed away the active blockers, the strength returned. One blocker had this effect whether they added it 10 minutes, 90 minutes, or four hours after stimulation.

This suggested that the connections needed an ongoing supply of nitric oxide to keep showing their added strength.

Adding nitric oxide alone did not produce the same lasting effect. A brief dose of a chemical that releases the gas strengthened connections for only a few minutes.

Keeping the tissue in a solution that released the gas caused a large but temporary increase in signal strength.

Prolonged exposure also appeared to damage the nerve fibers.

The team proposes that strong nerve activity starts a loop: the enzyme makes nitric oxide, and nitric oxide keeps the enzyme active.

Hochner said the work shows how different brains can solve a shared problem.

“It is a remarkable example of how evolution can give rise to similar principles of learning and memory through very different biological mechanisms,” Hochner added.

In well-studied examples from other animals, including the sea slug Aplysia, lasting changes in nerve connections depend on new proteins.

Blocking protein production in the mammalian hippocampus prevents the later, lasting phase of strengthening.

The team treated octopus tissue with anisomycin, a drug that blocks protein production, for two and a half hours.

Treatment began half an hour before stimulation, yet the connections stayed stronger for at least 10 hours.

To check that the drug worked, researchers used a glowing marker to label new proteins. Untreated tissue glowed brightly, while treated tissue showed very little glow.

In four lengthy experiments, blocking nitric oxide still reduced connection strength in tissue treated with anisomycin. The nitric oxide system could therefore keep working without new proteins.

When researchers reviewed 11 blocker experiments, they found two patterns. In five, the drug removed an average of 97% of the added strength, acting more than four times faster than in the other six.

After the drug washed away, another round of stimulation made these fast-responding connections about 2.6 times stronger.

It looked as though the earlier strengthening had been erased, allowing it to build again.

In the slower group, the blocker reduced strength by 72%, and further stimulation added almost nothing. Here, the drug seemed to suppress the earlier strengthening without erasing it.

The team thinks the faster response reflected a switch turning off in connections that also started out weaker.

Across the lobe’s five sections, fast responses appeared in the middle, slow ones in the outermost pair, and both in the sections between.

The researchers studied tissue in a dish, not octopuses learning a task.

Most comparisons involved only five or six brain slices per group, and the authors doubt this switch alone explains lasting memories.

Earlier work found that removing the vertical lobe after training did not stop octopuses from remembering learned tasks. The lobe may help animals learn before they store memories elsewhere, where new proteins could still matter.

Cuttlefish may use a different system: their vertical lobe shows no detectable activity of the gas-making enzyme, and connections strengthen on the output side of the circuit.

The team also does not yet know whether nitric oxide keeps its own enzyme active directly or through another enzyme.

Genetic studies show that octopuses and their relatives underwent major changes in how their DNA is arranged.

The authors suggest these changes may have helped turn older mollusk memory chemistry into the nitric oxide switch.

They now want to identify the specific molecular changes involved. That could help explain how this system developed and what role it plays in learning.

The study is published in The Journal of Neuroscience.

#6389. Your voice can now say things you never said

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

AI can replicate a person’s voice. That raises questions about who has the right to use it and what happens when its owner can no longer give consent.

AI technology can create realistic clones of people’s voices. The resulting proliferation of synthetic voices ushers in all sorts of new scenarios, good and bad. “Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type, and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, [of] anybody doing or saying anything,” says Hany Farid, a computer scientist at Dartmouth University.

Some of these voice clones are deeply meaningful to people, as in the cases of people who lost their ability to speak. But voice clones can also cause harm, as with scams and deepfakes. And some uses fall into murky gray zones, such as voice clones that “speak” after a person has passed away. What happens to a person’s digital voice after they’re gone?

In this episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me, hear more from Farid, as well as from a former hospital chaplain and AI researcher, and from Jules Rodriguez, a man who communicates with a voice clone. You’ll also hear about a choice Jules made about what will happen to his voice once he’s gone.

Laura Sanders: What’s a voice you like to listen to?

Kate Nilson: That is a great question. I hope my students don’t listen to this. I was having Snoop Dogg read their assignments to me the other day, just because I thought it was funny. But I don’t know if I would say that’s my favorite.

Sanders: That’s speech language pathologist and professor Kate Nilson. And if you’re wondering, this is a real, legitimate thing that anyone can do.

Snoop Dogg audio: Vector mathematics. Think about a car trip. Your displacement from your starting point is a vector.

Snoop Dogg: I’m glad to be the voice of reason so you can focus better, understand more, and enjoy listening to the internet in the voice of Snoop Dogg.

Sanders: Welcome to The Deep End, Talk To Me. In this episode, we’re stepping out of the lab and into the new digital world we all live in. We’re going to get into some of the good, bad and strange scenarios that come up when voices can be cloned and let loose in the world. Let’s talk about it.

[voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? Hi. Do you want to talk? That added layer of it being you. Hello? Your voice. Hi. Your voice is you.

Sanders: As we’ve heard in earlier episodes, ultra-realistic voice clones can be extremely meaningful to people who can no longer speak.

Jules Rodriguez: So when I first heard my cloned voice, it felt like I reappeared. When my wife first heard it, she cried because of how close it sounded like me before I lost my voice. I knew of the potential of this technology at that moment.

Sanders: These digital copies of voices have restored connections to their loved ones.

MA Fernandez: You know, the first thing he played for me, I was like chills all over.

Patrick Darling: The first time I performed with the AI voice, I was surprised how physically connected I felt with it.

Sanders: These voice clones have been transformative for people who have lost the ability to talk. But the existence of realistic digital copies of voices has effects that ripple farther out into society.

Hany Farid: So here’s where sort of state of the art is. Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, anybody doing or saying anything.

Sanders: That’s Hany Farid. He’s a computer scientist at Dartmouth College and cofounder of Get Real Security, a firm that sorts real from fake. I called him to ask how these voice clones have changed our world.

Farid: If you had asked me, I don’t know, five years ago, is this possible? I would say, yeah, maybe, but not anytime soon. And then all of a sudden, boom, it just came out of nowhere.

Sanders: This shift happened in a very, very short amount of time, and it has big implications, both good and bad.

Farid: And so we are living in, I think, in equal parts an exciting time and a terrifying time, and somehow those are coexisting.

Sanders: Farid tells me about some of his research, which asks people to decide whether something, like a voice or a video, is real.

Farid: My bread and butter is developing technologies to distinguish real from fake. And we work with media outlets and law enforcement and courts, et cetera. But one of the questions you always want to ask when you’re in my business is, well, do you need the mathematics and the computation? Just let somebody listen to it or look at it. And can they tell the difference?

Sanders: It turns out they cannot. In laboratory tests, people can’t reliably say whether a voice they hear was created by a machine or by a real living, breathing person.

Farid: It’s essentially like they’re flipping a coin.

Sanders: But there’s another, even higher bar for voice clones to pass. That’s whether they can mimic a specific person well enough to slip by undetected.

Farid: The other question too is what if I, for example, play a real voice sample of your voice, Laura, and then I clone your voice using my favorite AI cloning technology, and then I type something and I get you to say something, and I play those two samples to somebody, and I don’t ask them if it’s real/fake. I say, is this the same person? Is the AI not only able to make something that is natural, but is it identity preserving?

Sanders: Okay, give it a try yourself. Is this the same person?

[Sanders voice clone] And how about now? Is this the same person?

Farid: And when you ask them, is it the same person? They say yes, which means the AI has figured out with roughly 20 seconds or so of your voice how to make their AI sound like you, which is mind-blowing.

Sanders: In the earlier episodes of this season, you’ve heard examples of the good that’s been created by these technological leaps. In many cases, that good comes because these voices are both extremely realistic and extremely good at sounding like a specific person. People want their voice to sound like theirs.

Farid: People with ALS can speak with what sounds like their voice. We’ve seen beautiful examples of that. Translation, right? We can now translate things in real time from any language and it’ll sound like you. I’ve made videos of myself speaking any language I want and it sounds like me, and it’s amazing. It’s really cool.

Sanders: These new ways to connect are very impressive, but as with any technology, these powerful realistic auditory dupes can be repurposed to cause harm.

Farid: Some pretty bad stuff’s happening, right? So let’s just go through a few of these. So first, you’re seeing massive types of fraud. Everything from romance scams to people calling parents and saying your kids have been taken, pay a ransom, to geopolitics. People are getting on calls with who they think are leaders of other countries, and it’s not. It’s a deepfake. It’s an AI-generated voice or face.

Sanders:  What Farid is saying feels especially relevant right now. I’m recording this episode in the fall of 2026, and midterm elections in the U.S. are upon us. Political ads are everywhere. Some of these ads use deepfake audio and video to make opponents say or do things they never did. Here are a few recent examples of deepfakes compiled by the New York Times.

[Audio] Hi, I’m Zohran Mamdani and I’m Kathy Hochul and together, we’re making New York, don’t say affordable. I’m voting for Hochul because she basically gave me an early retirement. They stopped prosecuting people for crime, so now I get to sit back and play Candy Crush all day. Is New York getting a little expensive? I’m Kathy Hochul, and I’ve got just the thing. Clinton lover, Trump hater.

Farid: When you can steal somebody’s likeness, their voice, and their face, you can do some damage. We’re seeing people doing content credential resets at companies. They call up and say, oh, I’m employee X. Will you reset my credential? That’s how they’re now attacking companies. We’re seeing North Korean IT workers penetrating Fortune 500 companies by disguising their voices and their accents and their identities. So lots of bad things, and not unpredictably bad.

Sanders: There are romance scams, political scams, employment scams, money scams of all sorts. Farid was even involved in one himself.

Farid: My voice was cloned by an attacker. I was working a very sensitive case with an attorney. Not many people knew about it. And he got a call from my phone number in my voice talking about the case. And after about three minutes, got suspicious, hung up, called me back. Wasn’t me.

Sanders: Bigger picture, we’ve reached a point where it’s safe to say we can no longer automatically trust digital versions of other people. That applies to the images and sounds on my computer screen as I talked with Farid. Maybe this 2-D picture and sound coming from my laptop is a fake.

Farid: So this two-dimensional version that you and I are sharing now, all right, I can’t control that. That can be stolen. The three-dimensional is right now still me, right? We don’t have the robots that can mimic us. Yet is the end of that sentence.

Sanders: So my interview with Farid was alarming. There are parallels here to any new technology, though. Today, people talk about brain rot from junk online. But remember that television was also going to rot our brains.

[Audio] Its content affects us. So does the sheer weight of the hours we watch.

Sanders: Phones today are the downfall of society, but actual wired telephones encountered really similar resistance when they first started appearing in homes.

[Audio] In Chicago, Sharon Krall’s 15-year-old daughter Angie got so addicted to one teen talk line, she ran up an $850 bill in one month.

Sanders: No big technological advance has escaped this fear.

[Audio] We need teachers who are deeply concerned about how the modern media of communication are changing education.

Sanders: Electricity, bicycles, railways, novels, even the printing press all had their skeptics. So this fear of the new thing has been around a long time. Are synthetic voices created by AI any different? Here’s Karina Nagin from Bridging Voice.

Nagin: Taking off my Bridging Voice hat and just as like a human being in the world, I think there’s a lot of things about AI that I’m very concerned. Deepfakes, the ability to make videos and audio that sound and look just like someone saying something that they’re not saying, I think is a huge, huge concern to our news and public information.

Sanders: Nagin then pivots back to the good, the possibilities here.

Nagin: And then I put on my little hat in my space that I am like, this is how we can harness this to impact people’s lives in our space right now. And I think both conversations need to happen.

Sanders: It occurs to me that I’m seeing the ends of the spectrum here. The stories Farid told me were awful. And the stories that Jules and Casey and others have told me were really, really life-changingly good. Yet these ends of the spectrum are the easy ones. The ones you can look at and say, that’s a horrible way to use this technology. Or that is a powerful and good way to use a voice clone. Between those two poles is the middle ground. That’s the place where Snoop explains cell biology.

[Audio] The membrane separates the material outside the cell.

Sanders: Good, because it’s helping people learn more about mitochondria and who couldn’t use more of that in their lives. Bad, because Snoop never actually said those words, and it’s weird to pretend otherwise.

[Audio] The artists of the Renaissance said that man’s main concern should be for man.

Sanders: There are deepfakes of the late great physicist Richard Feynman delivering famous lectures.

[Audio] The problem is the laws of physics themselves. Let me start with something basic. The next star over from us is called Proxima Centauri.

Sanders: Good because it introduces some amazing physics to people who would otherwise scroll past? Bad because it’s somewhat disrespectful and possibly inaccurate? There aren’t easy answers here. This murky middle gets even murkier with the invention of griefbots. Those are digital versions of people who have passed away. And that means that special voices can keep talking to us long after the body that created them is gone.

I read a poignant post online written by a guy who had lost his dad after years of dementia. He missed his dad’s voice, he wrote, so he cloned it. He paid for the starter pack, submitted three minutes of his dad’s audio, and he wrote, quote, a few minutes later, I had a scarily accurate clone of my dead father’s voice. He goes on to write, quote, my family and I had a good cathartic cry upon hearing the results. I had his cloned voice read the Lord’s Prayer as well as ‘Twas the Night before Christmas. Just hearing his simulated voice again is such a blessing and is helping me in the grief process. End quote.

There are lots of companies now offering this exact thing. A casual search online gets me to a company that sells chats with dead loved ones. There’s a big orange button to click that says bring them back to life. A 2024 documentary called “Eternal You” follows the stories of people as they grapple with this idea. Here’s a little bit of the trailer.

[Audio] We are on the verge of a new era. Hi. It’s like, it’s the funniest thing. It’s like, what’s the first thing you say to someone that’s dead? Like, welcome back.

Sanders: Griefbots or digital avatars of loved ones offer a bridge from the past to the present, a way to remember vividly. But they are also a denial, of sorts, that all life must come to an end.

[Audio] And what I can tell you is that AI really is changing the way that we interact with death.

Sanders: That’s from a 2025 TEDx talk from Dylan Thomas Doyle. He’s a former hospital chaplain, current academic researcher at Northwestern University and self-described philosophy bro. His work explores death and AI.

[Audio] Imagine that you are at a funeral, and you’re sitting there in silent reflection, and all of a sudden, on the back screen in the auditorium, a woman’s face appears. And it’s the face of a woman named Marina. And her hologram, she starts talking to you, and she starts asking you how you’re doing today. And you answer her, and then you ask her a question back. And she responds as if she is still there.

Sanders: I called Doyle to ask about the implications of using technology this way.

Doyle: It was on my radar as a chaplain and a technology researcher, I started thinking through, well, what is the actual impact of this technology on people? So what is it like to hear the voice, in the context of this podcast, the voice of, say, your father who’s passed away while you’re actively grieving their death? And they’re not just repeating what they said or a journal entry in their voice, but like, creating new stories and new relationships through their voice. It gives a lot of people existential ick, is what I’ve heard. And that’s something that I really, I’m curious about.

Sanders: There’s tension here, Doyle tells me.

Doyle: So there’s this push force where you’re like, this is not right. We don’t have the narrative or cultural script to understand what’s going on there. But then as people are beginning to use it, there’s a comfort that comes out of it. So we’re working in that tension space between this comfort that comes, then you’re still dealing with this push away from this technology of it just being weird in a way that people are still grappling with language, I think, to describe.

Sanders: It’s not clear how these types of interactions might affect grieving. They could help or they could hurt.

Doyle: There is this tension between more healthy continuing bonds. So continuing that relationship by, say, writing letters to your dead loved one or, you know, talking out loud to them and continuing that relationship in a positive way that moves us through a healthy grief process and a grief journey. Or hanging on to our relationship with that person to a degree where we can’t actually do any sort of moving on.

Sanders: Doyle points out that we don’t have good data on how many people might be using griefbots.

Doyle: I just don’t want us to get ahead of ourselves when it comes to people like using these. So the capability to do everything we’ve talked about with griefbots is there. But the actual use cases of individuals in their homes using this, it’s still pretty unclear about the adoption of those technologies.

Sanders: But even if griefbots aren’t widespread, the questions they raise aren’t going away. These voices are blurring the lines between a memory and a present-day experience, between alive and dead. Here’s Karina Nagin again.

Nagin: It’s an interesting conversation that we’re having right now of what happens to your voice once you pass away. Some people are starting to integrate this into their wills or their sort of final wishes of, do you want your voice to be able to speak at your own memorial service?

Do you want to have messages saved in your voice that are for your child at graduation that they listen to? Who and when can use that? I think that these are things that people are starting to think about. Who owns your voice? Can your children use your voice to write a speech for their children’s graduation? Or do you want that voice to be deleted once you pass away? Very tricky questions.

Sanders: Rules about who can use voice clones are all over the place. Regulations vary by state and by country, and even companies have their own individual policies in place. There are no clear guidelines, and that makes sense given how young this technology is. Conversations about digital voices and how to use them are inherently very personal. There are as many different takes as there are people. I asked MA if she and Jules had talked about this.

MA: I love that question. Both of us love this question because it’s so important. And we talked about it before he got the trache. Like when he was already using the voice, we were talking about different things in bed at night. And he said, you know, I have a very clear request that my voice like dies with me, basically, that, you know, I ask that you don’t use the voice to keep me alive in any way,  that there’s no… And I was like, 100 percent clear. I hadn’t even thought about that. But yeah, it would make sense to be like, I miss him so much. I want to, whatever or. But no, as far as we’re concerned, his voice dies when he does. And his voice will live on in whatever videos or things we captured, whatever he’s left us intentionally. And that’s as far as that goes.

Sanders: So when Jules is gone, his voice will be gone too. But right now is a different story.

MA:  Well back in 2021, I was writing an Instagram post about something. It was him playing with Skylar in the backyard while he was already like, you know, had trouble with everything, but he was doing what he could. And I asked him like, you know, what, what do you want to caption it? And he just said that, right here, right now phrase, something else, and like right here, right now. And it became our family mantra. It became something that we wanted to just to share and in both a sense of like do the things that you want to do.

And also something that’s always been big for Jules that I’ve admired him articulate is that it’s not just about, oh, just go forward and do all the things and like suck the marrow out of life. It’s like just also, like, settle. Like it doesn’t have to be that extreme, you know. There’s a beautiful thing about that presence and that settling in. And again, with ALS being something where you’re given the diagnosis, which is terminal, it’s basically a death sentence. Most people are given, you know, two to five years. You don’t know where you’re going to fall in that. We’ve known people that have passed away in a year and a half. We’ve known people that are six years in like Jules, but can still kind of walk around, speak a little bit. ALS touches everybody really differently. So you really don’t know what’s coming. And there’s a lot of like forward thinking that you can do that detaches you from being in your life. So how are you here? And then there’s a lot of backwards, you know, reminiscing and grieving about all the things we’ve lost and how we wish things were different. But then that also takes you out of like this moment right now and this part of your story.

Sanders: This part of the story is the important part. Right here, right now.

On the next and final episode of The Deep End, Talk to Me. We’re going to look at what’s next for Jules and Casey and what’s next for the science racing to give voices back to people.

Vikash Gilja: We can see all the pieces coming together. All of the emphasis, capital, quite frankly, talent focused on advancing AI techniques and technologies. You know, our little corner can benefit from it, right? These tools weren’t available even five years ago.

Sanders: What’s next for the human voice?

Samantha Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

This is The Deep End, Talk to Me. I’m Laura Sanders. If you like this podcast tell your friends and leave us a review. It helps the show a lot. Send us your questions and your comments at podcasts@sciencenews.org.

Sanders: The Deep End is a production of Science News. It’s based on original reporting by me, Laura Sanders. This episode was produced and mixed by Ella Rowen. Our project manager is Ashley Yeager. #6388. More parents say no to vitamin K shots, and bleeding cases in babies are rising

Vitamin K deficiency rose among U.S. infants as fewer newborns received the shot that helps prevent dangerous bleeding.

Most babies in the United States get a vitamin K shot soon after birth to protect them from serious bleeding. But a growing share are missing it.

A new study found that recorded diagnoses of vitamin K deficiency more than tripled among babies between 2017 and 2025.

Diagnoses of bleeding linked to the deficiency more than quadrupled.

Elizabeth Wolf, a children’s doctor at Children’s Hospital of Richmond at VCU, led the study. She is also an associate professor in VCU’s Department of Pediatrics.

“We knew from prior studies that vitamin K refusal had been increasing in the U.S., and we wanted to learn if there were any real-life consequences of this trend,” Wolf said.

Vitamin K helps blood form clots that stop bleeding. Having too little is called vitamin K deficiency.

Babies start life with very little of this vitamin. Only small amounts pass from a mother to her baby before birth.

Newborns also lack the established gut bacteria that help produce vitamin K. Breast milk contains only small amounts, too.

The American Academy of Pediatrics has advised giving every newborn a vitamin K shot since 1961. The shot cuts the rate of bleeding that starts a week or more after birth by 98%.

Without enough vitamin K, a baby may struggle to stop bleeding. Doctors call this vitamin K deficiency bleeding.

One form starts between two days and one week after birth. Babies may bruise or bleed from the belly button.

Another form starts between one week and six months. It can affect breastfed babies who miss the shot and babies whose bodies have trouble taking in vitamin K.

Among babies with this later form, 30% to 60% have bleeding inside the skull. This can cause seizures, lasting brain damage, or death.

The team used Cosmos, a large collection of health records from places that use Epic software.

It brings together records from more than 2,300 hospitals and 50,000 clinics and other care sites, with names and other identifying details removed.

The study included about 11 million babies up to six months old who received care between 2017 and 2025.

All had been born at 35 weeks of pregnancy or later.

The team checked when doctors first found low vitamin K or bleeding linked to it, and whether babies also had bleeding inside the skull or brain.

The number of births in the records roughly doubled during the study. To make a fair comparison, the team worked out how many cases occurred for every 100,000 babies.

In 2017, 97.7% of newborns had a recorded vitamin K shot. By 2025, that fell to 95.0%, so the share without a recorded shot had more than doubled.

Low vitamin K rose from 11.8 to 37.3 cases per 100,000 babies. Bleeding linked to low vitamin K rose from 24.0 to 107.4 cases per 100,000.

Both rates were highest in 2025. That year, a little more than one in every 1,000 babies born in the records had bleeding linked to low vitamin K.

Doctors found most cases during the first week of life. That was true for 62% of babies with low vitamin K and 88% of those with bleeding.

About 97% of all babies in the study had a record of getting the shot. But among babies with low vitamin K, only 39.7% did.

Among babies with bleeding linked to low vitamin K, only 19.2% had a recorded shot. Babies without a recorded shot were a small part of the full group, yet they made up most of the bleeding cases.

Some babies also had bleeding inside the skull or brain. This affected 6.9% of babies with low vitamin K and 2.4% of those with bleeding linked to it.

An earlier study found that the share of newborns who missed the shot rose from 2.9% in 2017 to 5.2% in 2024. A study in Sweden also linked missing the shot to bleeding in babies.

Wolf’s team pointed to growing distrust of public health after the COVID-19 pandemic. They also noted more doubts about vaccines and more worries about medical care given to newborns.

The authors wrote that the vitamin K shot “may be a victim of its own success.” Because it has made this bleeding problem rare, many families may not know how dangerous it can be.

“Similar to the recent measles outbreaks, we are seeing the real-world implications of growing mistrust of doctors and public health professionals,” Wolf said.

“We need clear messaging from all levels of public health about the benefits of vitamin K administration for newborns.”

Some countries give vitamin K by mouth, either as the usual choice or as another option. These include France, Germany, the Netherlands, Switzerland, and Canada.

Vitamin K taken by mouth can work less well than the shot at preventing bleeding that starts later.

Still, the authors said U.S. doctors may need to consider it as a second choice if more parents refuse the shot.

The study cannot prove that fewer shots caused more bleeding. It also left out babies who received care outside health systems using Epic, so it may not show the full picture across the country.

Some records may have listed the wrong diagnosis or missed bleeding inside the skull. The team also looked for other reasons that might explain the rise.

Breastfeeding rates changed little over the past decade. Diseases that can cause low vitamin K, such as cystic fibrosis, did not become more common.

Wolf noted that these problems could keep rising if more parents refuse the shot.

“We need to better understand why parents are refusing vitamin K and what can be done to improve the uptake of this important medication,” she said.

The full study was published in the journal JAMA Pediatrics.
