#6332. How to Sing Karaoke Every Night, in Every Borough of New York City

In 1968, Daisuke Inoue decided he was going to be in two places at once. A musician who played in a backup band working Kobe’s nightlife circuit, Inoue soundtracked the evenings of soulful salarymen whom he befriended. With drums as his instrument of choice because “all you have to do is hit them,” he turned those relationships into business, arranging entertainment for their other engagements. As the legend goes, he couldn’t make it out to a gig he had booked at an insurance company’s trade show, so he invented the next best thing. Combining a standard eight-track tape player used in car stereos, a microphone, an amplifier, and a 100-yen coin slot, he placed his ghost in the machine, which he fashioned into the Juke 8. Inoue’s device—the progenitor to the modern-day karaoke machine—was a success.

A more rigorous history might question whether Inoue really invented the first such machine or whether that credit belongs to electronics manufacturer Shigeichi Negishi’s Sparko Box a decade earlier. But the meteoric takeoff of karaoke has soared far past its humble—and slightly murky—origins. A portmanteau of the Japanese words kara, meaning empty, and oke, meaning orchestra, karaoke evokes both loneliness and collective belonging. Nearly 60 years on, we still root for the little machine that could—and all the brave singers who bare their heart through age-revealing ballads and club classics.

An impassioned rendition of Celine Dion’s “It's All Coming Back to Me Now” transpires at Beats Karaoke Cafe in Williamsburg

Perhaps nowhere is karaoke’s full breadth more on display than in New York City, where, on one side, you’ve got lounges complete with floor-to-ceiling video walls and speakers with built-in auto-tune capabilities and, on the other, decades-old dives whose performers are as much an institution as the establishment.

A karaoke spot is the one place where post-prom dates, wedding parties, and career performers alike gather to spend their time and money on gloriously subpar entertainment, entirely without irony. When you’re the one behind the mic, it becomes something mythic—a reprieve from the passive consumption dominating much of the city’s nightlife. Tally up the past year’s most recent headlines, and you’d get the impression that we’re becoming less fun—we’re having less sex, drinking less alcohol, going to fewer parties, and hosting fewer of our own. The karaoke bar might be one of the last, thriving places in New York where we wait half an hour to openly embarrass ourselves, and for that it’s well worth our nights out.

With the hundreds of sing-along nights and 30-plus specialized bars in New York City listed on trackers like Karaoke Crowd, there was no way we’d be able to cover them all. So we visited one place a day for a week, crisscrossing the boroughs for a taste of the city’s diversity. We commenced our week in Koreatown, where some-dozen private rooms are conveniently concentrated on a single street, and continued our spree at an Irish pub on the Upper East Side, where shouting for sport and song are one in the same. We hit up a Staten Island dive of devoted locals and a year-old Astoria restaurant where, once the Tagalog ballads have begun, you must push the plate away and join in. These watering holes, old and new, are living proof of the many shapes karaoke takes and the unifying joy of belting it out together, even when so much else threatens to divide us.

A singer takes the stage at Iggy’s on the Upper East Side to perform Billy Joel and Elton John’s “Piano Man”

We began the week where many end it, on the dense corridor of West 32nd Street between Sixth and Seventh Avenues. Along this stretch of Koreatown, karaoke bars, podiatrists, escape rooms, and coworking spaces stack atop one another. Our crawl started at Gagopa, whose BYOB policy is a favorite among the large-group partiers and Midtown corporate crowd for fast-tracking camaraderie. The bar eluded us at first, not for a lack of signage but for its location on the fourth story of its building, and the search more or less provided a template for our crawl: a ride up an elevator the size of an airplane lavatory and head-scratching decor. At Gagopa’s sister bar, 32 Karaoke, this last item consists of Polaroids of visiting groups on the walls—the very karaoke canon that, once you’ve stepped through its doors, you become part of.

Anticipatory staircases aside, no amount of symbolic literacy can prepare you for a K-town elevator panel. Despite its abundance of labeled buttons, deciphering them only makes things more confusing. To reach Space Karaoke Bar and Lounge, for instance, you have to avoid accidentally ending up at Space Ping Pong, one of two Space sports bars, or the Space golf simulator. Take it as a sign to stop trying to make sense of things and just embrace the ride.

Across the street, Chorus Karaoke Lounge has a clubbier feel, with a purple-and-blue-lit bar. To the left is a hallway of private rooms, lined with porthole window portraits of Madonna, Morrissey, Elvis, and all the other greats. On the evening we visited, only one karaoke room at the end of the white hallway was occupied—by a lone singer crooning to himself. It may well have been a strict weekly ritual, the first step in a vocal warm-up regimen. “I sing, therefore I am,” read a sign near its entrance as we left, a reminder that although thinking may be proof of existence, song is proof of life. —Skyli Alvarez & Kat Chen

Pianist Mark Benjamin, left, accompanies performers at Sid Gold's Request Room on 26th Street, which has additional locations in Detroit, Nashville, and Washington, DC

In the liminal space between Chelsea and Flatiron, Sid Gold’s Request Room is a bit of an outlier. Sandwiched between an empty office space and halal buffet, its old-timey façade simply reads “piano” and “karaoke.” Both await you in the spacious piano lounge, tucked behind a pair of velvet curtains at the back of the cocktail bar.

We arrived around 9 p.m. and slid into one of the alcoved booths closest to the stage, a small black platform beside the bar centerpiece: a Baldwin baby grand. As we settled in, a singer, backdropped by pianist Mark Benjamin’s harmonies, wrapped up his performance to a crowd of now four; he then came to take our order. Fortunately, others trickled in: tourists and their New Yorker friends; Tuesday-night regulars; a dog named Henry. Many, as we learn, were here for Benjamin's performance—and succor.

As we came to find out later on in the week, karaoke works better in numbers, but Sid Gold’s makes the case for a small yet mighty group. A particularly moody evocation of Chris Isaak’s “Wicked Game,” prefaced by the singer’s memories of angst-ridden high school years, drew out lower-than-low notes. In what could only be described as a shouty but otherwise cheery cover of “Back to Black,” each verse’s forceful delivery was more unpredictable than the last. At some point Benjamin called upon someone named Eric, who kicked off his flip-flops to sing “Part of Your World,” a method for getting into character (one can only assume) that would be frowned upon everywhere else but here.

If you think you can evade the stage, Benjamin will make sure you get on up there. He’ll harmonize and improvise riffs even if he’s never heard the song (or wants you to think this); pause to match your pace; and convince you that it was made for you to sing. —S.A.

I was immediately given the cousin treatment when I passed the threshold of Barkada Social Club. In case there was any ambiguity about the cultural identity of this Astoria restaurant and bar, let it be known I walked into Bruno Mars’s “Risk It All,” with plates of lumpia and kwek kwek covering the tables. It was a good night to come—Barkada NYC, a separate but similarly named LGBTQ+ Filipinx community group, hosts its monthly Kikay Konek karaoke event here. Joey, a queer-affirming physical therapist by day and programming coordinator with Barkada NYC, was my gregarious host for the night. When I asked them about encountering struggles with finding kindred souls, they gave me a considerate look before breaking out into a smile and saying, “I honestly can’t relate.” This came as no surprise as I watched them record the “Toxic” floor routine for BNYC’s Instagram before rushing off to plan next month’s programming, discuss bringing BYNC to the Bronx, finalize plans for a hike three weekends away, and introduce me to their boyfriend. It takes a social whirlwind like that to bring together a collective of members from across all five boroughs, plus exotic reaches like Tenafly, New Jersey. The crowd is in constant flux, peeling off and joining in depending on what the song queue has in store. The one exception to the rule is when someone requests Jesse Zaragoza’s “Bakit Pa,” a sweeping Tagalog ballad from the ’90s about unrequited love that brings everybody rushing to the fore. “It’s like our national anthem,” Joey says. —K.C.

Tim sings at Steiny's Pub in Staten Island

At Sid Gold's, patrons are more than ready to be called up for a harmonized performance

At the site of the former Mayfair Bar and Grill, a favorite among St. George’s queer patrons in the 1950s and ’60s, Steiny’s Pub was once a low-key gay bar turned sports joint that now exists somewhere between the two. It’s fitting for a borough that’s often the butt of the joke, cloaked in its perceived suburban isolation, though an eight-minute walk from the Staten Island Ferry makes it surprisingly less difficult to reach from Manhattan than one might assume. We passed a small group of local 30-somethings smoking near the entrance and, once inside the dive, encountered a lively emcee who goes by the DJ name Nazz Raidience. We’re quickly singled out for not being regulars and handed a Sharpie and clipboard to add to a queue that Nazz only loosely followed.

As co-owner John Michael works behind the bar, a few seated patrons watch tennis and baseball while others belt it out to their backs. The L-shaped booth seating next to the DJ setup operates as the stage. Most who perform adhere to genre: bar patron Dia’s heavy metal numbers by Kittie are complete with death growls, Connor does Eminem with breakdancing and triple-threat delivery, and others insist on 1980s ballads. Nazz shepherds the queue at an auctioneer’s pace, sometimes joining in and always poking fun, calling upon you to spin the prize wheel that could lead to a free drink or 10 push-ups. Although they host karaoke nights across the city, Steiny’s is their favorite for the many different worlds it attracts, and they'll convince you to stay for the ferry sailors who, post-shift, are said to come singing around 2 a.m. When it became clear to us this would not be the night, we left without sea chanteys in our hearts but with a better understanding of the appeal of the city’s least-populated borough. —S.A.

Performing karaoke cosplaying as Shadow the Hedgehog, hands full with impulse purchases from Comic Con’s artist alley, is my penance. I had postponed this visit for too long, leaving me with no option but to come as I was. Bronx Beer Hall is nestled within a larger food hall in the historic Italian neighborhood of Arthur Avenue (please, try the veal). By the time Friday karaoke night is in full swing, all of the surrounding businesses are fully closed. From the outside the telltale sign that anything is happening is the ambient trail of music. Channel an ’80s B-movie slasher victim, and follow the noise into the darkness. Upon emerging into the light, you’ll see a hallway lined with T-shirts printed with lines like “Call it gravy, not sauce!” or “I’m not a gynecologist, but I’ll take a look.” As for the music selection, it’s what you’d expect from a generationally eclectic crowd. There’s tender performances of Bon Jovi and Air Supply following the crowd-rousing momentum of “NUEVAYoL” by a man wearing a snapback with what was certainly a record-breaking number Yankees logos embroidered on the design. Every three songs the DJ would queue up 50 Cent’s “In Da Club” to announce yet another birthday, and BBH turned out to be just the kind of place where an unrelated 24-year-old and 40-year-old blow out their candles together. Being Shadow the Hedgehog did not go unnoticed either. Our millennial bartender who grew up playing the original Sonic games requested “Live and Learn,” the main theme song of Sonic Adventure 2. As I took in the lyrics for the first time on the TV screen, I lived and I learned. —K.C.

The karaoke room at Iggy’s becomes rowdier as the night progresses

This Irish karaoke bar was our first reporting excursion, and it established a curious precedent. Between its Upper East Side location, Gaelic rafters, and portraits of 27 Club musicians, the place seemed tailor-made for Xennial dads. We assumed butt rock was inevitable and hedged our bets on at least one rendition of Hinder’s “Lips of an Angel.”

My hunch came from Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick, specifically her theories of homosociality: the nonsexual bonds between people of the same sex. Spend enough time at karaoke, and you’ll notice that “Lips of an Angel” is almost always performed as a duet between two men. For the uninitiated, the song imagines a phone call between a singer and an ex he still quietly yearns for, wishing she were there instead of the “girl” in the next room. Sure enough, two friends took up the mantle. Maybe it was simply a fun song to sing; maybe karaoke offered a safe conduit for expressing something else. We encountered the song at every subsequent karaoke night, always sung by two people of the same sex.

While some bars use online queues for song requests, attendees go analog at Iggy’s

As a week of karaoke draws to a close, you will come to find specific crowds come in waves. First come those who learned to love performance in youth-theater productions, usually in duos or trios, and take their sing-alongs seriously. Then there are the harder-to-place groups: coworkers, reunited friends, or couples using karaoke as a social buffer. Next come the balladeers and lone yearners, eager to broadcast exactly how they’re feeling, followed by the humble soloists who know they’re good and have nothing to prove. Finally, the rowdy late-night crowd of after-partiers spills in, at worst hogging the mic and at best uniting an entire room.

In our five hours at Iggy’s, the former theater kids delivered truly spectacular covers of “Defying Gravity,” the Irishmen shouted Irish pub songs, and the soloists flirted by way of song choice. Three dollars grant you one song that you select from an impressively up-to-date binder and scrawl onto a piece of paper, then the waiting game begins. “We just met in the photo booth” is how one performer introduced a B-side from The Cure, an effort to woo over a stranger who he knew shared at least one common interest. Karaoke gives singers permission to say what they otherwise cannot or will not admit, though the message is rarely subtle. —S.A. & K.C.

Though Seventh Heaven's evenings often begin with film screenings, watch parties, and other community events, they always end in karaoke

During a week when we spent every other waking hour thinking about karaoke-ing, we sometimes looked past dives and private rooms for other ambitious reinventions, like on a boat; in a taxicab en route to the airport; or in an East Williamsburg apartment turned karaoke rental. Still, it’s ultimately the most obvious spots that draw the crowds. Take Williamsburg’s Beats Karaoke Cafe, an eight-minute walk from the Bedford Avenue station, with a rustic bar on the first floor, leading to a hall of private rooms that continue downstairs. We eventually wound our way into film production coordinator Natalie’s group of eight, who told us this was their go-to whenever they “want to add a little divorced dad rock to the night,” and we had caught them testing out new material. Still, they made their way through classics like The Cranberries’ “Zombie” and “Time of My Life,” while also executing many Dirty Dancing lifts.

Farther along the L train, it was only appropriate that we ended up at a bar named Seventh Heaven. We were among the youngest crowd by far, at least in taste. Karaoke-goers swarmed the stage and fluently rattled off the romaji lyrics of “A Cruel Angel’s Thesis,” the theme song to ’90s anime Neon Genesis Evangelion. This bar gets its crowd, with a cocktail menu filled with allusions to the fandom, like the Apothecary’s Negroni fashioned after popular light novel series The Apothecary Diaries, or my own drink, the Boy’s Love G&T, which is named after the popular fiction genre that focuses on the romance between male characters. Turns out, there are plenty of effusive ex–theater kids who understand the assignment.

The DJ cued up our request, “Viva la Vida.” From the vantage point of the stage, the outstretched hands of the crowd looked not unlike the Eugène Delacroix painting of the Revolution of 1848, which Coldplay used as cover art their 2008 album Viva la Vida or Death and All His Friends. A notably resigned wedding party lingered at the back of the audience, while city newcomers hailing from nearby venue House of Yes gleefully accepted our mic to unleash a few verses. The karaoke-goers had in the very least not given up on tonight. —S.A. & K.C.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6331. The Sky Today on Saturday, November 7: Venus meets the Moon

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Venus is already primed to capture attention above the eastern horizon before sunrise. This morning, the Moon passes 1.1° due south of Earth’s sister planet at 7 A.M. EST.

You can easily catch the pair an hour before sunrise, some 6° high in the east and climbing as the sky begins to brighten. Magnitude –4.5 Venus blazes to the upper left of the delicate crescent Moon, whose western limb is just barely lit as the Sun sets across the lunar nearside. Look for earthshine on the already-shadowed portion of Luna’s face, as sunlight bouncing off Earth lights it up.

Near Venus is another bright light: This is Spica, Virgo’s alpha star, shining at magnitude 1.0 and also lingering in the morning twilight. This morning it lies 1.3° northeast of Venus, with the planet and star roughly side by side above the horizon. Use this view as an anchor point: By the 10th, Venus will have moved to stand due west of this star and will be located to its upper right.

Sunrise: 6:36 A.M.Sunset: 4:51 P.M.Moonrise: 5:01 A.M.Moonset: 3:40 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (1%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

#6330. The 6 Best Paper Shredders Destroy Sensitive Documents in Seconds

Get rid of personal data, credit cards, medical information, old IDs, and CDs securely … by turning them into confetti.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

There are two types of people who have a paper shredder at home: Most folks are what I like to think of as “casual” shredders, who shred paper bank statements, medical notices, snail mail credit-card or life insurance offers from time to time. Home-office workers, gig workers and freelancers, small business owners, retirees, and anyone wary of identity theft. Then there are the “serious” shredders—doctors, lawyers, accountants, government workers, or anyone who regularly handles no-one-else-needs-to-know information—who may need to obliterate foot-high stacks of documents day after day, which requires a powerful, secure, durable machine that can monotonously masticate without jamming or overheating.

Whether you’re a “casual” or “serious” shredder, everyone wants to find a home office workshop that doesn’t cost too much but can handle their workload swiftly, smoothly, and securely. Within both camps, there are significant features that can make or break a shredder: longer run and shorter cooldown times, bigger bins, quieter motors, safety features, casters, and compact designs that let you tuck an infrequently used shredder discreetly under your desk. There are also special features that can make life easier, like anti-jam protections and solutions, ever-smaller particles, and automatic paper feeding. It’s easy to pick a paper shredder, bring it home, and hope for the best: But if you’re reading this guide, chances are you’d rather not leave your information security to chance.

And that’s why we’ve tested many of the most popular shredders on the market. We’ve found the best options for a wide spectrum of specialties. Whether you need to crush a foot-high pile of papers every morning or a few envelopes every week, we’ve found a shredder whose power, capacity, conveniences, and price all cater to your needs.

Paper shredders are more home office tech than conventional consumer electronics: Most of us don’t plan on upgrading our paper shredders regularly. As a result, the tech inside evolves far more slowly than gear like laptops, phones, and even printers. As a result, many of the best models stay at the top of the heap for years.

Given that reality, I try to look for the best of the best, not the “latest and greatest.” Ideally these are machines that you can invest in and trust to meet your needs for years and years. In fact, I’ve owned and used my personal shredder, an old Fellowes MS-450Cs shredder, for two decades.

While selecting which shredders match specific purposes for this guide, we considered mostly real-world factors as well as tech specs, such as:

Since our last roundup, I’ve tested an expanding range of models, from cheap shredder-mechanism-over-trash-bin designs to full-fledged micro-cut and auto-feed machines. I also widened my search beyond familiar shredder brands to lesser-known and retailer-exclusive models where performance, features, price, and consumer history warranted consideration. Some of these often-unknown brands can be surprisingly difficult to contact, which makes where a shredder is sold—and what help that retailer provides if something goes wrong—part of our value equation.

The Fellowes Powershred LX220 is the most versatile shredder I’ve tested, and works equally well in a home office, pulverizing an occasional pile of household paperwork, or tackling the more substantial workload of a professional team. My testing revealed its stated specs met or even exceeded its rated 20-sheet capacity and 30-minute runtime. Plus, Fellowes’ IntelliBar provides visual feedback on bin fullness, runtime, and sheet capacity, while SafeSense stops the cutters when hands approach the paper opening.

Best of all, Fellowes’ proactive “100-percent Jam Proof” system is designed to detect overambitious stacks and head off paper jam interruptions before they happen.

Notice, I said designed to. During our testing, we did manage to jam the supposedly 100-percent-jam-proof LX220. In its defense, I was actively trying to choke it rather than accidentally overstuffing it in a fit of shredding enthusiasm.

Under more normal conditions, Fellowes’ anti-jam system works incredibly well. Combined with the LX220’s other talents and relatively few shortcomings, it’s still the shredder we’d recommend to the widest variety of buyers.

For $75, the Sam’s Club-exclusive Member’s Mark C249-A delivers a robust set of functional and convenience-minded features, including some options you’d expect only on a higher-priced shredder.

It has a rather surprising skill set, anchored by a 12-sheet capacity, P-4 micro-cut security, 30-minute runtime, and an auto-reverse to help clear jams. It also has a “safety interlock/shred safe” feature—a helpful safety precaution that prevents operation when the bin is missing or not seated correctly. It’s common in high-end shredders, but a huge get at this price.

Surprisingly, it also handles nearly all the non-paper office detritus likely to find its way into a shredder—staples, credit cards, CDs, and what Sam’s Club describes as “small” paper clips. Again, this kind of power is normally reserved for more expensive models.

Not only do you get capacity, stamina, security, and convenience for not a lot of money, but you have the convenience of taking it back to Sam’s Club if something should go wrong with it.

If your shredding needs lean toward the occasional, choose one that won’t hog otherwise valuable floor space. Better yet, get a shredder that’s essentially invisible when not in use. At roughly 15 inches tall, and barely a foot wide, this compact Aurora AU870MZ may not be a ninja, but its ability to simply slide beneath your desktop makes it as unobtrusive as a shredder can be.

Not only does this Aurora—not to be confused with its older and less capable sibling, the AU870MA—disappear beneath most desks or easily slip into a closet, it can also make up to eight sheets disappear at a time.

There are some compromises. This Aurora’s 3.9-gallon bin will fill faster, and its five-minute runtime won’t be enough time to take care of even a small pile of accumulated scraps in one session. But if you consider this a JIC shredder, being able to hide it is likely more important to you than its lack of workhorse attributes.

While compact, this Aurora doesn’t skimp on shredding security or capability. You get a P-4 micro-cutting mechanism that also can chomp non-paper credit cards, staples, and small paper clips.

Nearly everyone would rather do almost any other kind of office work than shredding. So, instead of feeding and watching, this HP (made by Royal and sometimes listed as the 91032T and/or the AF809) lets you load up to 80 sheets into its clever fold up/down automatic feeder which frees you up to do something more important, like grab a snack or cup of coffee.

However, in the real world, the small 3.8-gallon bin doesn’t hold the bits from all 80 shredded pages without some help. Once I reached around 50 pages shredded, the HP stopped and waited until I pulled out the bin and leveled its shredded contents. After shoving the bin back in, the HP finished the remaining 30 pages without any trouble. But even with this bin shuffling, the 80 sheets got chewed up in just around five minutes.

Other than its mismatched auto-feed and bin capacities, this surprisingly affordable, speedy, and compact machine—it’s less than 17 inches tall—includes P-4 micro-cut security and can also masticate credit cards, staples, paper clips, and CDs through its 9-sheet manual feed slot.

If you’re the paranoid type—rather extra extra careful like me—about completely obliterating confidential documents—purchase a shredder that’s capable of mincing personal papers into the most minuscule, irrecoverable particles possible at a price that doesn’t require a bond issue.

The relatively new Effeluviate Q9 deploys P-7 cutters—a shredding security level normally associated with much pricier specialist machines and here for something approaching a consumer price—pulverizes a document into tiny 1 × 1.7mm particles (3/64 x 5/64, or 0.05 x 0.08, of an inch), a fraction of the size of a P-5 shredder produced particle.

Other than its ultra-secure P-7 rating and its resulting paper powder, this Q9’s remaining specs are almost boringly conventional: a relatively low seven-sheet manual feed, a decent 30-minute runtime, and a mid-range 5.23-gallon bin (not 6 gallons, as rated). And while the Q9 can crush plastic credit cards, staples, and CDs, it’s apparently allergic to paper clips.

Its sub-56dB noise rating, however, makes the Q9 about 10dB quieter than most shredders so mincing documents won’t disturb your co-habitants either day or night. I’m a little skittish about recommending a relatively unknown brand, but the specs are incredibly impressive.

If you must macerate massive masses of documents on a daily basis, the Bonsen S9221 is about to become your new best friend. Lift up its top, load up to 320 sheets into its flatbed feeder, and walk away. In 30 minutes, all 320 sheets will be transformed into tiny 2 × 10mm specks.

The S9221’s 8.1-gallon pull-out bin is appropriately roomy for the kind of 320-sheet jobs its auto feeder invites. Although you can leave large jobs to the auto feeder, a separate manual slot handles up to 10 sheets in smaller batches along with staples, paper clips, and credit cards—but not CDs.

One thing to keep an eye out for when you go to buy: There’s an older version of the S9221 with a slightly lower 300-page capacity and only P-4 micro-cut security instead of P-5. Since it has the same name and similar features to the new model, it would be very easy to buy the old model without noticing. Please make sure to check the listing before clicking “buy.”

I recently evaluated the top shredders under $100, and there are a few sub-$100 models that work great and are more widely available than the Member’s Mark, including the Amazon Basics 12-Sheet Cross-Cut ($59), the Staples ST62150 ($82), which is loaded with safety features, and the Bonsaii C275-A 12-Sheet Cross-Cut ($65), ideal for infrequent emptying.

You may not be able to control where your digital data ends up. But you know exactly how you can securely dispose of your paper records. The trick is deciding which shredder will best satisfy your serious or casual shredding needs, which usually comes down to a handful of features.

Once you start your shredding chore, you’d rather not be interrupted by problems with your shredder. Runtime tells you how long you can keep feeding paper into a shredder before its motor overheats and shuts down, forcing you to wait 30 to 45 minutes, depending on the model, for the machine to catch its mechanical breath.

A small personal shredder may run for only five or 10 minutes, which is plenty if you dispatch only a few documents at a time. If you’re regularly confronted by larger piles to pulverize, look for a runtime of 30 minutes or more.

Once you choose a shredder with longer runtimes, don’t obsess over the advertised cooldown time. You may fill the bin before the shredder overheats and, by the time you’ve disposed of all that confetti, the motor already has had a chance to cool before you return with an empty bin.

A shredder is still largely a mechanical device, a motor driving a set of cutters, augmented in many models by sensors and electronic controls. And as with any mechanical object, failure is often less a question of if than when. Long-term owner shredder reviews are especially useful for spotting recurring problems with motors, sensors, switches, and other parts that may not misbehave during short-term testing.

Unfortunately, getting help directly from some shredder brands can be harder than clearing a paper jam. During our ongoing shredder research, we’ve encountered multiple manufacturers failing to respond to repeated emails and phone calls. Some brands don’t even provide a U.S. customer-service number.

That doesn’t automatically make shredders from these contact-resistant brands a bad buy. Purchasing from an established store or online retailer with a clearly stated return or replacement policy gives you a more reliable resource to turn to if your new shredder turns out to be a lemon. Before buying—particularly from an unfamiliar brand—check both the manufacturer’s warranty and especially the retailer’s return/replace policy.

Unlike the shredders you may remember from old movies, most modern machines no longer turn documents into long linguini-like strips. Cross-cut shredders slice paper both lengthwise and crosswise into small rectangular scraps. Micro-cut models slice and dice those scraps into even tinier bits, leaving hundreds or even thousands of petite particles.

For most home and home-office use, either cutting method provides plenty of protection. Most shredders these days offer micro-cut machines with either P-4 security, which makes reconstructing a document the most puzzling jigsaw puzzle ever, or P-5 security, whose even more diminutive document destruction methods are favored by MDs, CPAs, JDs, or by other professionals with initials in their titles.

The larger and more powerful your shredder, the more sheets it can generally chew through at one time. Just don’t treat the number printed on the box as a dare.

Manufacturers’ rated sheet capacities are best-case numbers, usually based on neatly aligned standard-weight bond paper. Thicker stock, folds, staples, uneven piles, and stuffed envelopes can quickly turn a “12-sheet” machine into something more comfortable with eight or nine. Feeding a few sheets below the rated maximum is one of the easiest ways to avoid jams and unnecessary strain.

Manual shredders require you to stand there feeding paper in batches. Auto-feed machines let you load a stack, walk away, and get something else done while the shredder eats.

Here again, don’t take the rated auto-feed sheet capacity too literally. An “80-sheet” or “200-sheet” auto feeder may accommodate that many pristine sheets under ideal conditions, but real paperwork is rarely pristine. Wrinkles, folds, different paper weights, staples, and uneven stacks can reduce how much you can reliably leave it to swallow unattended. Plus, the bin on a high-capacity auto-feed model may fill before the maximum number of sheets are fed into it.

Auto-feed mechanisms also add more rollers, sensors, and jam-clearing compartments. And more moving mechanical parts create more places for something to eventually go wrong.

However, if you routinely accumulate large piles, the time a highly rated auto-feed shredder saves can easily outweigh the added complexity and potential mechanical issues.

A bigger bin means fewer trips to empty it, but gallon capacity tells only part of the story. Pull-out drawers are lighter and easier to clean and empty. Bins that require lifting the often heavy shredder mechanism off the top of a wastepaper basket can potentially scatter loose particles still in the cutter mechanism.

Also pay attention to what happens when you pull that drawer out. Paper confetti has an impressive ability to cling to plastic, pile up behind a bin, and otherwise escape the container designed to hold it. An easy-to-remove bin that keeps most of its shredded paper actually in the bin will save you emptying and cleanup aggravation, especially if you don’t wait until the bin is filled to its brim.

Shredders may look sturdy and impervious, but most are actually quite finicky eaters. Nearly every shredder will eventually jam if you feed it too much at one time or feed it the wrong type, shape, or mix of paper. More advanced models with more advanced anti-jam systems sense an overload before one occurs, or either automatically reverse or allow you to manually reverse to relieve the jam before you need to perform paper-removal surgery from the cutters with tweezers or needle-nose pliers.

The cheapest jam protection, however, is restraint. If a machine claims 12 sheets, regularly feeding it eight or nine instead will lower your odds of spending quality time violently tugging mangled paper back out of its teeth.

Most current shredders can swallow staples and paper clips, and many can also chew up plastic credit cards. CDs and other thicker media such as metal cards are less universally welcome.

Check the manufacturer’s instructions before you buy for what non-paper materials a shredder can successfully chew and before feeding anything other than paper into its cutters. A shredder capable of mincing a stack of tax records can object like a microwave forced to cook metal—something it wasn’t designed to eat.

Probably less than you think. For most people who dispatch a few bills, receipts, financial statements, or junk-mail offers every few days, well under $100 can buy a perfectly capable shredder.

Spending more generally buys stamina, convenience, and durability: longer runtimes, larger bins, higher sheet capacities, auto-feed, better jam protection, sometimes finer-cut security, and years if not decades of service. Those features become worth paying for as the amount and frequency of your shredding increase.

As with nearly all things, don’t be penny wise and pound foolish. You will find you will shred more than you anticipated—it’s just human nature to use a new device more than you though you would. Overall, shredders costing several hundreds of dollars make the most sense for people who regularly devour large stacks or have a specialized need. Don’t decide what to spend simply by asking how private your paperwork is; ask how much of it you need to turn into confetti and how often both now and in the future.

The most important shredder “spec” may be how little time it forces you to spend with it. Sheet capacity, runtime, security level, and bin capacity are the headline numbers I’d look at first. Runtime is particularly useful because it tells you something about how much work the machine can comfortably handle before demanding a rest.

But some of the things that most determine whether you’ll love or hate a shredder aren’t specs at all. Nearly every decent modern shredder can reduce ordinary documents beyond casual recognition. The bigger differences are how often it jams, how easily those jams clear, how cleanly the bin empties, and how much confetti winds up everywhere except inside it.

Check owner reviews for recurring complaints about jams, overheating, finicky sensors, messy bins, and other annoyances. AI agents on online sites can summarize customer reviews to answer many of these before-you-buy questions.

With shredders, old doesn’t necessarily mean obsolete. Sometimes it means proven.Unlike most consumer electronics, shredders don’t become outdated because they lack this year’s faster processor, new operating system, wireless standard, or other bleeding-edge technology. An older model that’s still attracting buyers and good reviews may actually offer something a brand-new machine can’t: years of accumulated evidence about how well it holds up.

Before buying an older model, check whether the manufacturer has introduced a newer or revised version. When shopping online, search the manufacturer’s current lineup or, if the retailer provides an AI or shopping assistant, ask whether there’s a newer version of the model you’re considering. Then compare old to new rather than automatically assuming new means better.

The best shredder maintenance is self-restraint. Don’t continually stuff the cutters to their rated maximum, allow the bin overflow, or feed the machine materials it wasn’t designed to digest.

Lubrication requirements vary. Some manufacturers recommend shredder oil applied at regular intervals, others suggest pre-lubricated oil sheets, and some models claim to require little or no lubrication at all. Follow the instructions for your particular machine rather than assuming every shredder requires the same type of mechanical TLC.

Beyond that, maintenance should be pretty painless: empty the bin before the paper snow reaches the cutters, occasionally clean dusty sensors if the manufacturer recommends it, and clear jams rather than repeatedly hammering the reverse button and hoping for divine intervention.

Despite the name, most modern “shredders” no longer shred paper into long strips. While cross cut and micro cut are clues for how small the ultimate shred pieces will be, P-ratings, part of the DIN 66399 security standard, put an actual number on “small.”

P-ratings run from P-1 through P-7; the higher the number, the smaller the pieces produced. For ordinary household paperwork, P-3 is already plenty secure. A cross-cut P-3 machine reduces a document to hundreds of pieces, which is more than enough discouragement for anyone contemplating reconstructing your bills, junk mail, receipts, or other everyday paperwork. After all, a document pieced back together like a taped mosaic isn’t likely to fool many people.

P-4 is the sweet spot for buyers who want their paperwork diced considerably finer without spending much more, and P-4 is common among consumer micro-cut shredders. P-5 turns documents into even tinier bits and makes sense for especially sensitive financial, legal, medical, or professional paperwork. P-6 and P-7 go further still, into security levels intended for documents whose contents matter considerably more than last month’s Visa bill.

For most of us, then, P-3 is plenty, P-4 buys extra peace of mind, and P-5 is for paperwork you’d really rather nobody put back together.

Stewart Wolpin, based in New York City, has been writing about, reporting on, and reviewing consumer technology for nearly 40 years. He also serves as the unofficial historian for CTA (Consumer Technology Association), the trade group that produces the Consumer Electronics Show (CES), which he has attended and covered since 1984. He is also a huge Beatles fan and a METS season ticket holder.

The surest way to get a scratch from a feline is to go for a forbidden tummy rub. But why do cats hate being touched on their bellies?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dogs typically love belly rubs and will roll on their backs to get more. With cats, it's a different story: Most are visibly uncomfortable when someone touches their belly, and the same applies to their feet and tail.

When a cat is petted in these areas, its body language often changes. "They might do a quick head turn, looking at your hand, or they might start moving away from you or wiggling around a lot, basically trying to get away from the petting," Mikel Delgado, a cat behaviorist and senior research scientist at Purdue University, told Live Science in an email. "If these early warning signs are ignored, they might escalate to biting, hissing or scratching."

But why do cats dislike it so much when humans touch these specific areas?

Although there has been little formal research into this question, animal behavior experts proposed a few ideas for why cats don't like to be touched in certain areas.

"Cats are prey animals as well as predators and so they can be very protective of areas that are particularly vulnerable to injury during attack, such as the belly area," Sarah Ellis, head of cat mental well-being and behavior at the cat welfare charity International Cat Care, told Live Science in an email.

A cat's belly houses vital organs ‪—‬ such as the liver, stomach and intestines ‪—‬ without the protective bony cage that the ribs provide for the heart and lungs. Although cats have evolved a special feature called the "primordial pouch" —‬ basically a flap of loose skin and fat on their belly —‬ which provides a little extra padding to protect vital organs during fights, most cats still feel threatened when humans touch or rub their belly.

Cats have extra padding on their stomachs to protect their organs.

Dogs have a similar anatomy to cats, but they have to worry less about falling prey to larger animals. Cats, meanwhile, can be hunted by dogs, urban coyotes, and even birds such as hawks and owls, making it natural for them to be protective of their bellies.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

The tail is also a vulnerable area for cats. "When a cat is chased by another animal, including other cats, the tail is often the part of the cat's body that is closest to touch," Ellis said, "and the risk of being bitten at the base of the tail is high." Therefore, cats may be skittish about having their tail stroked.

When it comes to foot rubs, there are two possible explanations for why most cats hate them. First, a cat's paws are essential in threatening situations. Running away from danger is a cat's preferred survival strategy, and they rely on their paws as a means of escape, Ellis explained. If they can't run away, "a cat may resort to repelling any threats through swiping and scratching and it needs its paws free to do so," she said. "It is therefore predisposed to not enjoy having its paws restricted in any way."

Another reason could be that cats' paws are very sensitive. They have wrist whiskers (also known as "carpal vibrissae") and toe pads that are sensitive to various types of stimuli, like pressure and heat, Delgado said, "so it's not surprising that many cats are sensitive about having their feet touched."

If you're interacting with a cat, it's generally a good idea to stick to the areas where most cats like to be petted: the base of their ears, around their cheeks and under their chin. These areas are rich in scent glands, and cats tend to rub them against other cats they are friends with, Delgado explained. So essentially, cats like being petted in those areas because "they treat us as they do other cats," Delgado said.

But some cats go against the grain. "I've had a few who enjoyed belly rubs," Delgado said. Others enjoy having their tail stroked briefly and show their pleasure "by pushing their rump into the hand of the petter and holding their tail up in the air," Ellis said. (This behavior is sometimes called "elevator butt.")

As puzzling as it may be to humans, these varied preferences are a reminder that "each cat is an individual," Delgado said. Positive responses to petting of the belly, feet or tail can also signal close bonding to a human, Ellis said.

She advises people to "always take the cat's lead, learn what each individual cat likes and dislikes and respect these preferences."

#6328. Nov. 7, 1882: A Great Comet transforms astrophotography

In early September 1882, a comet was sighted from the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa. The comet brightened over the following weeks, reaching a magnitude of -2 on the 15th; at perihelion two days later, it was bright enough to be visible during the day. But at the time, David Gill, the director of the Cape Observatory, was busy observing minor planets Victoria and Sappho. It wasn’t until Oct. 12 that, his minor planet observations completed, he turned his attention to the comet and began photographing it.

Gill captured images of the Great Comet of 1882 on Oct. 12, 20, and 21, and Nov. 7, 13, and 14. The Nov. 7 shot was the one he would become famous for, though: It was not the first photograph of a comet, but rather would signal a change in astronomers’ uses of astrophotography. The photo was a 100-minute exposure, resulting an image that included stars to 10th magnitude and the comet’s 18-degree tail. Spurred by the large number of stars captured in his photo, Gill saw the potential for using astrophotography for star mapping and began the Cape Photographic Durchmusterung. (Durchmusterung means “close examination” or “scrutiny.”) The project would catalog nearly a half-million southern stars. Gill shared the successes of the program internationally, prompting the assembly of the world’s first major astronomical conference. As a result, astronomers worldwide began to move away from traditional, manual star mapping and towards more efficient and comprehensive photographic techniques.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#6327. 15 Best Arch Support Shoes for Long Travel Days

I grew up believing that sore and throbbing feet were a necessary evil of long travel days, until a physical therapist said three magic words: arch-support shoes. She’d noticed the inside forefoot and outside heels of my shoes’ soles were completely worn through—a sign of overpronation because I have no natural arch. With that kind of misalignment, it was no surprise that even a simple day of set-jetting through The Sound of Music sites in Austria or strolling through the compact center of Prague was wreaking havoc on my feet.

As it turns out, as much as 37% of the population is believed to have some degree of flat foot, according to a National Library of Medicine study. But how it affects everyday life can vary by person. Initially, I only noticed the pain on high step-count days, but when I started long-distance running 10 years ago, I knew it was time to invest in supportive shoes capable of going the distance.

So I visited my local Fleet Feet in Hoboken, New Jersey, where nowadays its complimentary Fit ID 3-D scan can get granular, most recently showing me that my two feet have different lengths, as well as varying ball and heel widths. Most blaringly, both my arch heights are on the lowest possible end of the scale.

What I’ve learned more than anything is that there is no one-size-fits-all supportive shoe that works for everyone, which is why individual fittings are so crucial. (In extreme cases, like when I got posterior tibial tendinitis after running a half marathon, be sure to consult a healthcare professional.) But for a dose of stability, here are 15 arch-support shoes that are primed for long days on your feet.

For the last decade, the Brooks Adrenaline GTS has been my go-to shoe—that’s what GTS stands for, after all. The shoe’s GuideRails technology works its magic not by trying to correct your stride, but by guiding it in the direction that feels natural. Not only did it get me through my first few races with New York Road Runners, and eventually NYC Marathon training, but it’s always the shoe I go back to when I crave stability with just a sprinkle of cushioning. Whenever I slip these on, I feel locked in. The new version, which launched on November 1, retains its trusted features, while refining the heel tab and tongue to be sleeker and more functional.

During the most wrenching times of my foot pain, when every step I took hurt, an orthopedic doctor encouraged me to get a pair of Hokas and start running again. The brand may have led the way with oversized cushioned soles, but one of its bestsellers is this stability shoe, with an H-frame to prevent arch-less feet from turning inward. The newest version features a tighter mesh upper on the inside portion of the shoe, adding support to its arch side while retaining that soft cushiony feel. It even bears an American Podiatric Medical Association (AMPA) seal certifying that it’s beneficial to foot health.

Oofos may be known for its slides and recovery footwear (I wore a pair for a week after the 2024 Boston Marathon), but the same lightweight support strategies are applied to this casual sneaker. Its trademark high-impact absorbing Oofoam soaks up 37% of impact compared to regular shoes. Best of all, it’s machine washable with a closed-cell foam that prevents odors.

Let’s face it: Hiking shoes can be a pain to pack—which is what makes this Columbia hiking boot that's disguised as a sneaker so brilliant. Without any breaking in, they were immediately comfortable yet firm, and have kept my feet dry through sudden downpours and even river crossings on a hike in Thailand. This fall, they doubled as a sporty shoe, as I ran and biked the 32-mile Moose Loop Trail around Anchorage over three days, including a drizzly four-mile run on the final day.

Most impressively, during my Intrepid Travel Kenya Safari Adventure earlier this month, rain started falling while we were planting trees in the Mt. Kenya region’s Intrepid-adopted forest until we were trudging through mud. But the Konos’s sophisticated underfoot system provided support with maximum cushioning and traction so that I never doubted my stability any step of the way.

During the worst of my foot issues, I thought I'd be confined to a life of bulky orthotics. That’s when Vionic saved me. Every shoe in its collection—from sandals to dress shoes—is powered by its podiatrist-approved Vio Motion technology with a deep heel cup for stability, shock-absorbing cushioning, flexible movement, and most noticeably, strong arch-support that realigns the body while improving balance. This casual sneaker merges all that into a lace-up design that’s as supportive as it is cute. Not only was there zero break-in period for instant comfort, but it also meets the One Planet sustainability standard.

As I learned during my most recent Fleet Feet fitting, arch support and heel stability are inherently linked—and Kuru’s own patented sole hones in precisely those two traits. Together, they turn these lightweight court shoes into a secret weapon, able to endure the miles without an inkling of fatigue. Plus the versatile style can be dressed up or down.

The 90-year-old brand from the Italian Dolomites is best known for its mountaineering gear—and it’s that kind of technical expertise that was used to develop its Pedrock hiking shoe. The visible 3F System ties together flexibility, fit, and support. The adjustable laces ensure that the shoe fits like a glove while an EVA plate provides stability, along with reinforced heel and toe caps. All together, the urban-to-mountain shoe transitions perfectly through every step of your travels.

When it comes to technical gear, there are so many bells and whistles to consider that it’s easy to overlook the basics—namely, support. Teva never goes wrong in that realm and uses its own Lite-Comf midsole for a cushiony step, along with a patented universal heel lock system and Vibram grip for traction on the outer, so there’s no reason to teeter, even on multiple-day hikes over varied terrain. Those looking for less bulkiness with the same support can also opt for the lightweight road-to-trail Aventrail R2T shoe, which launched earlier this year.

The dependability that comes with Merrell’s high-performing outdoor wear is merged with Gore-Tex’s gold standard of waterproofness in this simple yet powerful hiking boot. It's easy to see why it's become my go-to for the last few years. At 16.36-oz. per shoe, it’s a hearty design, which equals stability throughout. The Kinetic Fit–blend contoured footbed strengthens the heel and a molded nylon shank adds arch support, while Vibram traction on the soles prevents slipping on slick surfaces, eliminating any flat-footed hiker’s worries—and taking me on adventures I thought were out of my range.

Cold weather footwear has long been a struggle for me—until I met this travel-friendly ankle boot from my trusted Vionic. Its classic design is easy to pair with anything from dresses to jeans, and the full-length zipper makes it easy to slip on and off. But don’t underestimate its durability, equipped with a completely waterproof leather upper and sealed seams to ensure not a drop seeps in. Plus, it conquers my fear of slippery sidewalks with articulated pods that provide traction for steady steps while still feeling cushiony.

The Kizik brand may seem like a novelty, focused on the ability to step in and out of shoes hands-free—yes, even these boots with laces (that don’t actually need to be tied). But the Juno 2 goes beyond just speeding you through TSA checkpoints. It’s chock full of support, boasting a molded EVA foam midsole for comfort and an Arch Form insole that molds to your foot shape.

Here’s what Vionic does best—take the patented footbed it's known for with orthotic-grade arch support and apply it to styles that don’t disclose your foot problems. This everyday loafer, made with post-consumer recycled materials, combines that solid support with extreme flexibility and a grippy sole. But the best part for travelers is how packable these loafers are—the upper (which comes in either super soft leather or suede) squishes easily, yet retains its shape and support. I’ve worn these to conferences and events, and often get asked who makes them, as it’s rare to find business casual shoes that are so supportive. I stocked up with three pairs waiting in my closet for when my first ones wear out—though after more than a year, they’ve shown no signs of aging.

A ballet flat with actual arch support? Only Birkenstock can make that possible with its trademark cork-latex footbed known for its firm arch support, along with a natural leather insole and suede lining. All that support may sound stiff, but it’s evened out with EVA cushioning. All together, it’s that free-flowing feeling from its famous Big Buckle sandals wrapped in a cozy exterior.

This leather slip-on may look like an everyday flat, but its comfort features are where it shines, starting with sturdy arch-support designed for all-day wear. Unlike most shoes of this genre, it has a removable footbed to slide in custom orthotics (I’m used to having to tear them out of flats!), plus a lightweight rubber outsole to keep you on your feet. Available in regular and wide, the Larisa also proudly wears an APMA acceptance seal.

The first time I slipped on the Aetrex Collette loafers, I immediately stood up straighter. There’s something about its sloping arch-support that directed not just my feet but my entire posture into a more confident stance. It turns out the footbed is designed to follow the natural curvature of each person’s foot, alleviating issues from plantar facilities to heel pain. The brand puts an emphasis on personalized fit, with the strap across the shoe cleverly doubling as an adjustable Velcro and, making them feel more like snug sneakers than loafers.

While it may seem like only people with flat feet or low arches require arch support, that’s not the case. “Anyone with tired feet or discomfort may benefit from a more supportive shoe,” Jenny Simpson, three-time Olympian and Fleet Feet’s chief running officer, tells Traveler. She adds that the specifics of your foot will dictate the support that works best. Generally, those with low or flexible arches can benefit from stability shoes, while those with high and rigid arches might do better with more cushioned shoes.

What to look for in an arch-support shoe?

Simpson cautions not to choose a shoe based on arch height alone: “Support should feel like it is meeting your arch, while the heel should feel secure,” says Simpson. Only you can tell what feels right once it’s on your foot, as “how you move and what feels comfortable to you” are the ultimate factors.

No singular shoe will address soreness for everyone. “The right choice depends on what is causing the discomfort, how your foot moves, and whether you need more cushioning, more stability, or a combination of both,” says Simpson. Since no product photo or descriptions can replicate how shoes will feel on your feet, in-person fittings are the most valuable.

Are arch-support shoes good for heel pain?

Simpson says that insoles can definitely be “an excellent tool for anyone looking for more tailored solutions for their footwear.” In particular, for those dealing with plantar fasciitis-induced heel pain, the extra support can reduce strain. Alternatively, cushioned shoes—like Hoka is known for—can make standing and walking more comfortable.

What brands design the most supportive shoes?

Running and walking shoes are built to endure the long days that travel requires, as Simpson calls out Brooks, Hoka, Asics, New Balance, and Saucony as strong options. She suggests trying different models since two styles from the same brand can have totally different fits. Other lifestyle shoes aren’t necessarily designed for the same level of wear. “My strongest advice is not to shop by label alone,” Simpson says. “Many shoes are labeled ‘supportive,’ ‘stability,’ or ‘orthopedic.’ They can be useful descriptions, but your foot gets the final vote. The best shoe is the one that fits your anatomy, supports your activity and allows you to move comfortably.”
