#6252. Frontier Shakes Up Leadership Team

Frontier is reshuffling its leadership team, hiring a new chief operating officer, and announcing the departures of two senior executives.

Michael Delehant will join the carrier as executive vice president and chief operating officer on Nov. 30. He will oversee all airline operations and report to CEO Jimmy Dempsey, Frontier said Monday.

Delehant most recently served as group managing director at Wizz Air, overseeing operational and commercial activities. He previously held senior positions at Vueling, including chief strategy and network officer, and worked in several leadership roles at Southwest.

Dempsey said Delehant’s experience would be “instrumental as we continue growing our airline and executing against our strategic priorities.”

The appointment comes as Trevor Stedke, senior vice president of operations, and Alex Clerc, senior vice president of customers, prepare to leave Frontier on Nov. 13. The airline did not give a reason for their departures in its announcement.

“I want to express my sincere gratitude to Trevor and Alex for their dedication and contributions to Frontier,” Dempsey said.

Frontier also promoted James Fenner to senior vice president and chief revenue officer. His responsibilities include pricing and revenue management, loyalty, and network planning.

Fenner has spent more than a decade at the airline, most recently serving as vice president of revenue and loyalty.

Bobby Schroeter will move into the role of senior vice president and chief marketing officer, overseeing the airline’s brand and customer experience. Both Fenner and Schroeter will report directly to Dempsey.

The changes follow Frontier’s third-quarter results, which showed a $104 million net loss, compared with a $77 million loss a year earlier. Excluding special items, the carrier reported a $40 million profit on record revenue of $1.36 billion.

#6251. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

Not true (unless something changed) stayed here in May 2023 and got Globalist benefits

#6250. I Found $1.70 Burritos At Denver Airport. Thank You, Taco Bell.

While I usually just make a beeline for the Capital One Lounge while in Denver International Airport, I recently noticed that Taco Bell is back…now airside instead of landside..and from a cost perspective, probably the best deal for food in DEN.

If you’ve flown from Denver for years, you might remember that there used to be a Taco Bell in the Jeppesen Terminal in the food court above the security checkpoint. At some point that closed while the airport was refurbishing that area and did not re-open.

But was I (very pleasantly) surprised to see a Taco Bell Cantina in Concourse A (near Gates A47 and A49) during a recent trip through DEN. I had no idea!

Even better? The prices were street pricing, not airport pricing. $1.70 for a burrito? What a lovely way to get your junk food fix without breaking the bank.

And street pricing not ubiquitous in the airport. I had a salad with some pulled brisket at Brothers BBQ and it was almost $20….

I also want to note that I tried the more “local” option, called Denver Street Eats, located in The B Gates, which offers street tacos. A steak taco was $6.25. That may seem reasonable at first glance, but it was just a small flour tortilla with very little to it: a bit of steak, a couple spinach leaves, and a few tiny slices of picked onions. It was good, but sorry, Taco Bell is better.

So if you’re looking for an affordable meal at Denver Airport, Taco Bell is your best bet.

And for new readers, yes, I have a strong affinity for Taco Bell…wherever I am in the world. Check out the archive.

#6249. Awkwafina Takes Us on a Nostalgic Food-Tour of NYC's Koreatown

“It's so cool that in this city you have SoHo and Times Square but also these enclaves where you can totally belong,” says Nora Lum, the actor and comedian also known as Awkwafina. We're upstairs at the 24-hour Miss Korea, her go-to spot in Manhattan's Koreatown, picking our way over a lavish Korean barbecue spread of assorted banchan and gleaming chargrilled short ribs. “I love this!” she says, before popping a clump of braised burdock into her mouth.

Lum, who is Korean-Chinese American, has just wrapped filming Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook, an unscripted Apple TV series that she hosts and executive-produces. A descendant of the family behind the legendary Cantonese American restaurant Lum's, which her great-grandfather ran in Flushing, Queens, from 1953 to 1982, she spends eight episodes gathering cooking tips from the nation's Asian communities, particularly its Chinatowns. She heads to America's oldest Chinatown, in San Francisco, to cook with chef Martin Yan, who, using “insane” knife work, “absolutely destroyed a chicken in 16 seconds”; Texas for a barbecue-fueled road trip with comedian Jimmy O. Yang, making pit stops at Korean-American-owned Eaker Barbecue in Fredericksburg and Thai-American Curry Boys BBQ in San Antonio; and Los Angeles to wait tables at the dim sum joint Golden Dragon. All these experiences lead to her own pop-up revival of Lum's in Manhattan's Little Italy, where she serves beloved staples like orange chicken and barbecue beef to friends and family.

Lum crosses 32nd Street in the heart of New York City’s Koreatown.

At its heart Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook is about heritage, community, and small-business immigrant entrepreneurship. “After the pandemic so many mom-and-pop shops were closing and Chinatowns were declining,” says Lum. “The show is about exploring that phenomenon but then also seeing who in my generation is keeping it going.”

Our first lunch stop is Miss Korea, on 32nd Street between Broadway and Fifth Avenue, the stretch where Koreatown first emerged in the late 1970s. Then home to a Korean-language bookstore and a smattering of restaurants, it's since evolved into an around-the-clock entertainment hub for anyone looking to pick up K-pop memorabilia, sing karaoke, and eat everything from Korean corn dogs at Jongro Rice Hotdog to a Michelin-starred tasting menu at Joo Ok. For Lum it's a nostalgic stretch of the city. “I went to MK, Maru, Circle,” she says in reference to nightlife spots frequented by Korean American party kids coming of age in 1990s and 2000s New York. “Oh man, I've been so messy on this one block.”

Patrons fill the tables at the ever-popular BCD Tofu House, which specializes in soondubu.

We cross the street to BCD Tofu House for crispy seafood pancakes, spicy marinated crab slicked with red pepper seasoning, and Lum's favorite: the signature soondubu, a tofu stew bubbling in a clay pot. Since opening in 2008, the Los Angeles export has increasingly drawn long lines—a testament to the growing popularity of Korean food across the US. “Twenty years ago customers were 70 to 80 percent Korean,” general manager Alex Kim tells us. “Now it's a lot more non-Korean.”

Lum notes that, for a long time in the US, immigrants selling their traditional cuisines were often met with gratitude within the culture yet distrust outside of it. Adaptation followed: the invention of chop suey, for example, and wok-fired cooking of non-Chinese vegetables like broccoli. Her great-grandfather experienced this himself with Lum's, and local appreciation for the restaurant's Americanized Chinese classics like egg rolls and shrimp with lobster sauce has remained long after it closed. “I learned to think about it less as my family's attempt at just making money but rather, ‘Hey, this is the cuisine that we ate growing up,’ ” she says. “It's a fascinating story of belonging and acculturation.”

We wander over to Woorijip, a fast-casual institution for snacking and soju drinking to pick up kimbap, and then to food hall Food Gallery 32. “This is where I get the fish!” Lum says of bungeoppang, the fish-shaped pastry introduced to Korea by Japanese colonists in the 1930s and popularized again in the '90s. In Manhattan this is the rare spot to find it.

Freshly made bungeoppang lined up at Food Gallery 32

While filming, Lum prioritized places that are moving the needle forward while still preserving their communities' culture, like Phoenix Palace in Manhattan's Chinatown. The Cantonese American restaurant hosts local elders at affordable rates and buys plates from Wing on Wo & Co., a porcelain shop dating back to 1925. Lum recalls co-owner Cory Ng's father appearing with ingredients sourced from the neighborhood.

“Chinatown is totally a local economy,” she says. But it's also where immigrants can speak their native languages, play mahjong, eat dim sum, and celebrate Lunar New Year. “So when you see Chinatowns decline, it's a bigger problem”—a problem she hopes her show can help resolve.

In San Antonio, bright pink barbecue spot Curry Boys BBQ run by three childhood friends dishes out Southeast Asian–Texan blends like oak-smoked brisket with green curry. “They're combining their own cultures into something that's so authentic to where they're from,” says Lum.

For the show, Lum waited tables at classic banquet hall Golden Dragon in Los Angeles's Chinatown, which, with its traditional dim sum service, has remained a stronghold for 64 years. Step outside, says Lum, and “it looks like a movie set.”

Lum stopped by Oahu's Kō Hana Distillers while visiting Hawaii to learn about the tiki culture that inspired her great-grandfather's drinks menu. Come here for its farm-to-bottle selection using homegrown sugarcane.

In San Francisco, the nation's oldest Chinatown “serves the community in a different way from elsewhere,” says Lum. She also loves the comparatively younger, yet still landmark, Mister Jiu's for its Western take on Cantonese cooking.

#6247. A Flight Only Bookable With Points Offers Amazing Winter Sun

I often tell people that the best unkept secret with Avios is, in fact, the Avios app. Separate to the British Airways app, the Avios app allows users to set flight alerts and goals, but also gives a heads up about opportunities before they appear anywhere else.

Case in point: before a press release had even hit my inbox, the Avios app alerted me that an ‘Avios only’ flight had just launched. This isn’t the first time Avios has launched a flight only bookable with points, but it is the first time they’ve done one to CAPE TOWN, during peak winter break time.

British Airways and Avios have collaborated on a flight only bookable with Avios, where every seat on the plane is available for sale with points. First, business, premium and economy, all available using Avios. The flights depart as follows…

As noted, these flights are now bookable and if history repeats itself, they won’t be available for long. This plane only has 8 seats in first, so get in quick! One amazing thing about Avios is that they aren’t just the currency of one airline, but a whopping seven. If you have any points with Finnair, Iberia, Qatar, Aer Lingus, Logainair, Vueling or British Airways you can pool points together to book these flights.

Avios is also a transfer partner of Amex, Bilt, Capital One, Chase and plenty of other global financial institutions, so there should be ample opportunity to convert bank points into Avios and get these booked. Hot tip though, ensure there are seats available before you make your transfer, since this will be a hot commodity.

I love any airline rewarding members with flights entirely bookable with points. What makes this one different is that it’s not some off peak, off season destination. It’s Cape Town, easily one of the toughest tickets with any currency, during peak time, perfect for people looking to ditch the weather for the holidays and catch NYE in one of the best cities on earth.

Yes, Cape Town is by far one of my favorites and for any oenophiles, a trip to nearby Stellenbosch or Franschoek is a must. Standard luggage limits apply, so definitely bring enough suitcases to haul back wine. Fin. Head to British Airways website to book.

#6246. American Airlines Vs. United First Class: Boring Chicken Dinners That I’d Happily Order Again

I realize if you just read my blog it looks like I’ll eat anything thrown in front of me and to some extent that is true on airplane, but a pair of flights, one on American Airlines, the other on United Airlines, featured chicken dinners much closer to my what I usually eat at home. Let’s compare them in this week’s Meal of the Week.

Let’s start with American Airlines. I was flying from Los Angeles to Chicago and received a same-day upgrade (as a mere Advantage Gold!) and thus was not able to pre-ordered. Onboard the choices were chicken or pasta (described as a chicken breast with rice or pasta shells with tomato sauce). I chose chicken.

The chicken breast was covered in a white sauce and served with white rice on the side and green beans on top. On the side, a small green salad with sun-dried tomatoes and a ramekin with what appeared to be parsnips, carrots, and cabbage with croutons…at least I think so (whatever it was, it was nice).

While not an exciting dinner, I really appreciated just eating a lean chicken breast and green beans…it’s very similar to what we eat at least a couple nights per week at home.

Dessert was raspberry sorbet…I miss the Häagen-Dazs ice cream that used to be on these flights (and the real ice cream sundaes before that).

On to United. Same route. The current “signature entree” out of Los Angeles is described as:

Pollo asado chicken thigh Pollo asado chicken thigh with charred corn farro, street corn style zucchini and asado sauce

The AA dish was fine, but this folks was excellent. The flavor of the chicken was excellent and the corn farro and zucchini were really nice…we grow zucchini in our garden at home and cook it in the oven with our chicken so this really felt close to home. The corn was a nice treat and I ate every bit of it.

The sale on the side had sun-dried tomatoes and sliced cucumbers and the meal also came with a cornmeal roll and a slice of “hot chocolate” cheesecake, which I passed on.

Both were rather boring meals, but both were very delicious. Simple is often better.

#6244. Air India CEO Wants ‘More Widebody Aircraft’

Air India is looking to buy more widebody jets as it expands overseas and works to return to profitability.

“We want more widebody aircraft,” CEO Tewolde Gebremariam said Tuesday at the Aviation India and South Asia summit in New Delhi, according to Reuters. The carrier has held talks with both Airbus and Boeing. Gebremariam did not say how many aircraft Air India might buy.

The airline’s most recent Boeing order, announced in January, was for 30 narrowbodies: 20 737 MAX 8s and 10 MAX 10s.

The carrier is also updating the widebodies it already flies. In April, Air India took delivery of the first of 26 older Boeing 787-8s slated for cabin retrofits. The aircraft went from two cabins to three with the addition of premium economy.

Gebremariam, who previously led Ethiopian Airlines, described high operating costs as a “major concern” but said he expects Air India to return to profitability “very soon.”

Air India Group lost S$3.56 billion in the fiscal year ended March 31, according to financial disclosures from Singapore Airlines, which owns a 25% stake in the group. The loss came as the carrier dealt with disruption from the war in Iran and Pakistan’s closure of its airspace to Indian airlines.

#6243. Cheers At The Gate As American Airlines Pilots Save My Flight From Cancellation

Never have I been so happy to board a delayed American Airlines flight…because we actually took off when I thought we were certain to face cancellation. And it culminated in a way that left me smiling.

American Airlines is famous for its rolling delays and I recently encountered one on a flight from Chicago to Los Angeles. While AA has promised that it going to do a better job of communicating delays and trying to predict actual departure time based on aircraft placement, it still has some work to do.

My flight was originally supposed to leave at 7:10p but I received a text message in the afternoon that it would be delayed until 8:15p, which actually was idea for me. I showed up to the airport at 7:30p, had a quick bite to eat in the Admirals Club, and prepared to board…but boarding never began. Instead, the delay was pushed to 8:45p. Then it was pushed to 9:00p. Then 9:30p. Then 10:15p. Then 11:30p. Then 11:55p.

The other AA evening flight to Los Angeles was facing similar delays.

Why? The aircraft was on the ground and at the gate. It had been there since 7:45p.

One of the agents in the Admirals Club turned her screen to me and said, “See look, you’ve got no pilots.”

Sure enough, no pilots were assigned to my flight, though it made no sense to me…this was an A321 and were in Chicago O’Hare, a hub. Does AA have no reserve pilots there that can fly an Airbus?

During this time I went back and forth between the gate and the lounge, because the rolling delays notifications often came late and while I know you usually get a text message when boarding starts, that is not always the case and I did not want to miss the flight (like Andrea Sachs).

The poor gate agents were fielding the angry mob…people were livid and many were freaking out that the flight would not cancel. The gate agent didn’t exactly help by stating his belief the flight would cancel, but I appreciated his candor.

Back in the Admirals Club, suddenly the pilot positions were filled. They were being flown in from Dallas, said the agent.

Seems like a product of poor planning, but okay. I was offered a hotel room if I wanted to bail and rebook for tomorrow (“But it aint gonna be at the Hilton”) but I really wanted to get to LA without a short night in a hotel room.

Back at the gate, we were told that though the pilots had been assigned, it would be up to them determine whether they wanted to accept the overtime assignment and fly the flight…the gate agent once again was on the pessimistic side. Many passengers were (understandably) irate.

But around 11:15p, the Dallas flight pulled up to the gate. We all waited anxiously.

Suddenly, a first officer rounded the corner and the whole gate area broke out into cheers. Someone called out, “Are you our pilot?!” and he flashed the thumbs up sign.

Moments later, the captain showed up to another chorus of cheers.

The trip was on! Boarding soon commend and we were on our way…very late, but on our way.

And as an added bonus, since so many passengers bailed, I got a first class upgrade at the gate, minutes before boarding. Better than three seats in economy class? Probably not, but certainly better than just an open middle in Economy Extra and I ended up enjoying a delicious salmon dinner enroute to LAX and still enjoying a nap for a couple hours due to the late hour.

I wish AA would get their act together, but after hours of rolling delays, I was just thankful to get home without having to overnight in ORD.

Bonkers but I do like the salmon grain bowl or whatever they call it. One thing I really like about AA catering is that they don’t skimp on the veggies.

I have friends who work for major carriers here in the US, my question is how long was the food sitting on the plane? When a rolling delay happens in most cases the plane is catered for the original delayed departure time which in this case was 8:15 pm. However due to rolling delays it appears they didn’t leave the gate until 11:55 pm. At that time of night is it highly unlikely catering came back and re-catered the flight. Several of my friends have told me one of the most frustrating things they face as flight attendants during rolling delays is trying to get a flight re-catered and 9 times out of 10 the operation center refuses the request to re-cater the flight.

It is quite possible the food sat on the airplane for at least 4 hours without refrigeration if catering catered the flight for a 8:15 pm departure.

Glad this one worked for you, Matthew. This is why investing in operational resilience, reserves, properly paying and supporting crews and workers, all the above matters. Create the right incentives, get better staffed and maintained aircraft, less disruptions, actual duty of care, etc. I still think we need better guardrails, a sturdier baseline, meaningful air passenger rights like an EU/UK 261 in the US, regardless.

A very long day and those rolling delays are a pain. I could have gone home, rested, had a meal and/or nap and still had time to get to the flight on time.

I think after the first delay was extended I’d be looking at availability on United

Believe me I did, but UA has no late flights from ORD-LAX.

Oh man, you’re right.. they definitely used to have one around 9:30p

Very similar thing happened to me at ORD this week. Storms in Miami cancelled the last two incoming planes, rebooked the next morning. BUT Admiral’s Club agent saved the day by getting us the last seats on the last plane out. Every irregular operations at AA in the past 12 months has been solved quickly and satisfactorily. I see real improvement.

I wonder if either the FO or Captain were actually on their phone as they approached the gate…or fake calling to avoid any pax interactions? Just an observation…

#6242. Denver Airport Taco Bell Worker Sues Over Unpaid Security Time. So Much For My $1.70 Burritos?

I had barely finished celebrating $1.70 burritos at Denver Airport when View From The Wing highlighted a lawsuit that might help explain why airport food usually costs so much more. No, we did not coordinate our Taco Bell coverage. Apparently, we just had different concerns about what happens before someone hands me a burrito.

A former Taco Bell food preparer at Denver International Airport is suing the restaurant’s operator over allegedly unpaid time spent passing through security and traveling to the restaurant before clocking in. The Colorado state court lawsuit also alleges failures to provide paid rest breaks, according to Law360.

Meanwhile, I had just written about finding surprisingly affordable Taco Bell food in Concourse A. A reader noticed the coincidence and wondered about the relationship between my cheap burritos and Gary’s discussion of employee compensation.

My first instinct is to distinguish getting to work from doing the job. Most employees do not get paid for their commute, even when traffic makes it miserable. An airport restaurant operator does not control the security checkpoint, either.

But Colorado’s wage rules give the worker a substantial argument. They specifically include security or safety screening, and waiting for it, among activities that can constitute compensable time worked. The rules also provide circumstances in which travel between work locations must be paid once work has begun.

That raises a question beyond the checkpoint itself: if required screening starts the paid workday, does the subsequent journey to the restaurant count too?

At Denver Airport, getting through security does not necessarily mean you are anywhere near your workstation.

Taco Bell can reasonably argue that the screening and journey remain part of the commute and the lawsuit, on its own, does not establish that wages were unlawfully withheld. Still, Colorado’s express inclusion of security screening makes this a claim worth taking seriously.

I often roll my eyes at airport food prices. My recent Denver visit included a nearly $20 barbecue salad and a $6.25 street taco that left me much less satisfied than Taco Bell.

But this dispute illustrates a genuine expense associated with operating inside an airport.

If employees must be paid while waiting for screening and making their way to the restaurant, the operator is paying for time before anyone starts preparing food or serving customers. That expense has to be absorbed somewhere. Some of it could end up in menu prices. Indeed, it must.

Every overpriced airport meal is not suddenly justified, but workers should not forfeit compensation required by law so I can enjoy a cheap lunch. It is a more convincing explanation for a price premium than simply charging more because passengers have nowhere else to go…

I hope those $1.70 burritos stick around. After praising them, I would prefer not to discover that I had written their farewell tribute.

But if airport employees must be paid for additional time getting through security and reaching their workplace, higher operating costs will put pressure on those bargains. I can appreciate affordable food and recognize that providing it inside an airport comes with expenses the neighborhood Taco Bell does not face. Gary and I managed to cover both sides of that equation without even comparing notes!

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

Personally I just enjoyed yesterday’s Denver dichotomy, but I suppose Part 3 of the Taco Bell Trilogy will need to include a discussion of the economics of a loss leader item like the rice and beans burrito. Presumably there is some interest in continuing to keep that item at a lower cost to help drive traffic – whether that $1.70 goes up to $1.99 who knows (only “the market” I suppose), but probably won’t go to $2.50. As with any classic loss leader item, it often leads to the purchase of a higher value item in tandem – in your case, a still relatively modest $3 steak burrito.

Of course, you ended up adding steak to the $1.70 rice and beans burrito making it cost $3.50 instead of $1.70. Was that worth it versus the $3 steak burrito? Inquiring minds and all.

You are a careful reader. I like the bean/rice burrito because it comes with jalapeño sauce, which otherwise would cost 70 cents to add since Taco Bell doesn’t let you “swap” sauces on almost every item. But both items were fine.

But Wait! I thought if we increased the operating costs to run a business, the costs to the consumer WON’T go up!

Because that’s what 1990 always says when he wants to implement EU261 in the US, or wants higher compensation for delays, or wants delays out of the control of the airlines to be considered “within their control”, or wants airlines to increase reserve aircraft and crew coverage, etc. etc. etc. He says that can be done without increasing air fares.

Oh well. Cue to “anti-worker” or “anti-consumer” or “pro-fat-cat-corporation” label to be thrown my way.

Yes, sometimes those consumer protections create a far more smoother, predictable, and thereby efficient system and those who “pay a little more” actually don’t lose, because they are protected too.

Sort of like we don’t need “free riders” who claim they don’t need health insurance because of “muh freedom” but then clog ER waiting rooms when something goes bad because they know that they will not be turned away.

After some delays, United Airlines is one step closer to launching service on its posh new domestic plane.

The airline on Thursday evening announced it recently took delivery of its first Airbus A321neo “Coastliner” plane.

It’s a premium-heavy aircraft that will feature United’s new Polaris business-class suites and a true premium economy cabin.

And it will soon be a fixture on the carrier’s top transcontinental routes.

United shared a sneak peek of the new jet on social media Thursday evening —  well ... the outside of it, at least.

As expected, the exterior sports a special wrap featuring the “Coastliner” decal.

That’s because United plans to exclusively use this plane on its most premium coast-to-coast flights.

Once in service, you’ll see it on routes from Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and San Francisco International Airport (SFO).

It will likely also figure into the carrier’s plans at John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), once United makes its long-awaited return to JFK.

While United had hoped to launch service on the Coastliner this past summer, delays at Airbus pushed the debut back a few months.

The jet is now slated to make its inaugural flight in early 2027, United said this week.

It will certainly be an upgrade to the airline’s prime transcontinental service.

Passengers flying in those suites will get access to United’s Polaris Lounge facilities.

There are also 12 Premium Plus recliners across three rows in a two-by-two configuration.

Plus, in economy there’s a walk-up snack bar.

The whole interior is very similar to the Airbus A321XLR that United debuted late this summer. That longer-range jet is slated to start flying to Europe in the coming months.

United’s looming introduction of the Coastliner comes as a growing number of U.S. carriers are upgrading their top transcontinental products.

This fall, Alaska Airlines revealed it will add lie-flat suites and premium economy to a future subfleet of Boeing 737 MAX 10 jets.

American Airlines last year launched coast-to-coast service with the A321XLR, which sports its latest-generation Flagship Suites up front.

Delta Air Lines, meanwhile, rolled out a version of the Airbus A321neo that doesn't have lie-flat seats (at least not yet) but does have a whopping 44 domestic first-class recliners.

Plus, JetBlue recently announced that passengers flying in its lie-flat Mint cabins would be entitled to enter its new airport lounges in New York City and Boston, even when flying domestically.

United has 50 of these Coastliners (along with 50 of the XLR jets) on order for the coming years.

So this aircraft will be a big part of the carrier’s most lucrative domestic service for years to come.

#6240. Can Dubai Become the World's Fittest City?

At 6 a.m. on Sunday, November 22, Dubai's Sheikh Zayed Road will fall silent. For one morning only, the city's six-lane superhighway—usually a blur of Nissan Patrols, taxis, and delivery scooters—will belong to tens of thousands of competitors as Dubai Run takes over the city’s skyline at dawn, following in the footsteps of a record 307,000 participants last year.

Leading the charge is usually Dubai's Crown Prince Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, the driving force behind the Dubai Fitness Challenge (DFC) and one of the city's most ambitious experiments: to turn itself into the fittest city in the world.

"The people of Dubai have created an inspirational fitness movement, sending a powerful message that traveled far beyond our city,” Sheikh Hamdan said during a previous edition of the challenge. “Together, let us transform Dubai into the fittest city in the world.”

An athlete himself, the Crown Prince has long championed cycling, diving, and long-distance running, but the challenge—now in its tenth year—is his most visible legacy. Launched in 2017, it calls on residents and visitors alike to commit to 30 minutes of exercise every day for 30 days each November. Since its inception, more than 16 million people have taken part, transforming what began as a simple invitation to get moving into one of the world’s largest community fitness initiatives.

This year’s landmark edition is running until Sunday, November 29 under the theme What’s Your 30x30?, inviting residents and visitors to find their own way to complete 30 minutes of daily activity. With four flagship events, three free Fitness Villages, and more than 30 Community Fitness Hubs, the program is among the most ambitious yet, transforming everything from beaches and public parks to shopping centers and major roads into places to exercise.

The first Dubai Fitness Challenge took place in 2017

Four major events headline the 2026 calendar: Dubai Ride, which opened the challenge on Sunday, November 1 with thousands of cyclists taking over Sheikh Zayed Road; Dubai Run, the world’s largest free community fun run, on Sunday, November 22; Dubai Stand-Up Paddle, a two-day festival of paddle boarding, kayaking and yoga at Hatta Dam on Saturday, November 7 and Sunday, November 8; and Dubai Yoga, which returns for its second edition on Sunday, November 29, bringing thousands together for a mass sunrise session beneath the DIFC Gate Building.

Three Fitness Villages—at Kite Beach, Zabeel Park and Al Warqa’a—act as free, all-day wellness hubs offering everything from boxing and beach volleyball to spin classes and meditation. More than 30 neighborhood Community Hubs have also been set up across the city, bringing fitness closer to home with pop-up runs, rooftop yoga, skateboarding lessons, padel tournaments, and family-friendly bootcamps.

The calendar aligns with a packed line-up of international sporting events, from the Dubai Premier Padel P1 and T100 Triathlon to the DP World Tour Championship and Emirates Dubai 7s. This year also brings the return of the Dubai Sail Grand Prix, with high-speed catamarans racing off the city’s coastline, while HYROX Dubai will see athletes tackle a grueling combination of running and functional fitness challenges. Elsewhere, the program includes obstacle races, mountain trails in Hatta, and community running events across the city.

It’s all part of what His Excellency Saeed Hareb, Secretary General of the Dubai Sports Council, describes as a lasting change in the city’s relationship with exercise. “It has helped establish a culture of active living, bringing communities together and making sport and physical activity an integral part of life in Dubai,” he said as the challenge marked its tenth anniversary.

Ahmed Al Khaja, CEO of Dubai Festivals and Retail Establishment, says the anniversary is an opportunity to reflect on how far the initiative has come. Speaking at the launch of the 2026 program, he credited the collaboration between government bodies, private businesses, and local communities with making exercise increasingly accessible across Dubai. The aim, he said, is to inspire healthier habits that continue long after the 30-day challenge ends.

The numbers suggest it’s working. Last year’s edition attracted a record three million-plus participants, up from 2.73 million in 2024. More than 307,000 people took part in Dubai Run alone, while Dubai Ride welcomed 40,327 cyclists. Since the challenge launched in 2017, cumulative participation has exceeded 16 million, a remarkable figure for an initiative that began with a simple invitation to exercise for half an hour a day.

The Dubai Ride closes the city's busiest highway for one morning each year

Ethan Matthews, Chief Operating Officer at Reset Fitness and a former professional rugby player and coach in Portugal and Italy, says that Dubai’s greatest fitness asset is its variety. “There are world-class facilities on every block now—not just gyms, but parks, cycling tracks, and sports complexes,” he says. “Try as many things as possible—team sports, group sessions, individual training. It’s about finding what challenges you physically but also what you actually enjoy. That’s how you stay consistent, especially on the tough days.”

For Matthews, the social aspect is just as vital. “The moment you find something you like—padel, CrossFit, running, whatever—you meet people. It opens doors, both personally and professionally. That’s what keeps Dubai’s fitness culture alive.”

Anthony Lee, a personal trainer and owner of Activ8 Lifestyle & Fitness who has spent nearly two decades as part of Dubai’s fitness scene, thinks the timing of the challenge is part of its success. “It’s clever,” he says. “It's just before Christmas, when everyone wants to feel a bit fitter before heading home for the holidays, and when the weather’s perfect for being outdoors.”

He describes the month-long initiative as “a push that gets people back into routine,” and a rare opportunity to sample new workouts without cost or commitment. “You can try boxing on Kite Beach one day, yoga in Zabeel Park the next. It breaks the monotony.” What stands out most, he adds, is accessibility. “You don’t have to be an athlete. It’s about being a better version of yourself—you versus you.”

For visitors, the challenge offers a very different way to experience Dubai as, during November, the city’s hotels, cafes and shopping centers adopt a surprisingly sporty rhythm. At Kite Beach, sunrise yoga sessions fill up fast, while the public running track buzzes with tourists and locals alike, and Zabeel Park hosts evening workouts beneath the skyline. There's no need to sign up—just show up on the day.

Outside of November, the spirit of the challenge remains. Dubai has built more than 557 kilometers of cycle tracks, with a goal of 1,000 kilometers by 2030, and the urban planning department is adding shaded walking routes to make exercise feasible for longer stretches of the year.

Lee, the personal trainer, believes Dubai’s fitness drive has found fertile ground because of the city’s demographic and design. “It’s a young place,” he says. “Most people are working-age expats, and with the beach and pool culture here, people want to look and feel good.”

But vanity isn’t the whole story. “Every new residential tower has a gym and a pool, so exercise is built into daily life,” he says. “When I moved here 18 years ago, you had a handful of hotel gyms and a couple of Fitness First branches. Now every neighborhood has options, from boutique studios to outdoor circuits.” He has also noticed a social shift: “Fitness has become a way to meet people. For newcomers, joining a class or trying padel is how you find your tribe.”

This year’s Dubai Fitness Challenge runs under the theme What’s Your 30x30?

The fitness calendar's cleverest invention, however, might be the Mallathon. With summer temperatures soaring past 45°C, nine of the city’s biggest malls were converted into indoor running routes between June and September, attracting 100,000 participants.

Dr Amir Firouzjaei, a general practitioner and traditional Chinese medicine expert who has lived in Dubai for three years, believes the movement taps into something deeper. “When a city moves, its energy moves,” he says. “It’s not only about training the body but refreshing the mind and spirit.”

He explains that the city’s blend of high-intensity exercise and restorative practices “keeps the balance between energy and recovery,” preventing burnout and encouraging people to “stick with it.”

The trend is filtering into Dubai's hospitality scene, too. New-generation hotels such as SIRO One Za’abeel pitch themselves as “fitness and recovery” spaces, complete with in-room stretching areas, altitude chambers and performance coaches. In Al Quoz, the Matcha Club—a blend of padel courts, co-working space, and cafe—has become the new social hang-out for the health-minded. Even Dubai’s famously indulgent brunches are getting lighter, with restaurants like Eat Well dishing up bowls, turmeric shots, and cold-brew coffee instead of the traditional Champagne towers.

Matthews, who moved to Dubai in 2017—the same year the first Dubai Fitness Challenge launched—says he’s watched the city’s attitudes shift dramatically. “Post-Covid, the appetite for fitness just exploded,” he says. “Gyms, studios and open-air facilities have multiplied, but more importantly, people’s reasons for exercising have changed. They’re doing it to feel good, not just to look good.”

He believes that’s partly because of education and access. “The government has played a big role through campaigns like 30x30, but accessibility is the real game changer. Whether it’s walking paths, beach gyms or purpose-built cycling tracks, there’s always somewhere to move.” For Matthews, that accessibility underpins a healthy, sustainable economy. “When people feel better, they perform better—at work, at home, everywhere. Fitness has become part of Dubai.”

Residents and visitors alike are invited to discover new ways to move, connect and build healthy habits that last beyond the challenge's 30 days

Firouzjaei, the doctor, sees Dubai’s fitness boom as part of a wider cultural shift. “It’s a fast city, and that creates pressure,” he says. “People here work hard and compete hard, so they need ways to recharge and reset.”

He points out that the city’s international mix has made wellness more mainstream. “Residents come from everywhere—Asia, Europe, the Middle East—and many already know yoga, acupuncture, or functional medicine,” he says. “They’re open to new ideas and they understand that health is an investment rather than a luxury.” In his clinic, he’s noticed that even patients who once focused purely on appearance now talk about sleep, stress, and balance.

Behind the lifestyle messaging lies the emirate's urban agenda. Dubai wants to be a ‘20-minute city,’ where every resident can reach work, shops, and recreation within a short cycle or walk. The health argument is compelling. Obesity and diabetes are major public health concerns across the Gulf, and studies show only one in five UAE children meets recommended daily activity levels. City officials believe that building infrastructure—parks, cycle paths, open gyms—is the surest way to shift behavior.

Already, habits are changing. Park footfall has risen 20% year-on-year, while corporate wellness participation has grown by 30%. The once-novel sight of commuters jogging to metro stations has become almost ordinary.

According to experts, Dubai's mix of international residents has made wellness more mainstream

For tourists, taking part couldn’t be easier. The Dubai Fitness Challenge app lists daily events, classes, and pop-ups across the city, most of them free.

Looking back on 18 years in Dubai, Lee says the transformation has been “massive.” When he first arrived, “there were far fewer gyms, and fitness wasn’t part of daily conversation.” Now, he says, it’s as visible as the skyline itself. “Sure, some people join the big events just for the photos—you’ll always have that—but for others it’s the start of something lasting,” he says. “Even if they only do the challenge for a month, it plants a seed. And that’s what counts.”

Matthews agrees, though he cautions against seeing Dubai’s fitness scene as something reserved for the elite. “The biggest misconception is that you have to be in peak shape to take part,” he says. “You don’t. Fitness here is for everyone, from people training for Ironman to those who just want to walk their dogs or join a weekend bootcamp.”

Dubai has always been a city in motion, but now it wants its progress measured not by the height of its towers or the size of its megaprojects, but by footsteps, pedal strokes and heartbeats. It's a city that’s, quite literally, on the move—and inviting the world to keep up.

Dubai’s biggest community running event transforms Sheikh Zayed Road into a traffic-free running track, with participants choosing between a 5km route through Downtown Dubai or a longer 10km course finishing beneath the DIFC Gate Building. More than 307,000 runners took part last year.

Where: Sheikh Zayed Road, starting near the Museum of the FutureWhen: Sunday, November 22, 6.30 a.m.How to take part: Register free at at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

Marking the finale of Dubai Fitness Challenge, thousands of yoga enthusiasts will gather beneath the iconic DIFC Gate Building for a mass sunrise session. The program includes guided breathwork, a sound bath and a 30-minute yoga session, with dedicated areas for families and women.

Where: DIFC Gate BuildingWhen: Sunday, November 29, sunriseHow to take part: Register free at at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

Dubai’s largest beachfront Fitness Village returns with everything from spinning and yoga to padel, beach volleyball, basketball and cricket. There are dedicated activity zones, bookable courts and daily fitness classes, with the Arabian Gulf providing a rather spectacular backdrop.

Where: Kite Beach, JumeirahWhen: Saturday, October 31 to Sunday, November 29; weekdays 3 p.m.–11 p.m., weekends 7 a.m.–11 p.m.How to take part: Register free on-site, with selected activities available to book at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

Zabeel Park’s Fitness Village returns with boxing, spinning, basketball, padel, and daily group workouts, alongside dedicated children’s activities. The village also serves as the official bib collection point for Dubai Run.

Where: Zabeel Park, Gate 2When: Saturday, October 31 to Sunday, November 29; weekdays 4 p.m.–11 p.m., weekends noon–11 p.m.How to take part: Register free on-site, with selected activities available to book at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

Set among palm trees and parkland, this neighborhood-style Fitness Village combines outdoor exercise with family-friendly activities. There’s a 2.8km running and cycling track, bike rentals, daily fitness classes, dedicated ladies-only areas and courts for padel, volleyball, football, and basketball.

Where: Al Warqa’a ParkWhen: Saturday, October 31 to Sunday, November 29; daily 4 p.m.–11 p.m.How to take part: Register free on-site, with selected activities available to book at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

#6239. Christmas Flights To Europe Cost $2,000 Each In Economy. Should I Book Now Or Gamble On Award Space?

I’m faced with a travel dilemma concerning holiday airline tickets and as I evaluate how best to handle it, I thought I would solicit your feedback, dear readers.

We want to spend Christmas in Germany this year and arrive the weekend before Christmas. My wife’s family is having a big Christmas party the weekend before and as many of her family is aging, it’s important that we are there.

My objective, as with every transatlantic trip, is to use points to pay for the ticket, preferably in premium cabin, and even more preferably on the outbound overnight flight to Europe.

But have you checked Christmas fares from the USA to Europe lately? They are through the roof! Last year, I had no trouble getting SAS business class tickets on Christmas Eve to Europe (though from Chicago instead of Los Angeles), returning on New Year’s. This year SAS has nothing and we need to fly earlier anyway…at the same time many others are also trying to go.

Economy class tickets are pushing $2,000 each and I don’t see anything close to saver space on the usual suspects (I’m monitoring space using Atmos, AAdvantage, Aeroplan, Avios, Flying Blue, and MileagePlus, I’m also using tools like Seats.Aero to track award space).

But at this point, there’s really nothing…and I’m not being picky. I’ll take economy class or long layovers, but I’m just not willing to pay 4-5x saver pricing or the current cash price.

I can handle this is one of three ways. First, I can just wait and hope that saver space opens. It’s too early to tell how full these flights will get, but waiting for saver space to open has generally worked in the past with a couple days of flexibility.

Second, I can buy the tickets now in case the price goes up later. If book with United, if the price goes down I can cancel and rebook, baking the residual as a future flight credit. If I wait and do nothing, I may end up spending even more as well get closer to travel because this trip is happening no matter what (God willing…).

The third option would be flying to Germany a week earlier and staying a week later…the luxury of time. My wife’s schedule would not allow it – she’s traveling on set dates regardless of cost (and yes, I’ve also been tracking single award seats for her).

I’m less worried about the kids missing school than me trying to work from Germany, which is great for blogging but not so good for the other work that I do.

#6238. United Airlines Pilots Defy ATC Orders To Fly Through “The Worst Part” Of A Severe Thunderstorm

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

United Airlines pilots scheduled to operate a nonstop flight from San Antonio International Airport (SAT) to Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) refused to accept the air traffic control's proposed routing to the US capital, after they identified that the route would take them directly through a severe thunderstorm.

A recording shared by Aviation MP4 shows the moment the pilot questioned ATC's clearance, which, instead of routing the service around the worst weather, put the jet on a trajectory through the heaviest rain and thunderstorms. The pilot in command ultimately has the final say on whether the flight can operate, as they hold operational responsibility and safety for the flight. For this event, the pilots' concern was also backed up by United dispatch.

UA471 operates from San Antonio to Washington Dulles. It is believed that this incident occurred on Friday, but has not been confirmed by Simple Flying. As the plane pushed back from the gate and taxied to the runway, the recording captured the moment the crew questioned the proposed route. Initially, air traffic control had rerouted the Boeing 737-700 to depart south and travel around the severe weather.

During the flight's taxi, the moments shared had the flight crew challenging the decision, with the pilot noting that he was going to speak with United dispatch, and that the crew was refusing to fly through what would have been up to four hours of challenging weather conditions for the crew, and unfavorable comfort for the passengers onboard.

Simple Flying reached out to United for comment on Saturday, and the airline confirmed the flight landed safely.

Pilots onboard the flight quickly noted they could not fly the proposed route and instead requested the initial routing, which would have taken the Washington-bound flight south of the severe weather. The air traffic control (ATC) reevaluated the plan, while the United pilots spoke to airline dispatch, which backed them up, noting that they should not be flying through the adverse weather.

In the end, the crew was permitted to fly an alternative route, highlighting pilots' authority to reject an unsafe clearance request and choose an alternative. While air traffic control provides instructions and proposed flight paths, pilots in command have final responsibility for the aircraft's safety and the safety of everyone onboard, including passengers and crew.

UA471 has a scheduled departure time of 7:00 AM and an expected arrival time of 11:13 AM. The usual flight duration is two hours and 45 minutes. For the proposed route, flying through the thunderstorm would have added almost an hour of extra flying time, according to the pilot's commentary in the video shared above.

The lasting impacts of the unthinkable on ATC.

The Pilot-in-Command (PIC) holds final authority over an aircraft's operation and safety. They can challenge or disagree with air traffic control or airline dispatch if they believe the situation could be unsafe. Pilots have specific rights and protocols they can use.

This can include rejecting clearance and requesting an alternative. They can also declare an emergency and deviate from any air traffic control clearance without prior permission if safety is compromised.

From SAT, United and United Express maintain regular scheduled flights to Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD), Denver (DEN), Houston George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH), Newark (EWR), San Francisco International Airport (SFO), and IAD.

#6237. American, Delta, And United Accused Of Collusion To Keep Airfares High

American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, and other major carriers face new lawsuits alleging they share sensitive pricing and shopping data to keep airfares higher than they would otherwise be. While watching competitors’ prices is ordinary business, pooling information in a way that discourages competition deserves a much closer look.

View From The Wing highlights two proposed class actions targeting the Airline Tariff Publishing Company (ATPCO), its subsidiary 3Victors, and major U.S. airlines.

The Washington complaint names airline companies including American, Delta, United, Southwest, Alaska, Hawaiian, and JetBlue. A separate Virginia complaint targets ATPCO, 3Victors, and a smaller group of carriers.

A central question these lawsuits raise is worth examining: does greater visibility into competitors’ pricing help airlines offer better deals, or make them less inclined to offer deals at all?

ATPCO is an airline-owned company that has long distributed fares and fare rules. The complaints challenge an expansion into pooled shopping data, alleging that participating airlines exchange commercially sensitive information through a common platform and use it to coordinate pricing.

Shopping data can reveal demand before a passenger purchases anything. Searching for a flight generates information about the itinerary requested and the offers returned, even if the customer closes the browser without booking.

On its own website, 3Victors describes participation in Iris this way:

“The more you contribute, the more you receive.”

Its PriceEye description promotes alerts and tools that identify market undercuts and overpricing. Meanwhile, DemandView promises insight into where travelers want to go before they book.

Those descriptions explain why airlines would find the products useful but they do not, at least by descriptions alone, establish that using them violates antitrust law.

The plaintiffs’ concern is that exchanging this information reduces the uncertainty that encourages airlines to compete.

Consider this example. An airline has seats to fill and thinks a lower fare could attract passengers from a competitor. Cutting the price makes sense if it can win enough additional business.

But suppose its competitors can spot and match the discount almost immediately. The airline may gain little additional business while collecting less money from passengers who would have booked anyway. That could make discounting less attractive in the first place.

But there’s a difference between that (legitimate) concern and proving that these particular arrangements unlawfully suppress competition…we’d need to see evidence about what the airlines actually exchange and how they use it.

A sophisticated pricing dashboard is not necessarily evidence of a conspiracy, for I can think of a counterexample.

If American discovers that United is charging $100 less for a comparable flight, it might lower its fare. Passengers benefit. Better information about demand could also help an airline identify an opportunity to add service.

I use comparison tools when buying tickets…I would hardly expect an airline to set its prices without looking at what competitors charge.

The harder question concerns reciprocal access to sensitive information that competitors would not otherwise possess. What exactly is being contributed? How current and detailed is it? Does the arrangement support independent decisions or weaken the incentive to compete?

My concern as a passenger is straightforward. Airlines have become very good at identifying how much we might be willing to pay. I want them to remain equally concerned that another carrier will offer us a better deal. An industry in which competitors can readily anticipate one another’s behavior deserves scrutiny, particularly when the information comes from an exchange they collectively support.

If these cases proceed into discovery, I will be interested in what the contracts and internal communications reveal…I am not ready to declare these lawsuits winners or losers, though I think View From The Wing is probably right that this airlines appear to have th stronger arguments.

Two new lawsuits allege that major U.S. airlines are using shared shopping and pricing information to weaken competition and sustain higher fares. The companies’ public product descriptions establish that extensive competitive data tools exist, though that does not prove unlawful conduct.

Better information can produce lower fares. It can also make an airline more confident that it need not offer one. I want airlines competing aggressively for my business, and these cases raise a fair question about whether their shared data arrangements encourage that competition or undermine it, a fascinating lawsuit indeed.

#6236. Qatar Launches Two South American Destinations

Qatar Airways added two South American destinations on Wednesday, becoming the first Gulf carrier to serve Venezuela.

The new service flies from Doha to Bogotá, Colombia, then continues to Caracas, Venezuela, before returning nonstop to Doha. Qatar Airways will operate the route on Wednesdays and Sundays using a Boeing 777-200LR.

Flights are scheduled to leave Doha at 7:35 a.m. and reach Bogotá at 4:25 p.m. After a 90-minute stop, the aircraft continues to Caracas, arriving at 9 p.m. The return flight leaves Caracas at 11:30 p.m. and reaches Doha at 8:35 p.m. the following day. All times are local.

The airline originally planned to start flying the route in July but postponed the launch following an earthquake in Venezuela, according to Aviation Week.

Qatar Airways is also expanding its codeshare with LATAM to include domestic flights from Bogotá. The agreement will put Qatar’s code on LATAM flights to destinations including Medellín, Cartagena and Cali.

The additions bring Qatar Airways’ network in the Americas to 17 destinations. The carrier began serving South America in 2010 with flights to São Paulo.

#6235. 11 Gorgeous US Ski Vacation Homes Built for Fresh Powder and Easy Slope Access

I’ve been skiing my entire life, venturing out for nostalgic winter weekends on the East Coast and fresh powder-chasing adventures out West. Yet somehow, the anticipation of a new ski season never gets old. Like clockwork, every winter brings a new mountain to explore, a favorite run to revisit, and plenty of reasons to start dreaming about the next snowfall. With El Niño in the conversation and ski resorts across the US gearing up for opening day, there’s no better time to get your winter plans in order.

After all, a memorable ski vacation isn’t just about finding the right mountain (though I take my terrain very seriously). It’s also about the cozy ski towns, the lively après-ski scenes, the snow-covered scenery, and of course, the splendid place to retreat to when it’s time for boots to come off. When it comes to the best ski vacation homes, there are some amenities that really do take these trips to the next level: a hot tub to soothe your muscles, an in-unit washer and dryer to freshen up base layers, a nice fireplace or firepit to cozy up around, and a kitchen for easy meals at home—especially ideal after working up a big appetite on the mountain.

Some of the best ski vacation rentals in the US are every bit as enticing as the mountains themselves. Think glass-walled chalets, design-forward A-frames, and tucked-away cabins with easy access to the lifts. From New England favorites to Western powder havens, these 11 standout stays are worth building your next ski or snowboard getaway around.

Number of guests: 12Bed and bath: 5 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Hot tub, cedar barrel sauna, pool and ping-pong tables, arcade games, boot warmers

If you’re an avid East Coast skier, you’re likely no stranger to Killington’s buzzy ski resort, home to over 200 ski trails of terrain for any level shredder. This five-bedroom cabin makes a great launchpad for those staying in the area. The amenity-filled gem sits only four minutes away from Killington Resort, and comes with a game room, cedar barrel sauna, and mountain views for days. Use the boot warmers in the closet before hitting the mountain, then leave all your gear in the ski shed for storage once you’ve returned. In the evenings, fire up some food on the patio grill then cozy up around the wood-burning fireplace.

Where to ski: Killington Mountain ResortThings to do nearby: Killington Skyeship Base Lodge, The Lookout Tavern, Killington Village, Gifford Woods State Park

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3.5 bathsWhy we love it: Floor-to-ceiling windows, mountain views, fully equipped kitchen, in-unit washer and dryer

I’m adding this Vermont gem to my ski bucket list for a dozen different reasons, starting with the fact that the mountain access is second to none: This spruced-up, slopeside penthouse apartment sits steps from the ski lifts, less than just a five-minute walk to Stowe Mountain Resort’s six-passenger Over Easy Gondola. It’s also a 15-minute drive to one of my favorite mountains, Smugglers’ Notch, where the vibes are always high and the terrain is suitable for all kinds of skiers.

Back at “home,” this modern mountain aesthetic will refresh you after a long day on the slopes. A picture-perfect gas fireplace hangs in front of floor-to-ceiling windows that provide mountain views for days. Tasteful pops of color complete the dining space, comfy blankets line the couch, and the small-but-mighty kitchen has all the appliances you might need for cooking dinner.

Perched 60 feet above New York’s buzzy Hunter Mountain, with a ski (or hiking) trail just across the street, this rental is ideal for a fun-filled New York ski trip not far from the city. In true log cabin fashion, guests can admire the vaulted ceiling made of cedarwood beams, indoor fireplace, and mountain-facing sliding doors which open to a wraparound deck with a firepit. There are odes to nature everywhere, from framed landscape paintings to horns and antlers as wall decor.

The home’s slopeside location is the real draw: As one previous guest wrote in an Airbnb review, “you’ll feel like you’ll have your own backdoor to Hunter Mountain.” While it’s not a true ski-in/ski-out property, the home sits a quick drive or walk away from the Hunter North area, where you can gear up and take off.

While the prime location may be one of the biggest selling points, the decor and design make it even more enticing: The living room, for example, has classic Jackson Hole touches (note the antler chandelier and cozy fireplace), balanced out by light linens and airy textures. You might be hard-pressed to leave this homey adobe, but if and when you do decide to venture out, you can enjoy the two hot tubs and pool at the nearby Sundance Tennis and Swim Club.

Ski days here mean inviting terrain of wide-open slopes, steep chutes, and picture-perfect runs beneath the hulking silhouette of Lone Peak. Just 10 minutes from the resort itself, this gorgeous mountain home sits on a sprawling 23 acres of land in the Lower Beehive Basin neighborhood—a backcountry ski destination in and of itself.

Inside the home, you’ll find modern cowboy country design and swanky amenities in the places that matter. The state is one of the southern mountain regions set to see a spike in snowfall this winter thanks to El Niño. Lucky for those who book this cabin, you’ll be just 23 miles from Taos Ski Valley, and practically at the front door of Angel Fire Resort, a hidden gem famous for wide, smooth, groomed cruiser runs and gentler slopes. Mammoth is another mountain with an El Niño forecast worth keeping an eye on. Rising to 11,053 feet, the Eastern Sierra resort boasts California’s highest ski-resort summit and 3,500 acres of terrain, with plenty of room for everyone from first-timers finding their ski legs to seasoned riders chasing steeper lines. This unique mountain home near the base of the mountain takes its design cues from Japanese ryokans the host has frequented, with a soaring ceiling, dramatic dome-shaped window framing the surrounding peaks, and a loft-like den. The amenities are equally enticing: a hot tub, sauna, massage chair, optional tatami-and-futon sleeping quarters, yukatas, and an enormous shower room. Locationwise, it’s hard to beat: Canyon Lodge is less than half a mile away and walkable, while the Village and Eagle Lodge are both under a mile from the house. On especially snowy days, you may even be able to ski right down the hill and back home.

Where to ski: Mammoth Mountain Ski AreaThings to do nearby: Twin Lakes Vista, Mammoth Creek Park, Sherwin Lakes Trailhead, Mammoth Brewing Company, Canyon Lodge, Whitmore Hot Springs

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Slopeside and central location, heated pool, hot tub, private balcony

Where to ski: Aspen Mountain Ski Resort; Aspen Snowmass Ski Resort; Aspen Highlands Ski ResortThings to do nearby: Aspen Art Museum, Main Street, John Denver Sanctuary, White House Tavern

Number of guests: 5Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Ski-in/ski-out access, hot tub, gas fireplace, mountain views, outdoor seating on the patio

There’s something pretty splendid about staying at 8,300 feet, especially when the mountains are quite literally at your doorstep. This standalone cabin in Big Sky’s iconically named Cowboy Heaven neighborhood is a haven for folks who wish to spend their days outside, whether that means skiing straight from the deck in the winter or taking advantage of the area’s wildlife spotting in general.

It’s especially ideal for couples, small families, or friend groups, with one caveat for your crew: The second bedroom has a queen-over-twin bunk, so five adults looking for equal amounts of space may want to book elsewhere. A big plus? Big Sky’s tiny but endearing town center is less than a 10-minute drive away.

Where to ski: Big Sky Ski ResortThings to do nearby Lone Mountain Ranch, Moonlight Lodge, Big Sky Town Center, Gondola Mid Station, Montana Jack, Beehive Basin Trailhead

Which ski resorts in the US are on the Epic Pass?

The Epic Pass offers skiing and snowboarding at a sprawling collection of USresorts. Major destinations include Vail, Beaver Creek, Breckenridge, Keystone, Crested Butte, Park City, Heavenly, Northstar, Kirkwood, Stevens Pass, and Stowe. There are also regional and partner resorts with more limited access, so check the specific pass tier before booking a trip. Do note that blackout dates and access limits vary by pass, so read the fine print!

Which ski resorts in the US are on the Ikon Pass?

The Ikon Pass has a tempting lineup as well, especially if your winter plans involve chasing snow across the Rockies and Sierras. Its US destinations include Mammoth Mountain, Palisades Tahoe, Steamboat, Winter Park, Aspen Snowmass, Copper Mountain, Big Sky, Jackson Hole, Taos Ski Valley, Deer Valley, Alta, Snowbird, and Sun Valley. Out east, you can head to Killington, Sugarbush, Stratton, Loon Mountain, Sugarloaf, or Sunday River.

Where is El Niño predicted to bring snowfall this season?

For the 2026-27 season, a strong El Niño is shaping the forecast, with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) expecting wetter-than-average conditions across the southern US, from California and the Southwest through the Southeast, as well as along the East Coast. This could mean more opportunities for snowfall in higher-elevation ski destinations, particularly when temperatures cooperate.

However, wetter doesn't automatically mean snowier: NOAA also expects warmer-than-average conditions across much of the West and northern US Seasonal outlooks predict precipitation patterns, not specific snowfall totals, so keep an eye on shorter-range forecasts before planning a powder chase.

Read more about how El Niño is impacting ski resorts here.

The reason is simple: World of Hyatt is my favorite hotel loyalty program, and this card makes it even more rewarding to stay with the brand. Unlike cards that earn transferable rewards, this is very much a Hyatt-focused product. If you’re loyal to Hyatt — or want an affordable way to accelerate your progress toward higher status — it deserves serious consideration.

If there’s one reason why I continue paying the World of Hyatt card’s annual fee, it’s the anniversary free night certificate.

Each cardholder anniversary, you’ll receive a free night award valid at any Category 1-4 Hyatt hotel or resort. I’ve redeemed my certificates at The Standard, Brussels, Hyatt House Manchester in the U.K. and Andaz Mexico City Condesa. In each case, paying cash would have cost considerably more than the card’s annual fee.

Even better, you can earn a second Category 1-4 certificate after spending $15,000 on the card in a calendar year.

That’s the spending threshold I personally target each year. It unlocks another free night and an additional six elite night credits toward Hyatt status for even more value beyond the points you'll earn from that spending.

That said, for frequent Hyatt guests, this perk probably won’t be all that enticing since they’re likely to earn Discoverist status organically. The card becomes more valuable when working toward a higher status level.

Every calendar year, you’ll receive five qualifying night credits automatically, and you’ll earn another two qualifying night credits for every $5,000 spent.

#6233. Six Hours Of Sleep On An Eight-Hour Flight: SAS Business Class Delivered

I mentioned earlier this week we decided to take a last-minute trip to Europe, flying in SAS A330 Business Class. This flight could not have been smoother and I’m so thankful my kids are now such excellent travelers.

We connected through Chicago and spent some time at the excellent Delta Sky Club (it’s huge!) prior to boarding. The Air France Lounge is nice, but the Delta Lounge is even nicer. Full review coming.

Lingering in the lounge, we were among the last to board, finding our seats in the center sections of row one and two.

It was evening and we were tired, but would we be able to sleep?

Dinner service commenced after takeoff and the food on SAS is excellent.

Heidi ordered the fish and I ordered the short ribs, with the intention of sharing, which is something we like doing when we fly together. That said, the salmon was fine by the beef was really delicious, as were the appetizers.

Claire Marie and Augustine did the same thing, with one having beef and the other fish and then sharing. I loved how the kids were so quiet and well-behaved, enjoyed the in-flight-entertainment and also each other’s company.

After dinner the kids went to sleep immediately and Heidi and I soon did as well. A flight attendant asked if we wanted to be awakened for breakfast and we all said no, though I asked if I could have a cappuccino at the top of descent.

We all slept very well…six hours…which is pretty amazing for a flight that is only eight hours long.

As we began our descent, a FA remembered without even my prompting to bring over the cappuccino, which was enjoyable. Heidi slept a bit longer, awaking just 20 minutes before landing. She wanted coffee and was obliged…a great crew.

I’m happy to take family trips to together, though I hope the kids are soon old enough that they can fly economy class while Heidi and I fly business class. Why? Because they can sleep in any seat and the IFE is the same in business versus premium economy or economy. That’s a whole different issue that we can discuss at some future point.

Oh, the purser had an interesting “political” pin, which I’ll discuss next week. But a great flight. Hopefully no jet lag…
