#6232. Why The Boeing 777-9 Is Not A Straight Replacement For Every Airbus A380

minhanphotos & Tom Buysse | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Ethan is an aviation professional with a degree in Aviation Management with Flight from the Florida Institute of Technology. He previously wrote aviation and tourism features for Florida Tech’s student newspaper, The Crimson, where he developed a clear, reader‑focused reporting style. Aviation journalism has remained a consistent priority throughout his career.

He currently holds a Restricted ATP and Commercial Multi‑Engine Pilot certificate and works in aviation supply chain and aircraft component repair. Alongside his industry role, he is pursuing his Certified Flight Instructor rating and actively building flight experience.

A lifelong aviation enthusiast, Ethan spent countless hours at Raleigh–Durham International Airport’s observation deck studying air traffic and practicing amateur photography and videography.

Having been manufactured from 2003 until 2021, the Airbus A380 currently does not have a direct replacement available on the open market. The program itself was designed as a competitive option to a similar, superjumbo aircraft, the Boeing 747. The A380 has the distinction of being the highest capacity commercial jet ever produced, with its most dense example operated by Emirates, at 615 seats.

Due to a shift in a broader market trend of lower capacity, with less dense aircraft being prioritized by airlines, the A380 and 747 are left without a direct replacement. The closest possible successors to this type of jet include both the Airbus A350 and Boeing 777 families, both with high-capacity variants that approach, but do not exceed 500 seats. Some companies that opted for a purchase of the A380 during its production run made the unit a significant part of the network and fleet strategy; sourcing a direct replacement to fill the exact same niche has proven to be difficult for many.

On seat count alone, typical A380 layouts contain 500–600 seats, a window that no aircraft currently in production can comfortably touch with a multi-class layout. Airbus' official product page outlines that the A380 has a whopping maximum certified capacity of 853 seats, a figure that has not been touched by any airline in its operating history. Emirates' previous 615-seat configuration included the signature onboard experience that its customers are used to, at 32 inches (81.28 cm) of legroom. Mathematically speaking, an 843-seat A380 solicits significantly less legroom onboard. Comfort is not the goal with such a layout, but rather maximum capacity at the minimum legal threshold.

Typical 777-9 layouts are around 400–430 seats, with more than one cabin onboard. Flight Global reported back in 2018 that Korean Air once configured an A380 at 407 seats, in an all-business class layout, marking the lowest density example known to have flown. However, this example was exceptional, as it was primarily geared toward select missions as a charter.

Real-world seating differences by airline are of note. Regardless of an airline's configuration, whether it is a premium heavy model like France's La Compagnie, or an all economy 777 layout aboard IndiGo, the A380 simply has more square footage and a higher rated maximum capacity than the 777-9. While an airline can utilize a consistent ratio of economy seats to premium seats onboard, the total number of seats once available on an A380 route cannot be evenly transferred to the 777-9.

Why would an airline ever willingly choose fewer seats? Several different factors are involved, relating back to the four forces of flight: weight, lift, thrust, and drag. A smaller aircraft generally weighs less, requiring less lift to stay airborne and less thrust to maintain cruise speed. Generating that thrust requires burning fuel, while producing additional lift inevitably creates drag that must also be overcome.

Engine count alone does not explain the fuel-burn gap. According to Aero Corner, the 777-9's two General Electric GE9X engines each generate roughly 110,000 pounds of thrust, making them among the most powerful commercial jet engines ever developed. By comparison, the A380's Rolls-Royce Trent 900 and Engine Alliance GP7200 engines are typically rated between 70,000 and 84,000 pounds of thrust each. Combined with advances in bypass ratio, materials, and wing design, the 777-9 can achieve similar mission capabilities while relying on only two engines rather than four.

Boeing claims significant improvements through GE9X and aerodynamics; about 10% lower fuel burn than the Boeing 777-300ER

The A380's maximum takeoff weight (MTOW) is 1.27 million lb (575,000 kg), whereas the 777-9's MTOW is 775,000 lb (351,500 kg). The A380's MTOW is nearly double that of the Boeing, thus requiring nearly double the thrust to lift off and maintain flight. Further, the 777-9 offers a very high aspect-ratio composite wing, folding wingtips, improved lift-to-drag ratio, and fewer engine nacelles to provide an aerodynamic edge over the A380. With a larger wing span, at 235 feet, 5 inches (71.80 meters), it also benefits from an improved lift-to-drag ratio and lower induced drag.

The Airbus A380 can fly up to 16 hours nonstop. Here’s how its massive fuel capacity and range make ultra-long-haul flights possible.

If the objective is moving the maximum possible number of passengers through a slot-constrained airport such as London Heathrow Airport (LHR) or Tokyo Narita Airport (NRT), the A380 remains unmatched. On a high-demand route backed up by the high capacity of a full A380, the choice becomes economical for the operator.

However, airlines besides the A380 giants of Emirates, Qatar Airways, or British Airways do not optimize their fleets around a handful of peak-demand routes. Instead, such companies seek aircraft that can generate profits across a dynamic variety of markets, seasons, and demand conditions. This is where the 777-9's lower fuel consumption, reduced maintenance burden, and greater operational flexibility begin to outweigh its lower seating capacity.

An aircraft that burns approximately 2,000 fewer gallons (7570.82 liters) of fuel per hour than an A380 can often produce a stronger financial result even while transporting fewer passengers. This conclusion is only augmented during times of economic uncertainty and high fuel costs. Now more than ever, due to the Iran conflict, fuel efficiency is undeniably important. With an aviation marketplace that increasingly renders the A380 more and more difficult to operate profitably, where does its niche lie today?

In practice, airlines often use the 777-9 not as a replacement for an individual A380 flight but as a replacement for the role the A380 once played within a network. That distinction is important. Network planners evaluate total market demand, connecting traffic flows, slot availability, and seasonal variation rather than focusing exclusively on aircraft size.

Consider Emirates, Lufthansa, or Qatar Airways. Their largest hubs feed passengers from dozens or even hundreds of routes into long-haul banks. During peak periods, an A380's enormous capacity can be valuable. A380s are typically deployed on routes from Dubai International Airport (DXB), Frankfurt Airport (FRA), and Doha International Airport (DOH) respectively, to global hubs worldwide, like London and John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK). The 777 family can still reliably operate such routes, just not at the same scale as the A380.

A 777-9 gives airlines greater flexibility. During off seasons or weaker demand cycles, those same seats on the A380 become harder to sell profitably. Routes that may support 550 passengers in July might only support 400 in February. Rather than maintaining year-round A380 service, carriers can better match capacity to demand while preserving network connectivity.

What do you think is the real reason Airbus discontinued the A380?

The results of the 777 among other twin engine widebodies are visible throughout the industry. While Airbus ended A380 production in 2021 after delivering 251 aircraft, the Boeing 777X program accumulated hundreds of orders before entering commercial service. Emirates alone ordered more than 200 aircraft from the 777X family, despite remaining the world's largest A380 operator, serving as a strong signal that A380 operators are looking at the 777X program as a makeshift replacement.

Even airlines that continue to fly the superjumbo, including Lufthansa and British Airways, increasingly rely on twin-engine widebodies such as the 777, Boeing 787, and Airbus A350 families for the majority of their long-haul operations. Rather than replacing the A380 route-for-route, modern twinjets have largely replaced the network strategy the aircraft was designed around.

The success of aircraft such as the 777-300ER and later the 787 demonstrated that airlines often preferred operating more frequent flights with smaller aircraft rather than concentrating hundreds of passengers onto a single departure. The 777-9 represents the latest evolution of that philosophy, combining near-A380 range and premium-cabin capability with significantly lower fuel consumption and maintenance requirements.

By default, the end of the A380's production has forced customers to look elsewhere for an ideal replacement. With no commercial quad-jets currently available for purchase from either Airbus or Boeing, the market has pivoted to the highest capacity airframes in production. Fuel efficiency has become not only an added benefit of modern airliners, but also a reason for airlines today to continue the operation and, in some cases, as with Ethiopian Airlines, upgrade its orders.

The market response to each aircraft highlights the industry's shift toward efficient twin-engine widebodies. Airbus reports that it ultimately secured 251 firm orders for the A380 before ending production, while Boeing's 777-9 had accumulated 546 firm orders as of September despite not yet entering commercial service. Using each manufacturer's published list prices, those order totals equate to approximately $111.9 billion in potential A380 sales revenue and roughly $241.4 billion for the 777-9 alone.

While airlines rarely pay published list prices, the disparity nevertheless illustrates how strongly carriers have favored Boeing's large twin-engine strategy over Airbus' superjumbo approach. Boeing has already beaten the A380 in total production revenue, prior to the 777-9's first delivery. This is a solid indication of the program's success that is yet to come, and the broader market trend shifting to highly efficient twinjets in lieu of superjumbos.

#6231. Where to Eat Gluten-Free in Montreal

Recently I’ve noticed more and more food people going to Montreal—and who can blame them? This laid-back bilingual gem on the St. Lawrence River is one of North America’s very best food cities. Personally I’ve loved it since my first visit almost 20 years ago. Montreal’s wonderful food scene draws me back year after year, sometimes multiple times,and by now the six-hour drive from my home in New York City feels like a breeze. It helps to know that my top meals of the year are waiting just across the border.

But for the past two years, following my wife’s celiac diagnosis, I have been navigating the city a little differently. When I was younger, trips to Montreal meant poutine, bagels, smoked-meat sandwiches, and a plethora of other canonical Québécois favorites that happen to be full of gluten. These days we prioritize other local favorites and have developed a dependable roster of businesses we trust—and that don’t feel like a compromise. Luckily there are a ton of them; we’ve been thrilled to discover that Montreal is a paradise for gluten-free eating.

In my opinion the only gluten-free Montreal-style bagels worth sampling are located in Burlington, Vermont. But Montreal is a city that takes its baked goods seriously, and it’s home to a handful of excellent dedicated gluten-free bakeries. You will not miss the bagels. Instead how about a croissant?

Any gluten-free eater knows croissants are one of the hardest pastries to get right without gluten. As a rule my wife and I don’t really bother—unless we’re in Montreal. At Boulangerie Le Marquis, near Jean-Talon Market, and sister business Le Marquis Signature Santé, in Old Montreal, magnificent pains au chocolat and gluten-free croissants—available in plain, almond, and chocolate-almond varieties—arrive hot out of the oven all morning long. Flaky laminated pastry is a near-impossible feat in the gluten-free world, but Le Marquis has perfected it. We favor the pains au chocolat and almond croissants, but it’s tough to go wrong.

Even more unique is the gluten-free manouché at La Bolo à Lolo, a GF market and takeaway in the Plateau. Chef and owner Gordy Moufarrej emigrated from Lebanon to Montreal as a boy and uses his mother’s homemade za’atar in these addictive flatbreads. Made from Moufarrej’s proprietary GF flour blend, they are topped with a paste of olive oil and za’atar, plus cheese if you want (you do). A number of sandwiches made with the same base are available, but we’ve never gotten past the manouché—on our last visit to Montreal, we went three days in a row.

Perhaps unsurprisingly for a French-speaking city, crepes are another great option, and Montreal boasts an amazing spot for 100% buckwheat Breton-style galettes. At Crêperie du Marché, a bustling stall at Jean-Talon Market, cooks turn out a dedicated gluten-free menu of lacy galettes with both savory and sweet fillings. It’s a personal choice, but we like the cheeky selections that mix both: ham, cheese, eggs, potatoes, and a drizzle of maple syrup. Why not?

Nearby is cheery, quirky Cantine Panella, a dedicated gluten-free bakery and café run by the Peruvian chef Alessandra Perona. Her South American sensibility means breads are made with flours like quinoa, cassava, and sweet potato, which gives them a delightful chewiness. We like to stock up on a few of these to bring home, though they sometimes don’t last the drive.

Of all Montreal’s classic foods, rotisserie chicken might be my favorite. At Québécois-style rotisseries it’s slow-roasted on a spit and accompanied by gravy; at Portuguese spots it’s often spatchcocked and grilled over charcoal, then served with piri-piri sauce. In both cases gluten sometimes spoils the fun: Traditional establishments like the legendary Chalet Bar-B-Q and Portuguese eatery Ma Poule Mouillée both use wheat flour in their sauces. No matter—these are far from your only options.

Piri-Piri Chicken at Rôtisserie Coco Rico

At Rôtisserie Coco Rico, a Plateau institution open since 1970, the chicken is spit-roasted and served with GF piri-piri in a mélange of the two dominant local styles. On the side fries from a dedicated GF fryer are among the city’s best (and this is a city with great french fries), but don’t sleep on the roasted potatoes, full of savory chicken flavor.

More refined, and representing the French Canadian tradition, is Little Italy’s Rôtisserie La Lune, from the team behind überpopular restaurant and wine bar Mon Lapin. Gorgeous, plump birds are served with rich gluten-free gravy and excellent fries that come from a blessedly dedicated fryer. The same fryer is also responsible for the unbelievable Croqu’Ailes Farcies XL, which are deboned chicken wings stuffed with more chicken and deep-fried. Every meal here should start with these. But the kitchen has an equally deft hand with seasonal salads and veggie-focused sides—almost always gluten-free and an essential counterweight on the table.

Down the street from La Lune, Mon Lapin is equally adept at catering to gluten-free diners: On two recent visits most of the menu was in play. Dishes change with the seasons, but friendly servers will guide your choices (and help you navigate the impressive wine list). Make sure to save room for the restaurant’s signature buckwheat layer cake, accented with buckwheat honey caramel, fromage blanc, and crisp shards of buckwheat tuile. I’m not sure there’s a better gluten-free dessert on the continent.

Mon Lapin’s co-owners, chefs Jessica Noël and Marc-Olivier Frappier, and wine director Vanya Filipovic, are all alums of the trendsetting Little Burgundy eatery and wine bar Vin Papillon, whose chef and owner happens to be celiac. Best known as half of the duo that opened Montreal icon Joe Beef, Fred Morin now presides over those two restaurants, plus the rotisserie McKiernan and gastropub Liverpool House. His kitchens have airtight allergy protocols and are particularly sensitive to gluten-free diners because of Morin’s own celiac status. And because so many Montreal chefs have passed through Morin’s kitchens, his influence looms large over the city’s fine dining scene—and its spirit of hospitality toward those with allergies and intolerances.

While all of Morin’s restaurants are fantastic, Vin Papillon is the one we come back to every year—its Jambon de la Petite-Bourgogne is one of the world’s great meat-and-cheese plates, featuring house-cured ham, the Quebec sheep-milk cheese le Fleur des Monts, and a sneaky application of brown butter that brings together all the nutty, savory notes. For dessert the restaurant often serves a gluten-free carrot cake ice cream sandwich with caramel sauce in a silver goblet.

Another Joe Beef group alum, Ariel Schor, runs one of our favorite Verdun neighborhood spots with his brother, Pablo. Both natives of Argentina with Jewish roots, the Schors run a restaurant called Beba with a particular affinity for offal (organ meats) and a surprisingly light touch with creative veg dishes that change seasonally. Swiss chard leaves are stuffed with zucchini and chard stems and served with a sweet-and-sour condiment of onions, raisins, and pine nuts. Medjool dates are impishly filled with foie gras and topped with pistachio. Elsewhere on the menu expect things like tongue, rabbit, chorizo, and tripe—dishes that tend to be gluten-free.

When you’re craving Gallic comfort food, Montreal overdelivers. I used to think there were Leméac people and L’Express people, that one couldn’t possibly love Montreal’s two most prominent old-school bistros equally. I was wrong. The late local architect Luc Laporte designed both dining rooms, and they each have the buzzing, joyful energy most restaurants covet.

L’Express is my first love, a Montreal stalwart open since 1980 that I’ve been to more times than I can count. Its main virtues for gluten-free eaters are a dedicated fryer and incredibly good french fries—available as a stand-alone side or, even better, as part of steak frites. There are plenty of other GF mains and entrées, but room must be saved for the enormous île flottante, a classic French meringue-based dessert encased in a hardened caramel dome and surrounded by shards of candied almond. For something on the lighter side, try the unique crème brûlée with wild sweet clover from Quebec, sometimes called boreal vanilla.

Leméac does not have a dedicated fryer, so fries don’t work for celiacs. But I promise you won’t miss them. We favor the textbook duck confit, served with roasted potatoes and a bright green salad. For dessert there’s an unmissable gluten-free chocolate-and-banana moelleux, a decadent cake served with caramel and popcorn ice cream, along with many other classics, including crème caramel.

Montreal is also home to a number of fabulous Middle Eastern and North African restaurants, some of which can cater to gluten-free diners—albeit with asterisks. We love the standout Damas, a Syrian fine-dining spot on a pretty corner in Outremont, though gluten-free choices are limited. Still, it’s worth the trip for the ground lamb and eggplant kebab grilled over open charcoal and accompanied by charred pepper, tomato butter, and gobs of garlic labneh and the dreamy hummus topped with lamb shawarma and pine nuts, which can be served with crudités rather than pita. Both are among the best things I’ve eaten in recent memory.

Le Petit Alep, a neighborhood institution near Jean-Talon, offers more Syrian and Armenian options. The marvelous mezes are largely gluten-free and served—upon request—with crudités; savory, comforting mujaddara is made with lentils and rice, no bulgur, barley, or other glutenous grains. End with the house herbal tea, a beautiful floral mixture of cardamom pods, mint, rosewater, and orange blossom. I’ve tried to make it at home, but I can’t quite replicate it. That’s okay—I’ll be back next year.

If you’re a frequent traveler, scoring elite status with a major carrier like Delta Air Lines can make your journeys more relaxing and rewarding.

However, deciding which airline loyalty program benefits you the most is difficult. This is mainly due to the variations between complimentary upgrades, bonus points or miles, lounge access and other valuable perks. Plus, is it even worth pursuing elite status?

This guide breaks down Delta’s SkyMiles Medallion program, including its four public elite status tiers, how to earn status in 2027 through both travel and non-travel expenses, and the benefits of each level.

Here is everything you need to know about elite Medallion status in the Delta SkyMiles program.

Delta awards elite status to qualifying SkyMiles members each year. Elite status offers a range of benefits — from seat selection to priority boarding — that make travel more comfortable and convenient.

The airline has four published tiers of elite status:

Delta also has an invite-only status tier called Delta 360. While the airline doesn't publish its standard qualification criteria, big spenders could get an invitation to this very special club. Delta also says, “Members that have reached the 5 Million Miler milestone will receive an annual complimentary invitation for Delta 360° Membership.” That's a pretty sweet perk.

Visit our Delta Medallion glossary page for more details.

Flyers earn Medallion status based on their eligible activity during the preceding calendar year. Delta tracks travelers' activity through Medallion Qualification Dollars, which they earn by flying with Delta and its partner airlines, spending on select Delta SkyMiles American Express cards and booking Delta Vacations packages.

For Delta-marketed flights operated by Delta or a partner airline, members generally earn 1 MQD for every dollar spent on the eligible ticket price (including the base fare and carrier-imposed surcharges but excluding government-imposed taxes and fees). For eligible partner-marketed flights, MQD earnings are generally based on a percentage of the distance flown and the purchased fare class, according to Delta's published partner earning charts.

Note: Delta Main Basic tickets generally don't earn MQDs or qualify for Medallion upgrades.

Related: Your guide to Delta Air Lines Million Miler status

You can also earn MQDs on eligible award tickets and through everyday spending on the Delta SkyMiles Platinum, Platinum Business, Reserve and Reserve Business American Express cards. All four cards offer an annual 2,500-MQD Headstart, while eligible spending earns 1 MQD per $20 on Platinum cards and 1 MQD per $10 on Reserve cards.

Your status is valid through Jan. 31 of the following year. For example, travelers who qualify in 2026 will earn 2027 Medallion status, which would be valid through Jan. 31, 2028.

You must meet the applicable Medallion Qualification Dollar thresholds each calendar year to maintain that status.

Delta used to have several ways to earn status, but now the carrier uses only MQDs as qualification criteria. Below are the requirements to obtain 2027 Medallion status:

Delta did not raise the status requirements for 2027 status.

Here are some key benefits of each of Delta’s status tiers.

This is the entry tier in Delta’s program, and you’ll receive benefits like:

Delta’s mid-tier status includes Silver Medallion benefits, plus:

In addition to the Gold Medallion perks, you’ll also get the following:

You’ll get everything detailed above, plus some even better perks:

Check Delta’s website to review the full list of benefits available to SkyMiles Medallion members.

To make it easier to earn elite status, Delta gives eligible frequent flyers who also hold the following cobranded cards a head start on MQD metrics with a boost of 2,500 MQDs (per eligible card type) toward status qualification at the start of the year (and each year thereafter, until further notice):

Since the MQD head start is awarded per eligible card type, you’ll enjoy more than one 2,500 MQD boost if you have multiple eligible cards. Additionally, you’ll be able to enjoy bonus MQDs based on everyday spending on these cards.

Specifically, the Delta SkyMiles Reserve Amex and the Delta SkyMiles Reserve Business Amex will accrue 1 MQD for every $10 spent. Meanwhile, the Delta SkyMiles Platinum Amex and the Delta SkyMiles Platinum Business Amex will accrue 1 MQD for every $20 spent.

Technically, you could earn Delta Medallion status without ever stepping on a plane, simply by putting enough eligible spending on a cobranded credit card. But that doesn't necessarily make it a good strategy,

Even with the MQD Headstart, reaching the higher status tiers through credit card spending alone requires a large financial commitment. Before putting everyday purchases on a Delta card to chase status, consider whether the rewards and benefits justify the cost, when there are lots of other travel credit cards that could offer better returns for you personally.

If you earned Delta elite status in 2025, it’s valid through Jan. 31, 2027. If you qualify in 2026, your status will last until Jan. 31, 2028.

It’s critical to consider how much you’ll be traveling in the future to decide if Medallion status is worth it. If you push hard to reach Diamond Medallion status, the valuable perks outlined above apply only when traveling.

With the high MQD requirements, you would need to spend a significant amount of money with the airline or on a cobranded card to earn this top-tier status. So, you should ensure you're traveling enough to enjoy it.

That said, if you wind up within striking distance of the next tier, consider whether the benefits are worth it for you personally. There’s no reason to go out of your way for perks that don’t matter to you. Pursuing elite status with an airline you can’t realistically fly regularly isn't a great move. Look at Delta’s offerings from your home airport and whether it would be feasible to rely on that airline.

This elite-status hobby has many trade-offs, and one of the most common is deciding whether to use your preferred airline or hotel chain when neither is the most convenient nor the cheapest. Would you book a one-stop Delta flight if Southwest Airlines had a cheaper, nonstop option? If the answer is no, it may not be worth going out of your way to earn Delta elite status (or any elite status, for that matter).

The final consideration involves travel rewards credit cards. Many airline cobranded cards offer perks that mirror what you’d enjoy as an elite member. For example, the includes a free checked bag worldwide and a second checked bag when flying domestic, priority boarding and a 20% inflight savings in the form of statement credit. The card has no annual fee for the first year, then a $150 annual fee (see rates and fees).

Meanwhile, when you fly with Delta, the Delta SkyMiles Reserve American Express Card provides 15 Sky Club lounge visits each year (Feb. 1 through Jan. 31). Cardmembers also qualify for various complimentary seat upgrades and receive an annual companion certificate (valid for round-trip domestic and short-haul international flights to Mexico, the Caribbean and Central America in economy, Delta Comfort, Delta Premium Select or first class). To earn unlimited Sky Club visits each year, the total eligible purchases on the card must equal $75,000 or more between Jan. 1 and Dec. 31 each calendar year.

If you can pay a flat annual fee for one of these cards and gain access to perks that matter to you without going out of your way to earn elite status, that may be a good plan.

Delta Medallion status can make flying more comfortable, particularly if you're a frequent Delta customer who can take advantage of all the perks. But the value of those perks really depends on how often you fly and how much you're willing to spend to earn them.

For most travelers, the goal shouldn't necessarily be "reach Diamond Medallion." Instead, focus on the status tier that offers benefits you'll actually use and avoid spending more or booking less convenient flights just to earn a higher level of status.

If you’re considering switching your loyalty, we hope this detailed review of Delta’s elite status program has helped you make your decision.

#6229. How to Watch the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade

As the turkey thaws and a day of cooking prep begins, an equally integral Thanksgiving tradition is Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. Last year, 3.5 million spectators lined New York City’s streets to watch the procession of vibrant balloons and whimsical floats bob and weave through Midtown Manhattan to the beats of countless marching bands and celebrity performers. Beyond the city, a record-setting 34.3 million tuned into the NBC and Peacock broadcast, making the Emmy-winning production the year’s most-watched entertainment telecast. This year's promises to be even grander, as 2026 marks the 100th anniversary of the spectacle, which started in 1924 (though it wasn’t held from 1942 to 1944 because parade materials were reserved for wartime efforts).

“As a kid from the Bronx, it is an honor to bring this cherished tradition…to the city of New York every year,” the parade’s executive producer since 2021 Will Coss tells Condé Nast Traveler. The annual highlight for him is seeing the joyful expressions of spectators of all ages as the parade passes them by “showcasing some of the most iconic and recognizable pop culture characters and figures.”

This year marks the 99th anniversary of the Macy's Parade, an annual Thanksgiving tradition.

On the eve of the parade's centennial, the team—composed of painters, carpenters, animators, sculptures, welders, designers, engineers, and electricians—is honoring its past by way of revived classics like Felix the Cat and Underdog balloons. Ardent fans will also find a swath of newcomers that include a Fantasia-inspired Mickey, cowboy Minion, and a Peanuts duo. “The team at Macy’s Studios works year-round to make this historic parade bigger and better for our audiences every year,” Coss says. Here’s everything you need to know about the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in 2026—all its surprises, delights, and familiar joys.

When Macy’s first debuted its one-million-square foot New York City flagship store at 34th Street between Broadway and Seventh Avenues in 1924, the retailer threw a Christmas parade on Thanksgiving morning to boost holiday sales—with a much longer route starting at 145 Street and Covent Avenue. Balloons joined the lineup in 1927, starting with Felix the Cat, and the festivities were first broadcast nationally in 1947.

These days, the festive parade follows a 2.5-mile path from the Upper East Side to Midtown Manhattan. Starting at the corner of 77th Street and Central Park West, the route heads south to Columbus Circle and then turns east, heading along 59th Street to Sixth Avenue. From there, it goes straight down Sixth Avenue to 34th Street, ending in front of Macy’s flagship store in Herald Square.

Clifford the Big Red Dog in Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.

Coss recommends arriving early for a great view. Many spectators start to gather as early as 6 a.m. along the beginning of the route on Central Park West (approach from the west) from 61st to 75th Streets. Other prime spots include the south side of 59th Street between Columbus Circle and Sixth Avenue and the entire stretch of Sixth Avenue between 38th and 59th. Spectators should be aware there is no viewing on Central Park West between 59th and 60th Streets, or anywhere south of 38th Street.

Coss also reminds those bringing children to dress warmly for the chilly weather and to be prepared to entertain young ones for a few hours while waiting to spot the first float. He suggests avoiding strollers, large bags, backpacks, and umbrellas.

In celebration of its centennial, some 100 inflatables will fly. Returning after decades are much-anticipated Felix the Cat (the parade's first character balloon, introduced in 1927) and Blue Hippopotamus (from the 1931 parade), while Hello Kitty and Underdog (who appeared in every parade from 1965 through 1984) will also make cameos. New to the scene are Bluey, Buckaroo Bob the Minion, and Snoopy persona Joe Cool with Woodstock, among others. The procession will also welcome 52 floats, 31 clown crews, nine specialty units (such as trycaloons, or balloons ridden on tricycles), seven marching bands, and five balloonicles (that’s a balloon-vehicle hybrid).

TODAY’s Savannah Guthrie, Hoda Kotb, and Al Roker will host the live broadcast of the 100th Macy’s Parade. Though this year's performance lineup has yet to be announced, the 2025 roster featured 26 celebrity performers, ranging from Colbie Caillat and Christopher Jackson to Foreigner and Taylor Momsen, complete with a performance by KPop Demon Hunters’ HUNTR/X singing voices EJAE, Audrey Nuna, and Rei Ami. As anticipation for the parade's centennial only increases, Coss says this year will “bring new surprises and delights to the iconic holiday tradition and truly celebrate this incredibly special anniversary.”

For some, the majestic Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is an official marker of the transition into the Christmas season in New York City.

Americans can watch the live telecast on both NBC and Peacock on Thursday, November 26, from 8:30 a.m. to noon in all time zones, while Telemundo will air a Spanish-language simulcast hosted by Andrea Meza, Aleyda Ortiz, and Clovis Nienow. For late risers, an encore will air starting at 2 p.m. ET/PT, and the full broadcast will also be on NBC with live audio description on Secondary Audio Program channel (SAP). Behind-the-scenes footage will be shared on social media @macys and #MacysParade via Instagram, TikTok, and Threads.

To rev up for the turkey day excitement, “Countdown to the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade” will air on Wednesday, November 25, on NBC and Peacock. The primetime special will broadcast live from the parade starting line with exclusive previews and behind-the-scenes stories from the balloons and floats.

One of the most underrated—and free—ways to experience the parade is by attending the Thanksgiving Eve balloon inflating event on Wednesday, November 25, a “time-honored tradition and special peek into the parade celebrations,” Coss says. Since 1994, the Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade has invited guests to see the process the balloons undergo to reach their larger-than-life size and scale the afternoon before Thanksgiving. Last year’s took place between 1 p.m. and 6 p.m., with the line opening at noon.

Those interested can enter at West 72nd Street and Columbus Avenue, where they’ll be guided through a security checkpoint and then can roam between West 77th and 81st Streets to view the balloons. Note that prohibited items include bags or backpacks larger than 12-by-6-by-12 inches, lawn chairs, large coolers, alcoholic beverages, chairs, weapons, drones, pets, and umbrellas; participants will be screened before entering the route.

For the latest up-to-date information, visit macys.com/parade for details on the parade and nbc.com/macys-thanksgiving-day-parade for updates on the broadcast.

#6228. We Tracked The First Boeing 717 Ever Built For 24 Hours: Here's How Many Flights It Squeezed In

In Hawaii, a very important piece of aviation history is still flying between islands and continuing to serve passengers after nearly 30 years in operation. Using the Simple Flying Live Flight Tracker, we monitored registration N488HA through a 24-hour operating window, watching how the world's oldest surviving Boeing 717 churned through ten distinct sectors in a single day.

Observing this specific airframe in real time lays bare the relentless operational demands that define interisland scheduling. As regional carriers squeeze maximum productivity from aging twin-jets, following line airframe MSN 55001 offers a rare window into how classic engineering handles ten rapid cycles of takeoff, climb, and descent in a single calendar day.

The history of MSN 55001 begins long before its current life in Hawaii, originating in 1998 as Boeing’s flight testbed registered as N717XB, as per AirFleets. The airframe served as the foundational platform for certifying the MD-95 derivative before commercial assembly ramped up in Long Beach. Following that, the MD-95 program was then rebranded as the 717. This pedigree makes the aircraft not just a standard regional transport, but the literal genesis of the entire 717 production line: technically only the second ever produced, but the first to enter regular service.

Following its initial stint as a manufacturer test vehicle, the aircraft crossed the Pacific to fly commercial routes in the Southern Hemisphere. Airport-Data and Simple Flying aircraft analysis documents its tenure operating for Australian carriers Impulse Airlines and Qantaslink under registrations VH-VQA and VH-NXF. During this era, the twinjet proved its mettle on short-haul Australian domestic sectors, establishing the high-cycle durability that would later draw the attention of Pacific network planners.

Eventually, the airframe found its permanent home in the Hawaiian island chain, where it was rechristened with its current registration N488HA and the traditional Hawaiian bird name Puaiohi. Operating under Hawaiian Airlines' colors, it has spent over two decades mastering the short, high-density sectors connecting Honolulu to neighboring island airports. Ultimately, surviving decades of corrosive maritime air and relentless pressurization cycles attests to the robust structural margins engineered into the original Douglas-derived airframe.

According to Simple Flying's tracker replay data, monitoring registration N488HA through Friday, October 9, revealed a punishing schedule that highlights the twinjet's unmatched short-haul efficiency. The day's operations commenced bright and early at Daniel K. Inouye International Airport in Honolulu (HNL), where the aircraft departed at 07:07 local Hawaiian Standard Time (HST) on flight AS1013 across the brief 21-minute hop to Lihue (LIH). Following a rapid ground turnaround, the airframe immediately operated the return leg as AS1024 at 08:13 HST, setting the fast-paced tempo for a tough 24-hour operating cycle.

As midday approached, internal flight logs and tracking replay records show N488HA maintaining its relentless cadence across multiple islands without missing a beat. The aircraft cycled back to Lihue as AS1053 before returning to Honolulu, and quickly pivoted east toward Kahului Airport (OGG) on flight AS1096 at 12:43 HST. Each sector averaged 21 to 27 minutes airborne, showing how the high-thrust Rolls-Royce BR715 engines rapidly accelerate the airframe on short-stage climbs where traditional narrowbodies burn excess fuel during extended altitude transitions. Ground crews at each island destination successfully completed tight gate turnarounds, capitalizing on the aircraft's built-in airstairs to keep passenger boarding moving at peak efficiency.

The evening rotation pushed the aircraft further across the island chain before concluding its demanding operating day late into the night. After completing another rotation through Lihue, N488HA operated flight AS1120 from Lihue down to Kailua-Kona (KOA) with a 45-minute airborne duration, followed by the return sector AS1157 to Honolulu. The final assignment of the day came as flight AS1132, departing Honolulu at 21:19 HST and touching down in Hilo (ITO) at 21:53 HST after a 35-minute hop. Across all ten sectors, the airframe accumulated roughly 4 hours and 42 minutes of total airborne time while enduring ten full pressurization cycles, a testament to the robust durability engineered into line airframe MSN 55001.

Hawaiian Airlines has long depended on the Boeing 717 for its inter-island routes, making the aircraft an integral part of daily operations.

According to Simple Flying aircraft analysis, the 717 was structurally over-engineered for short-haul durability, tracing its lineage directly back to the ultra-rugged McDonnell Douglas DC-9and McDonnell Douglas MD-80 families. The now more common modern composite narrowbodies are designed for long-range fuel efficiency, whereas the 717 features a heavy-gauge aluminum fuselage and exceptionally robust landing gear designed specifically to absorb the relentless shock of short-field landings and rapid turnaround cycles. This explains why legacy airframes like MSN 55001 can endure decades of high-frequency island hopping without any premature fatigue.

The aircraft's powerplant performance is also custom-tailored for brief regional hops. As noted in manufacturer summaries, the twin rear-mounted Rolls-Royce BR715 turbofans deliver exceptional takeoff thrust and high climb gradients. On short sectors where an aircraft spends a disproportionate amount of its total flight time in transition, the BR715s allow the 717 to rapidly punch through low-level turbulence and reach efficient cruise altitudes before initiating an immediate descent toward neighboring island runways.

However, this relentless operating tempo pushes mechanical systems to their absolute limits. Reporting from AirInsight has shown that Hawaiian's 717s frequently operate up to 16 cycles a day, meaning that meticulous inspections of pressure bulkheads, wing spars, and landing gear attachments are needed. This punishing, high-cycle reality highlights why the aircraft remains irreplaceable for island networks, especially because the routes it serves integrate into carrier codeshare operations.

After the landmark merger between Alaska Air Group and Hawaiian Airlines, operational oversight of inter-island flying underwent a profound realignment. Hawaiian’s historic fleet of 717s now operates under consolidated commercial frameworks, evidenced by flight numbers transitioning to Alaska Airlines' familiar AS prefix, such as the early morning AS1013 from Honolulu to Lihue. Despite the updated ticketing and codeshare designations, the day-to-day cabin experience and local ground operations are still deeply rooted in Hawaiian's established island culture.

The unified network allows passengers connecting from mainland North American gateways on Alaska operated aircraft to seamlessly transition onto interisland 717 rotations under a single booking itinerary. Maintaining high-frequency regional connectivity is vital to sustaining economic mobility across the islands, so residents and visitors alike can travel between Honolulu, Lihue, Kahului, Kailua-Kona, and Hilo with minimal friction.

Tracking these merged operations within the flight tracker feature highlights the sheer complexity of coordinating high-density regional traffic under a single parent holding company. With air traffic control vectors and ground turnaround teams managing up to 16 daily cycles per airframe, the integration of AS flight numbers is a visible marker of how traditional regional carriers are adapting to post-merger realities.

The carrier will inherit these jets from Alaska Airlines.

Despite their unmatched reliability on high-frequency interisland sectors, the global 717 fleet is rapidly approaching an inevitable retirement finale. According to Simple Flying analysis, major operators are preparing to sunset the type as airframe maintenance cycles grow more complex and fuel-efficiency standards shift toward next-generation narrowbodies. Delta Air Lines, which operates the world's largest 717 fleet, has steadily laid the groundwork to replace its aging twin-jets with fuel-efficient Airbus A220 aircraft across key domestic hubs.

Meanwhile, in the Pacific, Hawaiian Airlines is mapping out its own generational fleet transition. As per Business Traveller, the airline's interisland 717 operations are slated to be phased out starting in 2028, with the carrier planning to transition those high-density short-haul sectors to Boeing 737-800s. Flight tracking logs for historic airframes like N488HA reflect this changing landscape; operational data show active tracked schedules tapering off after mid-October, signaling that these veteran aircraft face increasingly tight maintenance windows and scheduled deep-check rotations.

The eventual departure of the 717 will mark the definitive end of the DC-9 bloodline, closing an era of commercial aviation defined by rugged, rear-mounted engine airframes built to withstand punishing, multi-cycle daily rosters. Tracking aircraft like MSN 55001, therefore, provides a living archive of how robust engineering and dedicated maintenance teams keep aviation history airborne day after day.

Following registration N488HA through ten demanding sectors in a single twenty-four-hour window showed exactly why the 717 is so legendary among pilots, mechanics, and aviation enthusiasts alike. From its humble origins as Boeing flight testbed MSN 55001 to its decades of faithful service connecting Honolulu, Lihue, Kahului, Kailua-Kona, and Hilo, the aircraft embodies a masterclass in structural durability designed to conquer the brutal physics of short-stage, high-cycle operations.

The 2028 threshold is fast approaching, when Hawaiian Airlines begins transitioning its 717 operations to Boeing 737-800s and Delta advances its A220 rollout, so monitoring every remaining flight of the world's oldest active 717 offers a poignant glimpse into an evolving commercial landscape. You can continue following live fleet telemetry via Simple Flying's tracking channels as these iconic twin-jets gracefully approach their final decades of service.

#6227. Qantas Reaches Deal to Sell 44 Boeing 737s

Qantas has agreed to sell 44 Boeing 737-800s to British aviation aftermarket specialist AerFin as the Australian carrier prepares to retire most of its 737 fleet.

The deal includes the aircraft’s 88 CFM56-7B engines. AerFin said Wednesday it expects to receive the first jet before the end of 2026, with the rest transferring over the next seven years as Qantas retires them.

Qantas Domestic CEO Markus Svensson said the agreement gives the airline “flexibility to adjust the timing as new aircraft arrive,” in a news release.

Qantas operates nearly 80 Boeing 737-800s, according to data from planespotters.net. The carrier ordered 28 Airbus A321XLRs in 2022 to begin replacing the Boeing jets and later ordered another 20. Seven A321XLRs have joined the fleet, with 41 still on order.

AerFin, which supplies parts and engines to airlines and maintenance providers, said the acquisition is the largest in its history. The company said the deal would help it supply aircraft and engine parts to customers worldwide.

#6226. 8 Dreamy Hotels Our NYC Editors Are Booking This Winter

If there’s one thing the editors at Condé Nast Traveler love, it’s weekendmaxxing. We’re all about scouting the very best hotels upstate, or catching a quick flight to Miami, all before returning back to our New York City office by Monday. The art of the weekend trip becomes especially important in the wintertime, when the city closes its blinds and hibernates until spring. This is when an off-season jaunt to the Rockaways, or a hideaway in a Berkshires lodge, becomes all the more appealing. Essentially, we love a trip where you can get cozy somewhere else—because sometimes all you need is a simple change of scenery to tackle the winter blues.

From wellness sanctuaries nestled in the Catskills to country retreats in New England, these are the hotels our editors are eyeing for when the weather turns brisk, all within a few hours of NYC or a short flight away.

Where are you staying? Mayflower Inn & Spa, Washington, Connecticut

What drew you to this hotel? I visited Mayflower Inn back in spring 2024 with one of my best friends while she was pregnant with her second baby, and I’ve been dying to go back ever since. I don’t know if I’ve ever felt more relaxed than I did while there—we spent hours in the spa, chatted by the firepits, stuffed ourselves with farm-fresh meals, and feasted our eyes on some incredible interior design.

What are you eating? I won’t be leaving the hotel for food, that’s for sure. I’m always impressed by the F&B at Auberge properties, and the Mayflower Inn was no exception. The Garden Room offers creative but approachable seasonal cuisine from breakfast through dinner (don’t skip the burger), and the Tap Room is where you’ll find a tavern-style food menu plus a mixologist slinging delicious cocktails and mocktails.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? The Mayflower Inn is located in Washington, Connecticut, a small town in Litchfield County, a region beloved by many of my colleagues. Next time I visit the hotel, I’ll have to make a few stops along the way to see what all the fuss is about.

Where are you staying? Urban Cowboy Lodge, Big Indian, New York

What drew you to this hotel? Urban Cowboy Lodge has been on my weekend getaway wish list for years, and there’s something about it in winter that feels particularly charming—maybe it’s the delightful snow-filled view from the bathtub (pictured above) that drew me in. I’m imagining myself curled up with a good book by the lounge’s fireplace, draped in a Pendleton blanket, then dipping into the aforementioned copper clawfoot bathtubs. At just about two-and-a-half hours north of Manhattan, it’s a not-too-far excursion I’m saving for when I really need a break from winter in the city.

What are you eating? Phoenicia Diner, of course. I’m also keen to try out some of the many craft beers at Ralph’s Bar.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? I’m not a skier, so in the winter, heading to the Catskills comes with more of a stay-indoors-and-get-cozy vibe for me. Besides a pit stop at Phoenicia Diner, I imagine the furthest I’ll trek is over to the sauna and bowling alley.

Where are you staying? The Rockaway Hotel & Spa, Rockaway Park, New York

What drew you to this hotel? Aside from the ocean views—poetically perfect for New York in the winter—The Rockaway is home to one of my favorite wellness scenes in the city. The space transforms its outdoor pool area (which, in the summer months, is home to outdoor concerts and DJ-led pool parties) into the cozy Winter Pool House. The space gets decked out with outdoor cedar barrel saunas and the softest plush robes to wear while you transition to the heated outdoor pool. The warm water mixed with the ice-cold breeze coming off the nearby coastline is glorious.

What are you eating? I’ll be heading to Margie’s—the mood-lit hotel lobby restaurant—and ordering a juicy cheeseburger and a frosty gin martini. What better way to warm your soul?

What do you hope to get up to in the area? The beauty of visiting this hotel in winter? No summer beach crowds. I’ll likely bundle up, head to the beach for some meditation, and head right back to my cozy room at The Rockaway to soak up the views even more.

Where are you staying? Wildflower Farms, Auberge Collection, Gardiner, New York

What drew you to this hotel? I’ve had Wildflower Farms on my wish list for the past few years. Every photo I see of the property on Instagram looks so dreamy. It feels like a true escape from the city—quiet, cozy, and restful. Located in New York’s Hudson Valley, it’s a quick 90-minute drive from NYC, making it a convenient pick for couples or families seeking an easy getaway.

What are you eating? I’m most eager to have coffee and pastries around the fire at the Great Porch, Wildflower’s open-air communal space with sprawling views of the Shawangunk Ridge. And of course, I’ll be dining at the resort’s on-site restaurant, Clay, where the rustic American menu is full of seasonal ingredients from local farms.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? I usually try to pack as many activities and must-try coffee shops and restaurants as possible into my trip itinerary, but Wildflower Farms encourages you to slow down. You’ll find me at Thistle, the resort’s on-site spa where hand-harvested, small-batch oils and scrubs are used during tailored treatments.

Where are you staying? Inness, Accord, New York

What drew you to this hotel? Inness is resplendent in the summer, so I’ve always been keen to see a different side of it come hunker-down weather. Its cabins are certainly primed for rest, thanks to the fireplaces, but there’s also the outdoor pit with prime-time views of the Catskill Mountains decked in snow. I also love the central farmhouse, where cozy seats call out for a great book and a hot cocoa. And if you can drag yourself out, which you should, there are loads of hikes and walks, including those along the Ashokan Reservoir, which is one of my favorite spots.

What are you eating? Stacks of pancakes; comfort-food entrées like risottos; a round of Dorato Negronis at the bar.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? Spending the afternoons shopping and dining in some of my favorite nearby towns, like Kingston and Woodstock.

Where are you staying? Four Seasons Hotel at The Surf Club, Surfside, Florida

What drew you to this hotel? When one of my best friends announced she was celebrating her 30th birthday in Miami, a city I’ve shockingly never been to, the first place I thought of was the Four Seasons Hotel at the Surf Club; I remember reading about its incredible celebrity guest history, which includes everyone from Frank Sinatra to Elizabeth Taylor.

What are you eating? Perhaps we’d start with a toast at the on-site Champagne Bar, then move on over to dinner at Lido for seafood-inspired pastas.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? Laze around by the pool, enjoy the quieter beaches of Surfside, and maybe stroll through the Rubell Museum in Allapattah.

Where are you staying? Tourists, North Adams, Massachusetts

What drew you to this hotel? I love heading north of the city in the colder months—leaning in and getting even colder and cozier. And the words “reimagined motor lodge” are another form of catnip for me. I love the sense of nostalgia paired with very plush, updated interiors, ideal for hiding out for a wintery weekend.

What are you eating? I’d carve out time for the hotel’s restaurant, the Airport Room, ideally timed to one of the chef pop-ups they do—though given the three-and-a-half-hour drive from New York City, I’d probably also plot out an en route lunch in Kingston as well.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? Wintery hikes on the nearby trails, lots of reading by the fireplace, and maybe some of the arts and crafts activities—why not.

Where are you staying? Eastwind, Windham, New York

What drew you to this hotel? When I first caught sight of Eastwind, I was really into the property’s sprawl—there are different types of accommodations (cabins, hotel-style rooms), and everything is wound together via a small trail system lined with fairy lights, from the beer garden to the main house. It feels like a really great spot to get away from the noise of New York City.

What are you eating? The on-site restaurant, Dandie’s, serves up barbecue in a cozy, window-lined space—get some house-made gelato for dessert. And definitely make a detour for brunch at Phoenicia Diner on your way back to the city.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? Stop by Harriman State Park for a hike to stretch your legs on the way north. Once you’re there, you’ve got skiing options (Windham Mountain Club), more hiking trails (The Windham Path), and indoor activities (Helsinki Hudson for music lovers; Olana Historic Estate for museum enthusiasts).

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

There’s now a new reason to travel to the bottom of the world.

Silversea on Thursday officially opened The Cormorant at 55 South, a new luxury hotel near the southern tip of South America designed to transform the experience of traveling to Antarctica.

Located in Chile's Patagonia region near Puerto Williams, the world's southernmost settlement, the 150-room property will serve as a luxury base and launch pad for Silversea's high-end fly-cruise trips to Antarctica — journeys that begin with a flight from Puerto Williams to a research station at Antarctica's King George Island.

Once there, travelers board a Silversea expedition ship to explore Antarctica.

Related: How to get to Antarctica: The pros and cons of flying vs. cruising

“Silversea has always been about going further, and for our guests heading to Antarctica, that journey now begins here at the southernmost hotel on Earth, with the kind of welcome they’ve come to expect from us,” Silversea president Bert Hernandez said during an unveiling event at the hotel.

TPG is one of just a handful of travel media outlets getting an early look at the property this week.

Until now, Silversea's fly-cruise passengers have stayed in non-Silversea hotels in Punta Arenas, Chile ahead of a charter flight to King George Island. The less-than-ideal arrangement meant guests were booked across various hotels, while the line was left scrambling for additional rooms whenever bad weather delayed or grounded flights to Antarctica.

Now, with The Cormorant at 55 South, guests can relax in modern luxury overnight — or sit out bad weather — just minutes from their charter flight. Better yet, the expedition begins well before they step aboard their ship.

While at the hotel, guests will be able to try on or swap their Silversea-provided Antarctica polar gear, complete biosecurity checks that are necessary before visiting the continent, and clean any personal equipment they plan to take ashore, as well as attend an initial Antarctica briefing — activities that usually take place on the ship.

Related: I just camped on the ice in Antarctica; here's how you can, too

They'll also get a chance to explore Patagonia’s breathtaking wilderness on guided excursions around the hotel, including kayaking, hiking, birdwatching and horseback riding. A shuttle bus will also take guests into Puerto Williams.

“The idea was that this wasn’t a stopover hotel. This is the first and last impression that we make on our guests, and so we wanted that to be memorable,” Hernandez said at a press conference ahead of an official ribbon-cutting ceremony.

Initially conceived in 2018 as a turnaround hub for Antarctica, the Cormorant at 55 South has become a destination that by Hernandez’s own admission is “more beautiful than anyone ever envisioned."

Designed to blend in with the environment, the low-slung hotel features soaring ceilings, concrete floors, natural wood, stone and earthy textiles punctuated by pops of orange, yellow and green — colours that echo the surrounding terrain.

Floor-to-ceiling glass means the view is never far away, be it forest, sea or snow-scratched mountains, stretching from the jagged peaks of Dientes de Navarino to the Andes in Argentina.

Related: The best Antarctica cruise vessels

“It was always incredibly important that the hotel reflect the environment,” Silversea senior vice president of expeditions Conrad Combrink said during unveiling events. Elements of fire and ice inform the design, alongside the darkness of the Drake Passage and the Beagle Channel, just beyond the hotel.

Being in the “land of fire”, the hotel fittingly has a massive indoor firepit, surrounded by lounges and easy chairs. An outside terrace offers more places to sit and take in the scenery.

Rooms are simply designed, with a view of mountain or sea, and pair a soothing mix of local wood, natural textiles and green upholstery. There’s a Nespresso machine and a small bar fridge with water and craft beer from a brewery in Punta Arenas.

Latitude 55, the onsite restaurant, showcases regional flavors, including excellent empanadas and a stand-out asado barbecue served on the first night of any stay, slow-cooked over an open fire in the hotel grounds.. At Bar Sur, guests can sample Chilean wine, enjoy a pisco sour tasting or try a cocktail made with calafete, a berry indigenous to Puerto Williams. The Uncharted Boutique is the place to stock up on beautifully made Chilean handicrafts or last-minute polar gear.

More than a hotel stay, The Cormorant at 55 South marks a wider shift for Silversea,which will now base all its Antarctica expeditions out of Puerto Williams. Previously only sailings that crossed the Drake Passage left from Puerto Williams.

While most Antarctic operators base their fleets out of Ushuaia, Argentina, Silversea is the only cruise line running operations out of Puerto Williams. Located further south along the Beagle Channel, Puerto Williams provides a shorter, more direct launch point into the Drake Passage.

Silversea's fly-cruise trips allow Antarctica-bound travelers to skip a ship-based voyage across the Drake Passage — the notoriously rough, 600-mile-wide waterway separating the tip of South America and Antarctica.

Guests fly from Santiago directly to Puerto Williams for an overnight stay at The Cormorant, before taking a charter flight across the Drake to King George Island in Antarctica's South Shetland Islands, where their expedition ship awaits. Upon return, guests spend another night at the hotel before flying back to Santiago.

Related: The ultimate guide to expedition cruising to Antarctica and beyond

The opening of the Cormorant at 55 South coincides with Silversea's largest Antarctic season to date. Fly-cruise itineraries now dominate the line’s offerings in Antarctica, accounting for 29 of its 40 total sailings across three expedition vessels: Silver Endeavour, Silver Wind, and Silver Cloud. The hotel will currently stay open from October through March, but there is talk it will open year-round, for travelers to southern Chile looking for a soft landing after adventures.

More than a place to stay,  The Cormorant makes the journey south feel like an experience in its own right — a fittingly rugged starting point for what lies ahead, plus unique bragging rights of having stayed at the southernmost hotel on earth.

#6224. American Airlines Officially Welcomes Passengers Back To Flagship Dining At LAX After 6 Years

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

Travelers with American Airlines can now enjoy the carrier's Flagship Dining facilities at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX). The upgraded facility provides à la carte dining experiences within the Flagship lounge. The airline's premium lounge is available to travelers in premium cabins and those with AAdvantage elite status on long-haul flights.

According to The Points Guy, an enhanced guest experience awaits with table service and an a la carte menu, a vast upgrade from grabbing a plate and loading it up with food from the buffet. This complimentary sit-down meal service can include several courses.

The exclusive Flagship Dining experience is now open in Los Angeles, complementing the existing facilities open in Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) and Miami International Airport (MIA). These airports provide the dining experience within the carrier's Flagship Lounge. Historically, American limited Flagship Dining to passengers in the Flagship First Cabin only on the Boeing 777-300ER and Airbus A321 transcontinental service; however, recent changes from phasing out international first class have expanded access to additional passengers and routes.

American allows business class passengers access to the exclusive dining experience to those booked in the Flagship Business Plus seat on 787-9 Dreamliner or 777-300ER flights, and on those in business class qualifying transcontinental or Hawaii flights that have been marked as Flagship. This change for California departing passengers will allow business class domestic passengers on select transcontinental flights to allow access for those with a Flagship domestic first-class ticket (standard first-class ticket holders are not eligible).

Simple Flying reached out to American for comment on Saturday; however, an airline spokesperson could not immediately be reached.

Subject to availability, eligible passengers are able to arrive at the Flagship Lounge for a sit-down meal. During peak times, there may be a waitlist, which you can request when you enter the lounge. You can even order your meal via a QR code.

American previously had the Flagship dining experience at its John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) hub lounge. It now operates three premium lounges alongside British Airways within the airport's Terminal 8 (Greenwich, Chelsea and Soho lounges). For those departing from Philadelphia International Airport (PHL), À la carte menus are available within the regular AAdmirals Club.

With Flagship Dining now available at three major US airports, this also marks the upcoming end date for American's long-haul first class standalone product. The airline is phasing it out as it opts for Flagship Business as its premier cabin for international and Hawaii flights.

This has led to jets being retrofitted with new interiors and the addition of its highest-ever business class seat count onboard. These changes are expected to end on November 19, when the airline no longer offers long-haul first class. Transcontinental Flagship First is set to end in March 2027.

The carrier is opening its doors to more flyers as it rolls out lounge upgrades across the US.

American's Flagship Business Class offers a lie-flat long-haul and transcontinental experience with direct aisle access and upgraded amenities. Jets are configured in 1-2-1 reverse herringbone and staggered layouts on the 777 and 787, and select Airbus aircraft.

Dedicated priority check-in lanes, fast-track security screening at select airports, priority boarding, and expedited baggage handling all complement access to the airline's Flagship Lounge, where an à la carte menu provides delicious bespoke dishes, complemented by a range of hot and cold alcoholic or nonalcoholic beverages.

#6223. Bizarre: Lufthansa Group Now Requires Travel ID For Online Check-In

Most airlines encourage travelers to check-in online, given that it’s mutually beneficial — it saves time for the traveler, and saves resources for the airline. Well, Lufthansa Group is implementing a new policy that makes it more difficult to check-in online, as flagged by aeroTELEGRAPH, and that strikes me as rather backwards.

Lufthansa Group has the concept of a Travel ID, whereby customers have an account they can use to log-in across digital platforms belonging to all carriers, including Lufthansa, SWISS, Austrian, Brussels Airlines, Edelweiss, Discover Airlines, etc. This is separate from the Miles & More program, as the idea is that it simply creates a unified log-in for digital services across the airlines.

So along those lines, Lufthansa Group is progressively rolling out an initiative whereby customers need to have a Travel ID account in order to check-in online via the website or app.

Lufthansa Group is rolling out this requirement gradually. The Travel ID is required to check-in online as follows:

There are a limited number of exceptions for the Travel ID requirement. Specifically, you don’t need a Travel ID if you’re a traveler checking in at the airport counter or machine, if you’re traveling on a ticket issued by another airline, or if you’re on a flight operated by another airline with a ticket issued by Lufthansa Group.

Airlines love data and being able to market to customers. It’s one of the reasons that airlines create such strong incentives to sign-up for their loyalty programs (or in this case, a log-in that allows the airline to market to you). We’ve seen countless airlines roll out free Wi-Fi for those who are loyalty program members, and the logic is easy enough to follow.

However, in this case we’re talking about online check-in, which is something that arguably helps the airline more than it helps the customer. I can understand an airline wanting to add a step for something that entirely benefits the customer (like free Wi-Fi), but doing it for a basic function that saves the airline money? Well, that’s quite the approach to take.

In fairness to Lufthansa, I’m not sure this is actually a bad idea, or will backfire that much. Yes, it’s a minor annoyance, but:

Now, it’s still rather customer unfriendly, in my opinion, but that’s not exactly the first time we’ve seen something like that in the airline industry…

Lufthansa Group will start requiring passengers to sign-up for a Travel ID in order to check-in online. This is progressively being rolled out through November 30, 2026. Making it more complicated to check-in online seems counterproductive.

At the same time, clearly this is intended to encourage travelers to register for a Travel ID, so that Lufthansa can better track customer data and market to travelers. Usually we see incentives created to encourage this kind of registration, but in the case of Lufthansa Group, the airline is instead threatening to take something away if you don’t register.

What do you make of Lufthansa Group’s new online check-in requirement?

#6222. Allegiant Says MAX 7 Seat Cost ‘Loses Pace’

Allegiant prefers the economics of the Boeing 737 MAX 8 over the smaller MAX 7 as its plans for premium seating change how it evaluates the two aircraft.

The MAX 7 originally accounted for the majority of Allegiant’s Boeing commitment. In January 2022, the airline announced an order for 50 aircraft, split between 30 MAX 7s and 20 high-density MAX 8-200s, with options for another 50 jets.

The agreement, signed in December 2021, was Allegiant’s first direct Boeing order and marked a shift for a carrier that had largely built its business around buying used aircraft. At the time of the announcement, Allegiant operated 108 Airbus A319s and A320s.

Boeing said the new jets would reduce fuel consumption by about 20% compared with the older Airbus aircraft.

Speaking during the carrier’s third-quarter earnings call Wednesday, President and Chief Financial Officer Robert Neal said the MAX 7 initially offered an attractive balance between the cost of operating each flight and the cost per seat.

“When we did the order, we really liked the MAX 7 because we were looking at both the MAX 8 and MAX 7 at very high density,” Neal said. “And so you’ve got a really nice trip cost seat cost mix with the MAX 7.”

That calculation has changed as Allegiant expands its extra-legroom Allegiant Extra product and prepares to introduce Allegiant First.

“But over time, as you’ve seen us roll out incremental premium offerings at the moment through Allegiant Extra and eventually with Allegiant First, the seat cost just sort of loses pace with the MAX 8,” Neal said. “And so we prefer the cost economics of the MAX 8 at this point.”

Allegiant began shifting its order toward the larger variant in September 2023. An amended agreement retained the 50 firm aircraft but increased the number of MAX 8-200s, reduced the number of MAX 7s and expanded the option pool to 80 aircraft.

The MAX 7 faced years of certification delays, including work to redesign its engine anti-ice system. The FAA approved the variant on Aug. 3, after requiring changes to that system, flight-control software, and cockpit alerts.

The ultra-low-cost carrier added to its MAX 8 commitments last month, exercising six options for delivery in 2028. That brought its firm Boeing order to 56 aircraft, including 22 delivered through Oct. 23, with 74 options remaining.

#6221. Lufthansa Realizes 28 Business Class Seats Isn’t Enough For Boeing 787

In recent times, Lufthansa has started taking delivery of factory fresh Boeing 787s, featuring the carrier’s all-new Allegris cabins. Management at the airline has reportedly decided that the configuration of these planes isn’t quite right for many routes, so now it’s planning some updates.

That’s a sensible change, but it always just feels like Lufthansa is a step behind when it comes to acting logically and catching onto trends, no?

Lufthansa currently has a fleet of 20 Boeing 787-9s. Four of these were acquired secondhand (they were former Hainan Airlines jets), while 16 are brand new, and feature Allegris interiors. Not only that, but Lufthansa has at least another 22 of these planes on order, which will be delivered in the coming years.

In the long run, the Dreamliner is supposed to be the carrier’s primary long haul aircraft based in Frankfurt, complementing the Boeing 747-8s and Boeing 777-9s. Meanwhile Munich (MUC) is primarily getting Airbus A350s (including the A350-900 and A350-1000).

Lufthansa’s 787s are configured with 287 seats, including 28 business class seats, 28 premium economy seats, and 231 economy seats. Keep in mind that three of those seats aren’t even certified yet (but should be certified before the end of 2026), so actual business class capacity is currently just 25 seats.

Anyway, even with all seats certified, Lufthansa Group management has decided that the capacity doesn’t actually match demand on many routes, with CEO Carsten Spohr indicating that the airline is working on installing more business class and premium economy seats on upcoming Dreamliners.

Reportedly nothing has been finalized yet, as this is still in negotiations with suppliers, but the idea remains that the current configuration doesn’t offer enough premium seats.

Given the eventual size of Lufthansa’s Dreamliner fleet, it would also be reasonable to think the airline may have two configurations in the long run, to reflect the demand of different destinations. For example, one would assume that the potential customer demand profile would be different to New York (JFK) than to Columbus (CMH), both of which are going to be Dreamliner routes in the coming months.

I know ragging on Lufthansa is just too easy, from its challenging labor relations, to its botched Allegris rollout, and more. However, I can’t help but feel like the airline is a little behind on trends.

I mean, for how long have we been talking about the surge in premium travel demand? American is taking delivery of 787-9s with 51 business class seats, United is taking delivery of 787-9s with 64 business class seats, and British Airways is reconfiguring 787-9s with eight first class seats and 38 business class seats.

So Lufthansa just taking delivery of dozens of factory fresh 787s with just 28 business class seats seems a little off, especially since Lufthansa only recently started adding these planes to its fleet.

I get that demand differs between markets, and the 787 is actually supposed to be the less premium plane in the fleet, in the long run (with the Boeing 747s and 777Xs being the most premium Frankfurt-based planes), but still, 28 seats just doesn’t seem like a lot by any metric. Heck, the Airbus A330s that are slowly being retired have 42 business class seats, and that’s an overall smaller plane.

Of course the whole Lufthansa Allegris and SWISS Senses situation is just sort of messy, from the 3.5-seat first class cabin that makes no sense, to the need to install a weight on SWISS A330s to balance out the weight of first class, to the new Allegris seats delaying entry into service for planes by years, despite it not actually being that cutting edge at this point.

Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr has indicated that the airline is considering a new configuration for many upcoming Boeing 787s. Management has decided that 28 business class seats and 28 premium economy seats isn’t sufficient, which strikes me as a rather obvious, when you look at trends. Heck, these Dreamliners are partly replacing planes with 50% more business class seats.

I’m curious to see what Lufthansa eventually settles on for a premium Dreamliner configuration, because I agree, 28 business class seats isn’t a lot!

What do you make of Lufthansa reconsidering its 787 layout?

The whole Allegris philosophy was a gamble on one very specific aspect: segmenting customers with different seat types. The allegris business class seat is a very inefficient seat. It is essentially the same concept as united’s Polaris, except with more seat pitch, and every second row, just one middle seat instead of two. Lufthansa thought they could segment their business class customers, upsell certain seats (especially the throne seats, the long bed and the mini-first class at the bulkhead) and make up for the lost revenue of having such an inefficient layout and shrinking the size of the cabin (to maintain a large economy class cabin). But this gamble failed, because Lufthansa didn’t realise that by upcharging so many business class passengers even to simply select a window seat put a bad taste in many people’s mouths. Look at BA, AF and KL. all business class seats in their cabins are created more or less equal with the exception of the bulkheads. Furthermore, Frankfurt is a business heavy market, but has less point-to-point business traffic, and a lot of connecting traffic. It is easy for travellers who are not star-alliance loyal to simply connect elsewhere, or fly united across the Atlantic. Lufthansa wanted to create a segmented business class cabin, but instead created a business class “lite” and charged for extras after that. And now they’re stuck with a VERY expensive, delayed seat, which occupies way too much space on their aircraft, and as such they have had to make huge compromises like shrinking the first and business class cabins. They will seriously lose out in the long term.
